combinatorics-and-counting.title: Combinatorics and Counting

clauses.expected: Combinatorics and Counting

How many? The two basic rules, the four ways to choose r from n , what changes when repetition is allowed, how to correct an over-count, and the double-counting arguments that prove identities without algebra.
By the end you can choose the right rule, justify the choice, check the answer against a small enumeration, and invent the classification or the factor when no rule applies directly.
The basic rules come first, then the binomial coefficients and repetition, then corrections and bounds, and last the techniques that generalise them.
Sets, functions and induction.
Pick the right one of four rules
Ordered or not, repetition or not. The arithmetic is easy; the classification is where the answer is won or lost.
Count with restrictions
Complementary counting, cases, and knowing when to count the bad outcomes instead of the good ones.
Correct an over-count
Inclusion and exclusion for any number of sets, and derangements as the canonical application.
Prove an identity by counting
Count one set two ways and conclude the two expressions are equal — shorter and more informative than the algebra.
Invent the classification, or the factor
Choose the boxes so that ⌈n/k⌉ forces the conclusion, and write the factor that encodes each constraint so a generating function answers for every n at once.

Check every formula against an enumeration while the numbers are small. The counting lab lists the actual selections up to 400 of them, and a formula that disagrees with the list is wrong however good the reasoning looked.
Say out loud whether order matters and whether repetition is allowed, before writing anything. Almost every wrong answer in this course is a right calculation of the wrong quantity.
Do the combinatorial proofs in “Combinatorial Proof” twice: once by algebra and once by counting. The second is shorter and tells you why the identity is true.
Advanced enumerative combinatorics: species, the transfer-matrix method, and the deeper theory of generating functions. “Generating Functions” is an introduction, not a survey.
Design theory, Latin squares and error-correcting codes, which are the natural applications of this material but a separate subject.
Ramsey theory beyond the statement that R(3,3) = 6 , which appears in “The Generalised Pigeonhole Principle” as a pigeonhole application.

Combinatorics and Counting. Every count on this course is computed in exact big-integer arithmetic, so a figure like 52! is the number and not a floating-point approximation of it. Where the total is small enough to list, the lab lists it and checks the formula against the enumeration.

combinatorics-and-counting.rationale_text: Almost every wrong answer in this course is a right calculation of the wrong quantity.
combinatorics-and-counting.inverted_prerequisite: No knowledge of sets, functions or induction is needed.

discrete-probability.title: Discrete Probability

clauses.expected: Discrete Probability

Counting with a denominator. Every probability here is a ratio of counts, so Combinatorics and Counting does most of the work — and the parts that go wrong, conditioning and independence, go wrong for reasons that have nothing to do with arithmetic.

By the end you can compute a probability exactly, condition correctly, say what an expectation does and does not tell you, and build a distribution from its sample space — or bypass it with indicators.
The model is set up first, then conditioning, and last random variables and the two distributions worth knowing by name.
Counting, sets and functions.
Compute a probability from a sample space
Identify the outcomes, check they are equally likely, count the event, and divide — with the counting techniques of Combinatorics and Counting.
Condition without falling into the standard traps
P(A|B) and P(B|A) are different numbers, and the base rate is what separates them.
Use Bayes' theorem on a real question
The medical-test calculation, done properly, and the reason its answer surprises almost everyone.
Compute expectation and variance
From the definition, and by linearity — which holds whether or not the variables are independent, and is the most useful fact in the course.
Build a distribution, decompose a count, and tell the two distributions apart

Write P(X = k) from the sample space and check it sums to 1; split a count into indicators before reaching for a distribution; check the three binomial assumptions; and know that fixed trials is binomial and a fixed target is geometric.
Write the sample space down for the opening lessons, as far as “The Probability Axioms”, even when it is obvious. Most probability errors are errors about what the outcomes are.

Use the probability lab's outcome list. Every probability on this course is a count divided by a count, and seeing the outcomes highlighted makes conditioning concrete rather than formal. From “Random Variables” the distribution lab opens on each lesson's own worked example, so the numbers on the page are the numbers in the lab.

Do the Bayes calculation by frequencies as well as by the formula. The two agree, and the frequency version is the one that makes the answer believable. “Bayes' Theorem”’s lab does both on a million people, with every cell a whole number.
Continuous probability: densities, the normal distribution, and anything requiring an integral. Everything here is finite or countable.
Limit theorems. The law of large numbers and the central limit theorem are mentioned where they explain something and are not proved.
Markov chains, martingales and stochastic processes, which are the natural sequel and a course of their own.

Discrete Probability. Probabilities on this course are computed as exact fractions from the enumerated sample space, so 1/6 appears as 1/6 rather than as a decimal that is nearly it. The binomial and geometric distributions are summed term by term from their definitions and compared with the closed forms.

discrete-probability.rationale_text: Most probability errors are errors about what the outcomes are.
discrete-probability.inverted_prerequisite: No counting, sets or functions are needed.

number-theory-and-cryptography.title: Number Theory and Cryptography

clauses.expected: Number Theory and Cryptography

Everything follows from one theorem about division with remainder. Primes, gcds, congruences and modular inverses build up to RSA — which is generated, used and then broken here on primes small enough to check by hand.
By the end you can compute in modular arithmetic confidently, judge the parameters of the everyday systems built on it, and explain exactly what RSA's security rests on.
Divisibility and gcd come first, then modular arithmetic, and last the applications that use all of it.
Proof technique and induction.
Run the algorithms by hand
Division, Euclid, extended Euclid, fast exponentiation. Each with its trace, so the method transfers to paper.
Solve congruences
Decide solvability, count the solutions, and find them — including simultaneous systems by the Chinese remainder theorem.
Use Fermat and Euler
Reduce enormous exponents to small ones, and know exactly which hypotheses each theorem needs.
Explain RSA honestly
Generate a key, encrypt and decrypt, and then recover the private key by factoring — which is what shows what the security actually depends on.
Judge an application's parameters
Choose a hash modulus and say why a power of two fails, check the three conditions that give a generator full period, and validate an affine key — then break one from two letter frequencies.

Use the workbench lab in every lesson. Each mode prints the algorithm's trace rather than only its answer, and the point is to be able to reproduce the trace on paper afterwards. Every lab opens on its own lesson's example, so the first figure on the screen is one the text above it already states; change one input and watch which lines move.
Do the RSA lesson with the primes it starts with, then change them. Watching the key change and the ciphertext change with it is what makes the mechanism concrete.
Take the factoring demonstration in “RSA Encryption” seriously. The lab breaks the key it just generated, and understanding why that is easy here and hard in practice is the whole security argument.
Analytic number theory: the prime number theorem is quoted in “The Sieve of Eratosthenes” and not proved, and the Riemann hypothesis is mentioned only as context.
Elliptic curves, discrete logarithms and Diffie–Hellman. RSA is the one public-key system developed here.
Cryptographic engineering: padding schemes, key management, side channels and protocol design. “RSA Encryption” is the mathematics of RSA, and textbook RSA is not a system anyone should deploy.

Number Theory and Cryptography. All arithmetic on this course is exact big-integer arithmetic, because modular exponentiation with four-digit moduli already exceeds what floating point can represent. The RSA lab generates a real key, uses it, and then recovers the private key by factoring — on primes chosen small enough that it takes microseconds.

number-theory-and-cryptography.rationale_text: Watching the key change and the ciphertext change with it is what makes the mechanism concrete.
number-theory-and-cryptography.inverted_prerequisite: No proof technique or induction is needed.

graphs-and-trees.title: Graphs and Trees

clauses.expected: Graphs and Trees

The discrete structure that models everything with a relation on it: networks, dependencies, maps, molecules, schedules. Every theorem in this course is a claim about all graphs, and the lab lets you try to break each one.
By the end you can model a problem as a graph, run the standard algorithms, recognise a tree and rule out planarity by counting, and know which questions have easy criteria and which do not.
First the basics, then the structure of a graph, then traversals and paths, then trees, and last colouring and planarity.
Proof, sets, relations and counting.
Read and build the representations
Adjacency matrix, adjacency list and drawing — and know which makes a given question easy.
Apply the standard criteria
Euler's degree condition, bipartiteness as the absence of odd cycles, and the tree characterisation, each with the proof behind it.
Run the algorithms
Breadth-first and depth-first search, Dijkstra, Kruskal and greedy colouring, and say what each guarantees.
Tell easy problems from hard ones
Euler circuits are decided in one pass; Hamilton circuits are NP-complete. The problems look alike and are not.
Recognise a tree, and rule out planarity by counting
Any two of connected, acyclic and n − 1 edges give the third; the three traversal orders from a drawing; and E ≤ 3V − 6 or E ≤ 2V − 4 settling non-planarity before any drawing is attempted.
Use the workbench adversarially. Every theorem here is a claim about all graphs, and the fastest way to understand one is two minutes spent trying to build a counterexample.
Draw the small cases. Graph theory is one of the few parts of mathematics where the picture is the object, and most of these proofs were found by drawing.

Where a lesson has a worked example that fits, its lab opens on it: the preset "This lesson's example" is that graph, with the lesson's own weights where it has them, and the panel quotes the figures you should see before you change anything. “Shortest Paths and Dijkstra's Algorithm” and “Spanning Trees and Minimum Spanning Trees” carry weights; “Paths and Connectivity” names the bridges, “Rooted Trees and Traversals” prints all four traversal orders, and “Planar Graphs and Euler's Formula” runs the planarity counts.
Notice which criteria are one-pass checks and which are searches. That distinction is what Algorithms and Complexity formalises, and it is visible here first.
Directed graphs beyond passing mentions. Everything here is undirected unless stated; digraphs, strong connectivity and topological sorting are noted where they matter and not developed.
Network flow, matching algorithms beyond the bipartite criterion, and the algorithmic side of matching.
Spectral graph theory, random graphs and extremal graph theory, each of which is a course in itself.

Graphs and Trees. Every algorithm on this course runs in your browser against the graph you built, and every verdict names the vertex, edge or pair that decides it. The graph workbench caps at eight vertices for one reason worth noticing: the Hamilton search is exhaustive, and 8! is where exhaustive stops being instant.

graphs-and-trees.rationale_text: and most of these proofs were found by drawing.
graphs-and-trees.inverted_prerequisite: No knowledge of proof, sets, relations or counting is needed.

algorithms-and-complexity.title: Algorithms and Complexity

clauses.expected: Algorithms and Complexity

The course the rest of the path was building toward. Recurrences from Induction and Recursion, counting from Combinatorics and Counting and graphs from Graphs and Trees all reappear as the running time of something — and the last two lessons say what no algorithm can do.
By the end you can analyse an algorithm you are shown and recognise when a problem is likely to be intractable.
First what an algorithm is and what correctness means, then analysis, then design, and last the limits.
Especially induction, recurrences and graphs.
Prove a bound with witnesses
Big-O is an existence claim about a constant and a threshold. Producing them is the proof; quoting the class is not.
Analyse loops and recursions
Counting the operations of an iterative algorithm, and solving a divide-and-conquer recurrence with the master theorem.
Recognise the two design techniques
Greedy where it is provably correct, dynamic programming where it is not — and be able to say which and why.
Place a problem
P, NP, NP-complete, undecidable. Knowing which of those a problem is in changes what you should attempt.
Prove an algorithm right, and bound a sequence

An invariant for partial correctness and a decreasing measure for termination (“Correctness and Termination”); the cost of a whole sequence of operations rather than the worst single one (“Recursion Trees and Amortised Analysis”); and the lower bound no comparison sort beats (“Searching and Sorting”).

Produce the witnesses. Every big-O claim in “Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta” comes with a C and a k , and the lab searches for them; a claim without them is a slogan. When the relation is false the lab says so from the growth classes and shows the ratio diverging, because no finite search can refute a claim about every n .

Use the measured columns. The lab counts operations by running the algorithms, so the predicted growth can be compared with something rather than believed. Each lesson's lab opens on that lesson's own example — the invariant trace of “Correctness and Termination”’s POWER(3, 13) , “Analysing Iterative Algorithms”’s four loop nests, “Searching and Sorting”’s counts at n = 16 , “Divide and Conquer”’s 4T(n/2) + n , “Recursion Trees and Amortised Analysis”’s sixteen inserts, “Dynamic Programming”’s table to 8 — and every panel quotes what the lab prints there.
Take “Decidability and the Halting Problem” seriously. Undecidability is not a statement about current technology, and the halting proof is short enough to follow completely.
Data structures as a subject: heaps, balanced trees, hash tables and their analyses. They appear where an algorithm needs one and are not developed.
Randomised and approximation algorithms beyond passing mentions, and the average-case analysis that quicksort needs.
Formal models of computation. Turing machines are described in “Decidability and the Halting Problem” only as far as the halting problem requires.

Algorithms and Complexity. Every operation count on this course is produced by executing the algorithm with a counter, on a deterministic input, so the measured column is a measurement. Where it diverges from the predicted growth the reason is stated rather than smoothed over.

Overview
What it teaches

Reading price without indicators. The lessons explain how to label an unmarked chart bullish, bearish, ranging or in transition and name the level that would prove the label wrong; classify a boundary event as rejection, breakout, retest or sweep from its closes; decide from a pair of charts whether regime, location and trigger justify acting or waiting; match an entry rule to the model it describes; place a stop that expresses a thesis and size a position from its distance; judge participation against a bar's own baseline and leadership against a benchmark; and choose a long call or put whose expiration, strike and spread survive the thesis.
Who it is for

Anyone who can open a chart and wants a vocabulary for what is on it. No prior technical analysis is assumed — Market Structure Lab starts from a bare candlestick chart — and no platform, account, or subscription is needed. The lessons stay useful if you already trade and want a stricter definition of invalidation.
Concept dependencies

Entries are placed on pullbacks defined by market structure, ranges, breakouts, liquidity sweeps, and multi-timeframe context. Stops are placed at the structural levels those concepts name, and options contract selection prices the plan built from invalidation, stops and reward-to-risk. Each lesson ends with a way to test yourself.

Explanations, examples, interactive tools, and practice questions.

clauses.expected: Invalidation, stops & reward-to-risk

A stop should express where the trade idea is wrong—not where the loss becomes emotionally uncomfortable. Position size adapts to the structural stop; the stop should not be squeezed to justify a larger position. The drill at the end is the decision itself: pick the stop that expresses a stated thesis, then size the position from the distance that stop imposes.
The risk chain
Every number should derive from the thesis rather than from the profit you hope to make.
Invalidation
The price event that disproves the setup: a protected swing breaks, a breakout fails, or acceptance returns inside a range.
Position size
Risk budget divided by risk per unit. Wider structural stops require fewer units; tighter valid stops allow more.
R multiple
Potential reward divided by planned risk. It compares geometry, not the probability that the target will be reached.
Interactive risk planner
Change entry, stop, target, and account risk. The visual and calculations update immediately.
Position-size calculator
0.50% of a $25,000 account
Stop-quality drill

The rule for this setup: the long thesis is invalid only when the protected low breaks with enough room for ordinary noise. Pick the stop that says so — then size the position from the distance it imposes.
Which stop expresses the thesis?

Read as buyers stepping back in at the pullback: price stopped at 98.45 and the advance that followed carried through 104, where the previous advance had stalled. What that reading rests on is 98.45 — if price closes below it, the sequence that justified the long is gone, and the distance between the entry and the stop does not change that.
Three different stop problems
R describes payoff geometry. Setup quality, target realism, liquidity, gaps, and execution still matter.

clauses.expected: Learn to read the story of price.

Identify higher highs, lower lows, protected swings, breaks of structure, and reversals with interactive candlestick charts. The test at the end is concrete: label an unmarked chart bullish, bearish, ranging, or in transition, and name the level that would prove the label wrong.
Three structures explain most charts
Start with obvious swing points. Do not label every candle; label the moves that visibly changed direction.
Candle What one candle records

Each candle summarises one span of time — an hour, a day. Its body runs from the open to the close ; the thin lines above and below it, the wicks , reach to the high and low the span touched. A body in the up colour closed above its open; one in the down colour closed below it.
Close The price the rules use

A wick shows where price went; the close shows where it was accepted when the span ended. Every rule in this course keys on the close — “a close below the low”, “a close beyond the edge” — because a wick through a level that closes back on the right side of it is a level tested, not a level broken.
Swing A turning point

A swing high is a candle whose high stands above the highs on either side of it; a swing low is the mirror. Structure is read from the sequence of these turning points, not from single candles: label the moves that visibly changed direction and leave the rest unlabelled.
Bullish structure
The latest meaningful higher low is usually the level buyers must defend.
Read as buyers willing to pay more than they did last time: each dip is met before it reaches the previous low. A close below the low being defended is what would end that reading.
Bearish structure
The latest meaningful lower high is usually the level sellers must defend.
Read as sellers willing to accept less than they did last time: each bounce is capped before it reaches the previous high. A close above the high being defended is what would end that reading.
Range
Inside a range, apparent trends often fail. The edges matter more than the middle.

Read as both sides defending the edges and neither defending the middle: buying appears near the low, selling near the high. It stops reading as a range when price closes beyond an edge instead of turning back inside.
Structure explorer
Switch scenarios, move one swing at a time, and reveal the logic behind continuation and reversal.
What the chart is saying
The reading updates as you move through the swings.
Price is printing higher highs and higher lows.

Normally read as buyers stepping in at progressively higher prices: each pullback is bought before it reaches the previous low, and sellers have not been able to return price to where the last advance began. A close below 108 breaks that reading.
Use terms as evidence, not decoration
BOS Break of Structure
A meaningful swing breaks in the direction of the current trend. In a bullish market, a new high above the previous high is bullish continuation evidence.
CHoCH Change of Character
The first meaningful break against the existing trend. Treat it as a warning; confirmation normally requires the opposite swing sequence to form.
HL Protected low
In bullish structure, this is the higher low that launched the move through the prior high. A close below it weakens or invalidates the bullish thesis.
LH Protected high
In bearish structure, this is the lower high that launched the move through the prior low. A close above it weakens or invalidates the bearish thesis.
One stock can show several structures at once
Use the higher timeframe for direction and the lower timeframe for setup timing. Multi-Timeframe Market Structure Lab examines the same idea at full depth.
Daily chart
Read as buyers defending each higher low on the daily: the start of the last advance has not been given back. A daily close below the marked protected low would end that reading.
1-hour chart
Read as sellers controlling this pullback: each bounce stops below the previous hourly high while the daily low still holds. That is the two timeframes disagreeing, not the daily reading failing.
Example trade narrative
“Daily structure is bullish. The 1-hour chart is pulling back bearishly. I wait for the 1-hour to reclaim its protected high before considering a bullish entry.”
Classify the chart without labels
Choose the dominant structure. After checking, the important swings and explanation appear — and a second question asks for the level that would prove your label wrong.
What is the dominant structure?
Focus on the sequence of meaningful highs and lows, not the last candle.
A simple process beats more indicators
Start high, then zoom in
Read Weekly/Daily direction first. Use 4-hour or 1-hour structure to plan the setup.
Require a close
Use a candle close beyond the structural level for consistency. A wick can be a sweep, not a break.
Write conditions
“Above X, bullish. Below X, invalid.” Conditional plans are more useful than predictions.

Normally read as sellers meeting every bounce at progressively lower prices: each rally stalls before it reaches the previous high, and buyers have not been able to return price to where the last decline began. A close above ${level} breaks that reading.
Too early to read. One or two turning points show only that price moved; a boundary means nothing until the same area produces a second reaction.

Price has returned near the first low. If it turns here, the reading is that the same area is being defended a second time — but a matching reaction at the high is what would make this a range rather than a pullback.

Normally read as both sides defending an edge and neither defending the middle: buying appears near the low, selling near the high, and the space between shows neither. Acceptance beyond an edge — closing there rather than wicking through — breaks that reading.

Price has traded above the range high. Structurally this is an attempt to leave the range, not yet a successful one: the attempt only becomes acceptance if price holds and closes beyond the edge instead of turning back inside.

Price traded above the range high and came back inside. The usual reading is that the move beyond the edge found nothing behind it, and that the same boundary is again where price is being turned around.
Too early to read. The opening swings show only that price moved; nothing yet shows whether buyers will step in above the previous low.

Normally read as buyers stepping in at progressively higher prices: each pullback holds above the previous low, so sellers have not reached the start of the last advance. A close below ${level} breaks that reading.

Price closed below ${level}, the low the last advance had been defending. The reading that buyers were arriving earlier at each pullback has failed. What replaces it is unsettled — a change of character is the first break in the old pattern, not a finished new one.

A lower high, then a lower low. Read as the mirror of the earlier condition: rallies now stall below the previous high, and the low that had been defended was not defended. A reclaim above ${level} breaks that reading.

Look for the sequence. Are highs and lows rising, falling, staying inside boundaries, or changing direction?
You read it as falling. Trace the swing highs: each clears the last, and each low holds above the previous low. The direction of the sequence, not the colour of the last few candles.
Rising, not bounded. In a range the highs stop at about the same price each time; here each high clears the last one and the lows step up behind it.

You saw a change of character that is not there. Every pullback held above the previous low — none of the protected lows was closed through. A red candle or two inside a rising sequence is a pullback, not a transition.
You read it as rising. Trace the swing lows: each is below the last, and each bounce stalls below the previous high. Falling highs and falling lows.
Falling, not bounded. In a range the lows hold at about the same price each time; here each low undercuts the last one and the highs step down behind it.
Look for the break that should have started a transition: there is none. Every bounce stalled below the previous high; the lower highs and lower lows were there from the first swings.
Bounded, not trending. The highs keep stopping in the same area and the lows keep holding the same area; nothing has been closed through. A trend needs the highs and lows to keep moving.
Bounded, not trending. The lows keep holding the same area and the highs keep stopping in the same area; nothing has been closed through.
A transition is a trend that ends. Here there is no trend to end: highs and lows keep landing at the same two areas, so nothing was protected and nothing was broken.

The chart begins bullish, and if you stopped reading there you would call it that. It does not stay bullish: the last protected low is closed through, and a lower high and lower low follow. Read the sequence to its end.

The end is bearish, but that is not how it started. The first swings are higher highs and higher lows; what you are labelling is the change from one to the other, and the label for that is transition.

Not two boundaries — one break. Price was making higher highs, then closed through the low it had been defending, then made a lower high and a lower low. Nothing here rotated between the same two levels.
The chart reads bullish. Which close would end that reading?
A close below ${a[4]}
${a[4]} is the higher low the last advance began from. Close below it and buyers were not there before the previous low after all.
A close below ${a[5]}

A close below ${a[3]}
${a[3]} was the high that got broken — it confirmed the structure, it does not protect it. The level being defended is the higher low that launched that break, ${a[4]}.
The chart reads bearish. Which close would end that reading?
A close above ${a[4]}
${a[4]} is the lower high the last decline began from. Close above it and sellers were not there below the previous high after all.
A close above ${a[5]}
${a[5]} is the latest low. Bouncing from it is what every lower high in this sequence did; the reading fails only when a bounce closes above the high the last decline began from, ${a[4]}.
A close above ${a[3]}
${a[3]} was the low that got broken — it confirmed the structure, it does not protect it. The level being defended is the lower high that launched that break, ${a[4]}.

clauses.expected: Multi-timeframe market structure

The higher timeframe tells you the environment. The lower timeframe tells you whether the pullback is still unfolding or has produced a usable trigger. Context above; execution below. The drill at the end is the job itself: read regime, location, and trigger from a pair of charts and decide whether they justify acting or waiting.
The hierarchy
Timeframes answer different questions. Mixing their jobs creates contradictory signals.
Regime
Weekly and daily structure reveal the larger trend, major range, and important protected swings.
Location

Whether price is at support, resistance, a range edge, or an unhelpful midpoint. On a three-chart desk this is the intermediate chart's job; with the two charts this lab uses, the daily is read twice — once for direction, once for position.
Trigger
The lower timeframe shows the pullback, reaction, structure shift, and precise invalidation for execution.
Context + trigger lab
Compare the broad chart with the detailed chart. A lower-timeframe downtrend can be only a pullback inside a larger uptrend.
Top-down conclusion
The daily trend is bullish, price is pulling back into support, and the 1-hour chart has shifted back upward.
The lower-timeframe trigger agrees with the higher-timeframe direction at a useful location.

On the daily, read as buyers still stepping in before the previous low is reached: the pullback's lowest close held above the marked 110.2. On the hourly the same pullback stopped making lower lows and then took out its last lower high — the identical reading one scale down. A daily close below 110.2 breaks both at once.
The four-step workflow
Read from large to small, then define the invalidation at the execution timeframe.
Is the higher timeframe bullish, bearish, or ranging? Mark the protected swing.
Is price at a meaningful edge, prior breakout, protected swing, or merely the middle?
Has the lower timeframe actually changed character in the intended direction?
Invalidation
Which lower-timeframe swing proves the trigger failed without contradicting the higher-timeframe thesis?
Alignment drill
A useful analysis sentence
Price is pulling back into the prior daily breakout. The 1-hour structure remains bearish, so I will wait for a 1-hour higher low and break upward before considering an entry.

clauses.expected: Options contract selection

Translate a directional thesis into a long call or long put deliberately. Compare expiration, moneyness, directional sensitivity, time decay, volatility exposure, and quote quality instead of buying the cheapest contract. The drill at the end is the whole decision: choose the contract whose expiration outlasts the thesis, whose strike you can defend, and whose spread you have priced into the plan.
The words the table uses
Options Trading teaches options properly. This lesson needs only enough to read its own chain, so here is that much and no more.
Call, put

A long call is the right, not the obligation, to buy the underlying at the strike until expiration; it gains as the underlying rises. A long put is the right to sell at the strike; it gains as the underlying falls. Both cost a premium, and the premium is all a long option can lose.
Strike, moneyness
The strike is the price the right is struck at. A call whose strike is below the current price is in the money (ITM); at it, at the money (ATM); above it, out of the money (OTM). Puts mirror this.
Expiration, DTE
The last day the right exists, counted here in days to expiration. A thesis that needs ten days cannot be expressed in a contract that ends on day seven.
Premium, breakeven

What the contract costs per share, times the multiplier (100) per contract. At expiration a call is worth what the underlying exceeds the strike by, so it breaks even at strike plus premium; a put at strike minus premium.
Delta

How much the premium moves for a 1.00 move in the underlying. A 0.53-delta call gains about $0.53 per share when the underlying rises $1. The table shows its absolute value so calls and puts read alike.
Theta
What one day's passing costs the premium, all else equal. A long option pays it every day, and faster as expiration nears.
Vega, implied volatility

Implied volatility (IV) is the size of move the market has priced in. Vega is what one IV point is worth to the premium: a long option gains when IV rises and loses when it falls, even if the underlying does nothing.
Bid, ask, spread
The bid is what you can sell for now; the ask is what you must pay. The gap is paid twice, in and out, and as a fraction of the midpoint it is the friction the plan has to beat.
The contract decision stack
Start with the underlying thesis. The option is a wrapper around that thesis, not a substitute for it.
Direction
A long call expresses bullish exposure; a long put expresses bearish exposure. Define the chart invalidation first.
Time
Expiration must outlast the thesis. Extra time adds premium and changes theta and vega exposure.
Strike
Moneyness changes premium, delta, intrinsic value, and how much underlying movement the contract captures.
Liquidity
Evaluate the bid/ask spread and actual market depth. A good thesis can be damaged by expensive entry and exit friction.
Synthetic option-chain explorer
Select a row to inspect the tradeoffs. Prices and Greeks come from a simplified European-style model—not live quotes.
The selected expiration outlasts the expected 10-day thesis window.
Exit-value simulator
Estimate how the selected long option may respond to price, elapsed time, and unchanged IV. This is a model sensitivity exercise.
Selected exit point
Assumes the underlying reaches $108.00 after 10 days, 20 DTE remain, and IV stays at 35%.
Quote-quality evaluator
Enter an actual or hypothetical bid and ask. The spread is part of the cost of entering and exiting.
Contract-selection drill
This lab does not model assignment, exercise decisions, taxes, commissions, early exercise, broker approval, or suitability. Review the standardized options risk disclosure before trading.

clauses.expected: Pullbacks & entry models

A correct directional bias can still produce a poor trade when the entry is late, premature, or structurally invalid. Compare earlier entries with confirmation-based and continuation entries. The drill at the end holds you to it: match a stated rule to the entry model it describes, and say what that model pays in price or proof.
Three entry families
None is universally best. Each exchanges entry price, confirmation, and distance to invalidation.
Aggressive
Enter at the expected reaction zone before a lower-timeframe shift. Better location, but more false starts.
Confirmation
Wait for a reaction, local structure shift, and a defined swing that can serve as invalidation.
Continuation breakout
Enter as price resumes through a continuation level. Stronger proof, but usually a later price and wider chase risk.
Entry model comparator

Switch the pullback, then compare how each entry changes price, invalidation, and reward-to-risk — written as an R multiple: the distance to the target divided by the distance to the stop. Invalidation, Stops & Reward-to-Risk Lab makes R the unit of the whole plan; here it is the number that shows what each entry costs.

Direction alone is not an entry. Require a useful location, a reaction, a trigger, and an explicit invalidation.

clauses.expected: Ranges, breakouts & liquidity sweeps

Learn to separate a real break from a dramatic wick. The central question is not “Did price cross the line?” but “Did price close beyond it, hold there, and build structure?” The drill at the end asks for exactly that judgement: classify a finished sequence — rejection, breakout, retest, or sweep — from its closes alone.
Three ideas to master
A range is a negotiation zone. Its boundaries become meaningful because traders repeatedly react there.
Range
Price rotates between a recognizable high and low. The middle usually offers less information than the edges.
Acceptance
Price closes beyond a boundary, spends time outside, and either holds or forms new structure there.
Liquidity sweep
Price trades beyond an obvious level, then rejects and closes back inside. The failed break is the evidence.

Liquidity here means the orders resting just beyond an obvious level: the stops of traders positioned inside the range, and the entries of traders waiting for the break. A sweep trades far enough through the level to fill them, finds nothing behind them, and comes back.
Interactive boundary reader
Play each scenario candle by candle. Watch the close and the follow-through rather than reacting to the wick alone.
Read the evidence
The upper boundary rejects price without a confirmed close outside.
Price tested the high but has not demonstrated acceptance above it.
Read as sellers still defending the high: price reached the boundary and no candle could hold a close above it, so the rotation stayed inside. A close above 110 that holds would break this reading.
The boundary decision framework
Classify the sequence, not a single candle.
Rejection
Price reaches a boundary and rotates away without materially trading through it.
Confirmed breakout
A close lands outside the range and subsequent candles remain accepted beyond the boundary.
Breakout + retest
Price exits, returns to the old boundary, holds it from the other side, and resumes.

The failed break, completed: price trades clearly through the level — far enough to fill the orders resting beyond it — closes back inside, and the rejection often accelerates back through the range. Degree is what separates it from a rejection: a rejection reaches or grazes the boundary and turns; a sweep runs well past it and comes back.
Classification drill
Labels are hidden. Classify the completed sequence around the range boundary.

clauses.expected: Volume & relative strength

Price shows direction. Volume helps you judge participation. Relative strength asks whether the asset is actually leading or lagging its benchmark—even when both charts are green or both are falling. The drills at the end measure both: judge whether an event bar expanded against its own baseline, and whether the asset leads or lags once both series are normalized.
What each lens contributes
Neither volume nor relative strength replaces structure. They add evidence about participation and leadership.
Volume context
Compare current activity with the asset’s recent baseline. A large bar matters more when it is unusual for that market.
Follow-through
High volume can accompany continuation or exhaustion. The next candles reveal whether the price move was accepted.
Relative strength
Normalize the asset and benchmark, then compare performance. This is not the RSI momentum indicator.
Price + volume laboratory

Inspect the event bar, its volume relative to baseline, and what price does afterward. The baseline here is the average of the ten bars before the event bar — activity is judged against the market's own recent habit, not an absolute number.
Participation diagnosis
Price closes above the range on expanded volume and remains accepted outside.
Participation expanded during the break and follow-through held above the old range.

The bar that closed above 108 traded 2,240 against a baseline near 950, and no bar after it fell back to that baseline. Read conventionally, activity expanded at the new prices instead of drying up, which is what separates a break that holds from one that fades. A close back inside 108 would break the reading.
Relative-strength comparator
Both series start at 100, so their paths show percentage performance rather than raw price differences.
Leadership summary
The asset rises faster than the benchmark, while the ratio trend confirms improving leadership.
The asset/benchmark ratio is rising and finishes above its starting level.

You adjust rules repeatedly until they maximize results on the same historical sample.

There is no out-of-sample here: every adjustment was scored on the same trades. Proof would be the frozen rules holding on data they were never tuned against.
Equivalent to live trading
Live trading never lets you revise the rule after seeing the result and re-score the same trade. Repeated tuning on one sample is the opposite of live conditions.
Every sample contains noise, and enough parameter changes will fit it. The best combination found this way is usually the one that fits the noise — the third mistake this lesson names.
The rules may be fitting noise unique to that sample. Reserve unseen data for validation.
Which backtest most directly avoids look-ahead bias?
Chronological replay using only information available at each candle
Viewing the completed chart before marking entries
That is look-ahead bias itself: every entry is marked knowing what came after it. The replay labs in Breakout Setups, Reversal Setups and Trade Management hide the future for exactly this reason.
Selecting only clean examples
Choosing examples is selection bias, a different error that inflates results the same way. The valid setups that lost have to be in the sample, or the win rate is fiction.
Missed trades are part of the rule’s real result — a retest model that never got its retest earned nothing on that move. Removing them overstates what the rule would have delivered.
Chronological replay prevents future candles from influencing historical decisions.
A strategy shows +0.08R expectancy before 0.10R average costs.
The estimated net expectancy is negative
Costs do not matter
0.08R gross minus 0.10R of costs is −0.02R per trade. Costs are the entire difference between this strategy making and losing money — the cost-omission mistake in Risk-to-Reward.
Doubling size on a −0.02R expectancy doubles the loss per trade. Size cannot fix a negative edge; it scales whatever sign the edge has.
The edge is certain
The gross edge is +0.08R, the net is −0.02R, and both are estimates from a sample. Nothing here is certain, and what is likely is a small loss per trade.
Costs exceed the gross average edge, producing approximately −0.02R net expectancy.
In-sample results are strong and out-of-sample results are negative. What is the best interpretation?
A serious warning about generalization or regime sensitivity
The reserved segment is the only part of the test that could not have been fitted. Ignoring it keeps the number that was tuned and discards the one that was measured.
Increase risk because in-sample was strong
In-sample strength is what overfitting looks like. Raising risk on it puts more money behind the sample that was fitted and none behind the evidence that it failed.
Proof the strategy works
A rule that works only on the data it was built from has not been shown to work at all. The out-of-sample result is the test, and it came back negative.
The rules did not preserve the same behavior on unseen data and require investigation or rejection.

Acceptance
A close outside followed by continued trading or a successful retest is stronger than a wick through the level.
Room
A valid breakout is not automatically a good trade when the next opposing level is too close.

Breakout setup process
Separate the structural event from the decision to enter.
Define the boundary

Observe the break

What this is normally read as
Price is still rotating below the ${b.toFixed(1)} boundary. No close has settled beyond it yet.

The closes after the break stay beyond the boundary.

This is the reading a retest exists to produce: the old ceiling was revisited and behaved like a floor instead. It is more than the break alone because the level has now been tested from both sides — and a close back below it still ends it.

Price failed to accept outside and closed back inside the range.
The visible candles have not completed the breakout model.
Price closes above a range high, then the next two candles remain above it.

Rejection is a close back under the level. Price closed above it and two more candles held there, so the level did not reject anything.
A close beyond a range high that had capped every prior advance is the structural event this lesson is about. Two further closes outside make it acceptance rather than a probe.

Size comes from the stop distance and the risk budget; it has nothing to do with room. A bigger position in a trade with 0.4R of room is a bigger version of the same poor trade.
Setup validity and trade quality are separate. A valid break can still offer poor reward relative to risk.

Loss of the reclaimed boundary / retest structure
A red candle that holds above the boundary is what a retest looks like. The thesis is that the boundary now holds; it is disproved by a close back through it, not by colour.

A dollar figure can sit inside normal variation above the boundary and stop the trade while the thesis is still intact. Invalidation is a price the chart can disprove; size is what fits the dollars to it.
A headline is not a structural event. If it moves price back inside the range the boundary is lost and the trade is invalid for that reason; if it does not, nothing in the plan has changed.
The entry thesis depends on the broken boundary holding after acceptance or retest.

What this is normally read as
Higher highs at 108, 112 and 113.5, with higher lows at 103.2 and 107.4. The correction from 112 ends at 108.4, on the 108.2 breakout level, and price then makes a new high.

Normally read as buyers acting at successively higher prices, with the latest correction ending at the price the last advance began from rather than below it. That is one observation about location; it does not get stronger because a second tool measuring the same rising price agrees with it. A close below 108.2 ends the reading.
Price works up into the 106.3 range high over eleven candles, spending the later ones between 103.4 and 106.2, then closes above it at 107.6 — and the three closes after that stay above.

The usual interpretation is that a price which had capped every advance stopped doing so, and that repeated closes outside are acceptance rather than a single probe. The volume label on this chart is a premise of the exercise — no volume is plotted here — so it counts as evidence because the scenario states it, and for no other reason; nothing states relative strength, so nothing lets you claim it. A close back inside the range ends the reading.
Price swings between 100.0 and 104.4 and finishes at 103.4. Neither the 99.0 range low nor the 106.0 range high is reached.

There is no reading here, and that is the point: neither side has been tested anywhere that a reaction would mean something, so the swing says nothing about who gave way. A signal generated in the middle of a range is a signal about nothing in particular until price is somewhere that matters.
Every close in the series is higher than the one before it. There is no corrective swing anywhere on the chart.

A one-way advance is normally read as buyers paying up without waiting for a discount — but because price has never pulled back, nothing here shows how it behaves when the trend is tested, which is usually where a reading comes from. Every moving average and oscillator drawn on this series is a transform of these same closes, so of course they agree; that agreement is one observation restated, not several.
No evaluation yet. Select only evidence the scenario shows or states.
Relevant and sufficiently independent. The decision also matches the scenario.

Relevant, but over-claimed. ${extraNames.join(", ")} ${extraNames.length>1?"are":"is"} not shown or stated on this chart. A claim that cannot be checked is not confluence — drop it and evaluate again.
Evidence score ${score}%. ${missing.length?
Which set provides the most independent evidence for a bullish pullback?
20 MA + 50 MA + 200 MA
Three averages of the same closes agree with each other by construction. That set answers one question — is price trending — three times, and never asks about location or a trigger.
Bullish structure + support + local trigger
RSI + stochastic + MACD
Three momentum oscillators are three transforms of the same price series. They are one category, and it is not even one of the four this lesson uses.
Three bullish social-media opinions
Opinions are not market evidence, and three of them are usually one opinion repeated. Nothing in that set can be checked on the chart afterwards.
Structure, location, and trigger answer different questions. The other groups mostly repeat one category or add non-market evidence.
Price is above three moving averages. How many independent context categories does that usually represent?
Mostly one trend category
They are three lines, not three facts. Each is an average of the same closes over a different window, so when price rises they all end up below it together — one observation about trend, restated.
Six because slopes also count
Slope is derived from the same average, which is derived from the same closes. Counting derivatives of one input as separate evidence is the overlap this lesson warns about, multiplied.
Trend is real context and moving averages do describe it — the point is only that several of them describe it once. Count the category, and count it one time.
Different moving averages can add nuance, but they are highly correlated measurements of price trend.
A setup has excellent confluence but structural resistance is immediately above entry. What should happen?
Force a target through resistance
A target drawn past a level that has already stopped price is a target chosen for its ratio, not its structure. Confluence at the entry says nothing about whether price can get there.
Size follows the stop distance and the risk budget, never the strength of the evidence. More evidence with no room is still a trade with nowhere to go.
Reassess or skip because room is limited
Remove resistance from the chart
The level is still there whether it is drawn or not. Deleting it from the chart deletes the one fact that makes the trade poor — which is why the trade would still be poor.
Confluence does not repair poor location or insufficient room to the next opposing level.
What is the purpose of confluence?
No amount of agreeing evidence removes the need for an invalidation price. Confluence raises the quality of a decision that can still be wrong; it cannot make it right.
Combine relevant independent evidence
Maximize the number of signals
Requiring more independent evidence produces fewer trades, not more. A method that generates more signals is usually one that has started counting the same evidence twice.
Explain every outcome afterward
Evidence added after the entry cannot be tested, because it was chosen knowing the outcome. Confluence is assessed before the trade, and the second mistake this lesson names is doing it after.
Confluence increases evidential quality; it does not make a trade certain.

What this is normally read as

The advance to 112.0 corrects to 108.3, on the 108.2 decision area that capped the earlier advance. Price then closes at 111.0, back above the whole three-bar pullback, and the next dip stops at 110.1.

Normally read as the correction ending where the previous advance began, followed by buyers closing price through the level that had been holding the recovery down. Candles A, B and C are three different quantities of that same evidence at three different prices, which is what the confirmation model is choosing between. A close back under 108.2 ends the reading.
Eleven candles rotate under the 106.2 area, then price closes at 107.5 and 108.8 above it. The pullback returns to 106.5 and the next close is 107.2, back away from the level.

The usual reading is role reversal: the price that had capped every advance was revisited from above and held. Note that the break and the retest are two separate pieces of evidence, and the retest is the one that tests the level from the other side.

After the high at 111.4 price declines to 107.5, bounces to 108.4, then closes at 107.9, 106.8, 105.7 and 104.6 — the last three below the 107.3 decision area, and none of them back above the earlier 108.8 close.

The move to 108.4 is a reaction and nothing more: it never closed above the previous lower high, and price then made a lower low. Read the usual way that says the decline was interrupted rather than stopped, which is why no candle here satisfies the structure or retest model. The reaction model is different: it fires at A, because A is a reaction close by the same rule that made A the answer on the pullback tab, and it is stopped when 106.8 closes back under the area. That loss is the false start the earliest model pays for — the rule was followed, and it lost.
No candle selected. Use the labels on the chart and the chosen confirmation rule.
The scenario never completes the selected confirmation model.

This is the first qualifying reaction close — and the candles after it show the model’s cost: the entry is invalidated when 106.8 closes back under the area. Choosing ‘no valid entry’ here would have used those later candles, which the rule cannot see.
This is the first qualifying reaction close.
This is the first candle that completes the local structure shift or acceptance rule.
This is the first candle confirming that the retest held.
Your model requires a candle close above the last local lower high. Price only wicks above it.
Enter because the level traded
The model says close, and a wick is not a close. Entering on the wick is entering on a different rule from the one that will be tested and journaled.
Wait for the required close
Change the model to wick confirmation

Changing the rule at the moment it would have fired is choosing the rule by its outcome. Whatever the new rule is, it was not the one written before the setup, so nothing it does can be compared to anything.
The level is the trigger level the model was written against. Ignoring it leaves no rule at all, which is worse than either rule.
The written model requires a close. Intrabar trading beyond the level does not satisfy it.
A retest model never receives a retest after breakout and price continues higher.
Chase because the trade worked
Chasing enters at a worse price on no rule, after the evidence the retest model wanted never arrived. The trade working is what makes chasing tempting, and it is not a reason.
Record a missed trade and keep the model
Rewrite the entry afterward
A rule rewritten after seeing which entry would have won is a rule fitted to one outcome. The second mistake this lesson names is exactly this — and it makes every earlier result incomparable.
The structure is bullish and the plan was long; missing the entry does not reverse the thesis. A short here would be a trade against the evidence because the evidence was inconvenient.
A rule can miss valid moves. Consistency is necessary to test whether the model has an edge.
What is the main cost of waiting for more confirmation?
Later price and possible missed trades
More evidence is more evidence, not certainty — the retest model on the pullback tab can still be stopped. The cost it pays for that evidence is a later, worse price.
Risk always becomes zero
Risk is the distance to the stop, and a later entry moves the entry further from it — risk in points usually grows, not shrinks, as confirmation is added.
Waiting produces more data, not less. What it costs is the price that moved while the data arrived, and the trades where it never did.
Additional evidence usually arrives after price has moved, which can worsen entry and reward-to-risk.
When should the confirmation model be selected?
Before the setup resolves
After seeing the outcome

Chosen afterwards, the model will always be the one that would have won this time. That is hindsight, and it is why the failed tab scores the reaction model as an entry that lost rather than as no entry.
A model selected only on winning trades has been selected by the outcome. It cannot then be tested, because the losing trades were never counted under it.
It should remain undefined
An undefined model cannot be replayed, backtested, or journaled. Backtesting, Trading Journal and Performance Review depend on the entry being a rule that another reviewer could apply.
Predefining the model prevents hindsight from changing what counted as a valid entry.

Define trade setups, plan entries and exits, size positions, manage trades, and use records to review decisions.
Subject
Trading
Lessons
Format
Interactive
Overview
What it teaches

To write a conditional plan whose every line can be checked after the trade, place the zones it refers to from repeated reactions, and say which of the evidence for it is independent; to recognise a breakout, a pullback and a reversal — and the failed version of each — candle by candle; to pick the entry candle a stated model permits, put the stop beyond invalidation with room for noise, and set targets at structure rather than at a ratio; to compute risk, reward, break-even and expectancy, turn a risk budget into a rounded-down quantity, and manage an open trade to its plan while scoring discipline apart from outcome; to read a backtest for the number that would make you reject the rules, keep a journal another reviewer could use, and write one measurable improvement rule from it.
Who it is for

Anyone who can already read a chart and now wants a repeatable procedure for acting on one. Market Structure is the assumed background: this course places stops at structural levels and enters on pullbacks without stopping to define either. It also suits someone who trades already and cannot say, from records rather than memory, which of their setups actually pays.
Concept dependencies

Entry confirmation requires a named setup: breakout, pullback or reversal. Position sizing needs the stop distance established by stop-loss placement, and performance review needs records from the trading journal. Recording decisions and reviewing their outcomes makes the setup and execution work usable beyond an individual trade.
Lessons
Explanations, examples, interactive tools, and practice questions.
15 lessons

Educational use only — nothing here is trading advice. All charts, trades, prices, fills, and performance results in this course are synthetic educational examples. The pages contain no live market data and no trading signals, and nothing on them is a recommendation or a forecast. Real outcomes can differ because of spread, slippage, commissions, gaps, taxes, liquidity, assignment, exercise, implied volatility, time decay, and other factors. Trading carries the risk of losing money.

How the handoff works

Trading Journal keeps your entries in your own browser's local storage and exports them as a JSON document stamped trade-journal-v1 . Both pages run entirely in the browser: nothing is uploaded, and there is no account anywhere in this course.

The schema linked beside this is the contract between them. It is worth reading if you would rather keep the journal in your own spreadsheet or script and only bring it here for the review: match the shape and Performance Review will read it.

Aggregate expectancy is positive, but one setup is negative across a meaningful sample.
Investigate that setup separately
Ignore it because total results are positive

The total is positive because the other setups are carrying the weak one. Filter the sample to that setup on the lab and the aggregate stops hiding it — using aggregates only is the second mistake this lesson names.
Increase risk on the weak setup
More size on a negative expectancy loses more, faster. Risk is not a lever for fixing a setup; the setup is investigated, revised or removed.
Delete its losing trades
Deleting losses turns the journal into the selective record Trading Journal warned against. The losses are the evidence; the review exists to read them, not to remove them.
Aggregate results can hide a weak component. Segment-level behavior should be examined before changing the whole system.
Trades that followed the plan average +0.35R; deviations average −0.60R.
Improving adherence is a high-priority hypothesis
The setup rules must be replaced immediately
The rules made +0.35R when they were followed. The losses came from not following them, so replacing the rules attacks the part of the system that works.
Adherence has no relevance
A 0.95R gap per trade between followed and deviated is the largest single number in the review. It is exactly what the plan-adherence chart on the lab is for.
Stops should be widened

Nothing in the two numbers concerns stop distance. Widening stops would change the tested rules in response to losses that came from breaking them — and Stop-Loss Placement says it reduces size for no structural gain.
The difference supports testing a process intervention before changing market rules, assuming sample sizes are adequate.
A mistake appears twice in a sample of five trades.
Treat it as a hypothesis requiring more data
Declare it the permanent root cause
Two in five is 40% of a sample that the lab itself flags as too small below twenty trades. It is worth a rule for the next sample, not a permanent diagnosis — the third mistake this lesson names.
Never record it again
Not recording it is how a real pattern stays invisible. The tag keeps being applied; what changes is the confidence, which rises only with the count.
Size has no bearing on a recurring execution error, and doubling it doubles the cost of the error while it is being investigated.
The frequency is notable, but the sample is too small for a stable conclusion.
What is the best improvement cycle?
Choose one measurable change, test a defined sample, then review
Change entries, stops, targets, and setups simultaneously
If four things change and the next sample improves, nothing says which one helped — or whether one of the four hurt and the others hid it. The first mistake this lesson names is this one.
Rewrite rules after every loss

A rule rewritten after every loss never accumulates a sample, so it is never tested. Losses are expected under any positive-expectancy rule; the review cadence is fixed so that they are counted, not reacted to.
Review only when profitable
Reviewing only when the account is up selects the samples that look good. The review is scheduled by sample size, not by result, so the losing periods are read as carefully as the winning ones.
Changing one prioritized variable preserves the ability to attribute any performance difference.

Long option position sizing
Invalid per-unit risk. Entry and stop must create a positive planned loss.
Risk budget is smaller than one unit. The trade does not fit the selected account risk without changing the instrument or skipping it.

Position rounded down. ${c.detail}; planned risk is ${money(c.actual)}, leaving ${money(c.unused)} unused. The position’s notional is ${c.equity>0?pct(c.notional/c.equity*100,1):"—"} of equity — sized for risk, which says nothing about whether that concentration, or the instrument’s liquidity, is acceptable.
Account risk is $200 and per-share risk including costs is $2.50. Maximum whole-share size is:
100 shares is $200 ÷ $2.00 — the stop distance without the costs. Per-share risk including costs is $2.50, and 100 × $2.50 = $250 exceeds the budget.
50 shares would be $200 ÷ $4.00. At $2.50 per share, 50 shares risks only $125 and leaves $75 of the budget unused for no reason.
500 shares × $2.50 = $1,250 of planned risk against a $200 budget. That is the budget multiplied, not divided — the share count is risk ÷ per-share risk.
The structural stop becomes wider while account risk stays fixed. Position size should:
A wider stop means more dollars lost per unit if it is hit. The same budget therefore buys fewer units, not more — quantity moves opposite to stop distance.
Same quantity at a wider stop is more dollars at risk: 100 shares × $2 is $200, and 100 shares × $4 is $400. Holding the budget fixed is what forces the quantity down.
Doubling the quantity when the stop widens multiplies the risk twice over. Budget ÷ per-unit risk is the only rule, and a wider stop is a larger divisor.
Per-unit risk increases, so fewer units fit within the same dollar risk budget.
A long option costs $3.00. If the full premium is treated as maximum planned loss, one contract risks approximately:
$3.00 is the quoted premium per share, and one listed equity contract covers 100 shares. The dollars at risk are $3.00 × 100 = $300 before costs.
A contract is 100 shares, not 10. $3.00 × 100 is $300 before costs — an order of magnitude more than $30, which is the kind of error that oversizes an options position tenfold.
That would be a 1,000-share multiplier. Standard equity options are 100 shares per contract: $3.00 × 100 = $300 before costs.
One listed equity option contract generally represents 100 shares, so $3.00 × 100 = $300 before costs.
Why can an option premium stop be imprecise relative to an underlying chart stop?
Premium also changes with Greeks, volatility, time, and spread
They always move one-for-one

Only a deep in-the-money option moves close to one-for-one, and even then time and volatility move it as well. The premium at the underlying stop is an estimate, which is why the lab offers full premium as the conservative planned loss.
Option prices are fixed intraday
Premiums change continuously with the underlying, with implied volatility, and with the passage of time. That is the reason the exit premium cannot be known from the underlying price alone.
There is no difference

Options Trading explains the difference; for sizing, the point is that an underlying stop at a given price does not fix the premium you will exit at, so the planned premium loss is an estimate and the size should respect that.
The option price depends on more than the underlying price, so realized premium risk may differ from the plan.

What this is normally read as
Higher highs at 108.1, 111.8 and 113.4, with higher lows at 103.4, 107.5 and 109.5. The 114.5 first objective sits above every candle on the chart.

The entry side is readable: each correction has ended higher than the last, which is normally read as buyers acting at progressively higher prices. The objective is not readable from this chart — nothing has happened at 114.5 here, so it is an assumption carried in from elsewhere and should be treated as one.
Rallies end lower — 109.5, then 106.8, then 104.0 — and price closes down to 98.0. The 96.0 first objective sits below every candle on the chart.

The entry side reads as sellers acting at steadily lower prices with buyers arriving only after each decline. The objective has no history here: nothing has reacted at 96.0 on this chart, so it carries none of the evidence the entry side does.
Price turns down from 106.0, falls to 98.9, and recovers to 103.3. The 105.8 first objective sits at the area that turned the earlier advance back.

That earlier turn is why 105.8 is an obstacle rather than an arbitrary number: it is the one price on this chart where an advance has already been stopped. Placing the first target under it is a decision to take money off before price reaches the level that stopped the last attempt — not a claim that it will stop there again.
Structurally grounded targets. Target 1 respects the first obstacle, and the extended plan matches the selected method.

Recheck target placement. The first obstacle is ${s.levels[0].toFixed(2)}, which is ${targetR(s,s.levels[0]).toFixed(2)}R from this entry and stop; a first target beyond it is a number chosen for its ratio, and one well short of it leaves reward on the table. ${targetMethod!=="single"?
:""} Your Target 1 is ${r1.toFixed(2)}R and Target 2 is ${r2.toFixed(2)}R.
A long trade has major resistance at 1.4R and no clear structure until 3R. What is the first target consideration?
Force a 3R target
Price has to get through the 1.4R level to reach 3R, and that level has already stopped an advance. A 3R target drawn past it is a ratio, not a place where anything has happened.
The levels are the only evidence on the chart about where price has been stopped before. A plan that ignores them is a plan with no structural target at all.
Move the stop to create 3R

Tightening the stop to make the ratio moves invalidation inside the structure — the invalidation mistake in Stop-Loss Placement. The market does not owe a ratio, and the stop is not a dial for producing one.
The first meaningful opposing level affects available reward and should be included in the plan.
When is scaling out most defensible?
When multiple structural objectives exist
Whenever a candle turns red
A red candle is a feeling, not a level. Taking profit from fear is the third mistake this lesson names, and it makes the average win unmeasurable because no two exits follow the same rule.
Random percentages cannot be tested or repeated. Scaling is defensible only when the percentage and the level it fires at were written before the trade.
It is always superior

Scaling out gives up part of the position before the extended objective, so on a strongly trending trade it lowers the average win. It trades reward for lower variance — a choice, not a free improvement.
Scaling should connect to predefined objectives and a tested management rule.
What is a cost of trailing a remainder?
Some open profit is usually given back
There is no cost
A trailing stop is only hit after price has turned against the position, so the exit is always below the best price seen. That gap is the cost, paid on every trailed trade.
It guarantees the maximum price
It guarantees the opposite: the exit comes after the maximum, once price has pulled back to the trail. Participation in extended moves is bought with that give-back.
It removes all initial risk immediately
A trail 1R behind price at entry is still the original stop. Risk falls only as price advances and the stop follows it — which is a milestone rule, not an immediate one.
A trailing method participates in extended moves by tolerating pullbacks before exit.
A target exists only because it creates exactly 2R, with resistance at 1.2R. What is wrong?
The target ignores visible structure
R multiples are mathematically invalid
The arithmetic is fine — 2R is a correct measurement of the distance. What is wrong is that the distance was chosen first and the level at 1.2R was ignored to get it.
Every entry must target 2R
That is the assumption that produced the mistake. There is no required ratio; there is a level at 1.2R that has already stopped price, and the plan pretends it is not there.
Move the first target past the first obstacle on the lab and read the verdict. A target that exists only to make a number is the first mistake this lesson names.
R is a measurement. The market does not owe a target simply because the calculation produces a preferred number.

Trend first

Location

Recovery

Pullback assessment

Pullback setup process

Confirm the impulse

Define the pullback area
Mark prior breakout structure, support or resistance, or another planned zone.
Monitor validity

Require recovery evidence
Use the exact reaction or structure-shift rule in the entry model.

There is no pullback reading left to make: price has closed at or through the ${w.builtOn}, so the sequence of ${w.sequence} that defined the setup no longer exists. This is what invalidation looks like — the reading is not weakened, it is gone.

A correction this shallow is normally read as ${w.side} unwilling to wait for ${w.wait}. Read honestly it also means price has barely separated from the ${w.away}, so very little sits between here and the level that would disprove the setup.

The reaction candle and the local shift are the first visible evidence that the correction has stopped.

Setup not evaluated. Adjust the pullback and choose a decision.
The correction has broken the protected swing, so the original trend-pullback thesis is invalid.
Structure remains valid and the selected reaction plus local shift satisfy the confirmation model.

An uptrend pulls back to prior breakout support, holds the protected low, and forms a bullish local structure shift.
Invalidation is a close through the protected low, and the description says the low held. A pullback that holds its protected swing is the trend continuing, not ending.

A breakout needs a boundary being crossed for the first time. This is price returning to a boundary it already crossed and holding it from the other side — the definition of a pullback to breakout support.
Trend, planned location, held protected swing and a recovery trigger are the four components of the pullback setup, and all four are in the description.
The trend, location, and recovery trigger are all present while structural invalidation remains intact.
Price falls below the protected higher low before any long entry occurs.
It is only a discount if the trend is still there to buy. Below the protected low the sequence of higher lows is gone, so the thing being bought at a discount no longer exists.
Cancel the original pullback thesis
The protected low was the invalidation because it is the price that disproves the setup. Moving it after price got there is choosing not to be disproved — the second mistake this lesson names.
There is no position yet, and adding to one whose structure has failed would be the same error twice. The plan said what price cancels it; that price printed.
Breaking the protected low invalidates the original bullish pullback structure.
A pullback reaches support but continues making lower highs on the execution timeframe.
Enter because support was touched

Touching support is location, and location alone was never the entry rule. Lower highs on the execution timeframe say the correction has not finished; the model is waiting for the close that says it has.
Wait for the required recovery trigger
Move the target closer and enter
The target has nothing to do with whether the correction has ended. Shrinking the objective to justify an early entry changes the reward without changing the missing evidence.
The execution timeframe is where the trigger is defined, so its structure is exactly the thing that cannot be ignored. Lower highs there are the absence of the recovery the model requires.
Location alone does not satisfy a confirmation entry model.
What should determine whether a deep pullback is tradable?
Move the depth slider: a 70% correction that holds the protected low is a valid deep pullback, and one that closes through it at 100% is not. The percentage describes; the swing decides.
Protected structure, location, and recovery evidence
Whether price feels cheap
Cheap is a feeling about distance travelled, and distance travelled is the first mistake this lesson names. A price can feel cheap all the way through the protected low.
A single oscillator reading
An oscillator restates how far price has moved, which is the same information as depth. It cannot tell you whether the protected swing held or whether a recovery trigger has printed.
Retracement depth is descriptive. Structural validity and the selected entry rules determine the decision.

Distinguish a temporary countertrend reaction from a reversal by requiring a break of prior structure, a retest, and opposite-side continuation.
Core concepts
Use these concepts as explicit rules rather than changing them after seeing the outcome.
Prior trend
A reversal setup begins with a mature trend approaching a meaningful location.
Structure change
The countertrend move must break a structural level that mattered to the prior trend.
New structure
A retest and opposite-side swing provide evidence and a usable invalidation point.
Interactive lesson
Change the inputs, inspect the chart, and evaluate the decision before revealing the answer.
Evidence sequence
Reversal setup process
Wait for evidence of control changing instead of predicting the exact top or bottom.
Identify the prior trend
Mark the protected swing and the structural level that would signal loss of control.
Observe the reaction
Look for rejection, sweep, exhaustion, or failure at a meaningful area.
Require a structure break
A countertrend candle is not enough; the prior sequence must be disrupted.
Use the retest and continuation
Confirm an opposite-side swing, define invalidation, and verify room to target.
Reversal evidence drill
Confirmation hierarchy
Common mistakes
Completion standard
Choose wait on the failed tab until the break actually fails, not before; choose reversal candidate only once the retest has formed the opposite-side swing that gives the plan its invalidation.
