Lower highs at 111.4 and 108.2, with lower lows at 107.5 and 105.7.

A mature downtrend is normally read as sellers repeatedly able to act at lower prices while buyers appear only after a further decline. Nothing here is a reversal — this is the trend the rest of the sequence has to overturn.
The decline continues to 101.2, just above the 100 support line. No reaction is visible yet.
Arriving at a level is not the same as reacting to it. All this says is that the trend has reached a price where a reaction would be meaningful if one appeared; so far none has.
Price closes at 99.4, below 100, then closes back above it at 100.6 and 102.4. The 104.0 structure level is untouched.

Trading through a level and closing back above it is normally read as the move below failing to attract continuation. It is a reaction, not a change of structure: the most recent lower high still stands, and that is the difference between a bounce and a reversal.
The close at 104.2 is the first above the 104.0 lower high, and the pullback that follows stops at 103.1 — above the 99.4 low.

That pair is what the model calls a change of character: buyers took price above the level that capped the most recent bounce, and the next decline ended higher than the last one instead of lower. A close back below the 103.1 higher low would end the reading — that swing is the invalidation the model hands the plan, and Stop-Loss Placement puts the stop just under it.
Closes at 104.7, 106.3 and 108.0 carry price above the 104.2 swing high.

Continuation past the prior swing high is normally read as the new sequence of higher highs and higher lows holding. It confirms what the earlier candles suggested; it says nothing about how far the move runs.
Higher highs at 101.4, 104.7 and 106.4, with higher lows at 100.8 and 104.0.
A mature advance is normally read as buyers repeatedly willing to pay higher prices. That is the trend the rest of the sequence has to overturn, not evidence of a top.
The advance continues to 110.8, just under the 112 resistance line. No reaction is visible yet.
Arriving at a level is not reacting to it. All this says is that price has reached somewhere a reaction would mean something; so far none has appeared.
Price closes at 112.4, above 112, then closes back below it at 111.1 and 109.6. The swing low that the advance has been holding is still intact.

Closing back under a level that was just exceeded is normally read as the push above failing to hold. It is a reaction, not a change of structure: the higher low that the advance is built on has not given way yet.
The close at 107.9 is the first below the 108.2 higher low, and the bounce that follows stops at 109.0 — under the 112.4 high.

That pair is the change of character: sellers took price under a level that had held every prior dip, and the next rally ended lower than the last. A close back above the 109.0 lower high would end the reading — that swing is the invalidation the model hands the plan.
Closes at 107.4, 105.8 and 104.2 carry price below the 107.9 swing low.
Continuation past the prior swing low is normally read as the new sequence of lower highs and lower lows holding. It confirms the earlier evidence and says nothing about how far the decline runs.
Lower highs at 111.3 and 108.1, with lower lows at 107.4 and 105.8.
A mature downtrend is normally read as sellers repeatedly able to act at lower prices while buyers appear only after a further decline. This is the trend the sequence has to overturn.
The decline continues to 101.4, just above the 100 support line. No reaction is visible yet.
Arriving at a level is not the same as reacting to it. Price has reached somewhere a reaction would be meaningful; none has appeared so far.
Price closes at 99.8, below 100, then closes back above it at 101.1 and 102.0. The 104.0 level the model requires is untouched.
So far this is indistinguishable from the bottom-reversal tab: a reaction at a level, with the last lower high still intact. Anyone reading a reversal here is reading it from the reaction alone.
The bounce stalls at 102.0, below the 104.0 level, and price closes back down at 101.2 and 100.1.
The reaction never became a structure break, so the sequence of lower highs is unbroken. This is where the two readings separate, and the honest one is that nothing has changed.
Closes at 98.7, 97.5 and 96.3 take price below the 99.8 reaction low.

New lows beneath the reaction low are normally read as the prior trend simply resuming. The reaction was real; the reversal was never established — which is why the model asks for a sequence rather than a reaction.

The prior structure has broken, the retest formed an opposite-side swing, and the model now has structural invalidation.
The countertrend reaction failed to break structure and the prior trend resumed.
The sequence has not yet established enough evidence for the reversal model.
A downtrend prints one large bullish candle but remains below the last lower high.
Confirmation needs the last lower high broken and a higher low formed after it. One candle, still below that lower high, has done neither — it is the first mistake this lesson names.
Nothing on a chart is guaranteed, and this candle has not even changed the structure: the sequence of lower highs is intact until a close above the last one.
An entry needs a model — reaction, shift or retest — and an invalidation. A single candle below the lower high gives a reaction at most, with nothing yet to put a stop under.
One candle does not establish a break of bearish structure or a new higher low.
After a downside sweep, price breaks the last lower high, retests, and forms a higher low.
Bearish continuation would mean the lower high held and a new low followed. The description says the lower high broke and a higher low formed — the sequence has changed sides.
A break of the last lower high, a retest, and a higher low are three structural facts in a row. That is the most information a reversal model can be given.
The retest is where the entry is decided, not where the trade ends. The target is the next opposing level above, which the description has not mentioned.
The sequence shows a countertrend break and an opposite-side swing that can define invalidation.
A possible reversal fails to break countertrend structure and then makes a new low.
Hold the reversal thesis
A thesis that survives a new low below its reaction low is a thesis without an invalidation. The structure it needed — a break of the lower high — never happened, and the trend has resumed.
Treat the reversal attempt as failed
The reaction low was the invalidation because a new low below it means the prior side is still in control. Moving it after the fact keeps the idea alive by refusing to let it be wrong.
Rename it a pullback
A pullback needs an established trend in the trade’s direction. There is none — the trend is the one that just made a new low — so the label would be a name for a losing position, not a setup.
The prior trend retained control and continued through the reaction low.
What distinguishes a reversal setup from an ordinary pullback?
The reversal candle is larger
Size is the first mistake this lesson names. A large countertrend candle that stays below the last lower high has changed nothing about the sequence.
Prior structure breaks and opposite structure forms
Every pullback in a trend changes candle colour. The difference is whether the prior sequence is broken and a new one forms — closes relative to swings, not colour.
RSI reaches one fixed number
An oscillator reading describes how far price has moved, not whether structure has changed. Trends spend long stretches at extreme readings without reversing.
A reversal requires evidence of control changing, not merely a temporary countertrend move.

clauses.expected: Risk-to-Reward
Measure price risk, planned reward, break-even win rate, and expectancy while keeping mathematical ratios separate from structural target validity.
Core concepts
Use these concepts as explicit rules rather than changing them after seeing the outcome.
R as a unit
One R is the initial planned loss from entry to stop. Outcomes can then be compared across trades.
Break-even rate
The average win-to-loss ratio determines the theoretical win rate required before costs.
Expectancy
Combine win rate, average win, average loss, and costs to estimate the average result per trade.
Interactive lesson
Change entry, stop, target, win rate, average loss and costs; every figure on the right is recomputed from the formulas further down the page.
Trade math
Estimated per trade before model uncertainty.
The balanced preset, worked
Every figure on the calculator comes from these five lines. Follow them once by hand, then change one input and predict the new figures before reading them.
Risk-to-reward evaluation process
Use the ratio to measure a structurally valid plan—not to invent one.
Validate entry and stop
Confirm price risk is structurally justified and on the correct side of entry.
Identify realistic targets
Use visible structure before calculating the reward multiple.
Calculate break-even rate
Understand the minimum hit rate implied by average win and loss size.
Estimate expectancy
Use backtested outcomes and include transaction costs and slippage.
Risk-to-reward drill
Key formulas
Common mistakes
Completion standard
Risk, reward, the R multiple, the break-even win rate and expectancy — and say why a positive result is only as good as the win-rate estimate behind it.

Correct the stop and target sides.
Invalid geometry. For a ${rrDirection}, the stop and target must be on opposite sides of entry.
Positive estimated expectancy. This depends entirely on whether the win-rate and average-outcome assumptions are valid.
Non-positive estimated expectancy. The assumed win rate and payoff do not overcome losses and costs.
A strategy wins 40% of trades, averages +2R on wins, and −1R on losses before costs. What is expectancy?
0.40 × 2R is +0.80R, but that is the wins alone. The 60% of trades that lose 1R each take 0.60R back: 0.80 − 0.60 = +0.20R.
The sign is wrong: wins contribute 0.40 × 2 = +0.80R and losses 0.60 × 1 = −0.60R. The win side is larger, so expectancy is positive, +0.20R.
Zero would need the loss rate to equal the break-even rate, 1 ÷ (1 + 2) = 33.3% wins. At 40% the system is above break-even by 0.40 × 2 − 0.60 × 1 = +0.20R.
0.40 × 2R − 0.60 × 1R = +0.20R before costs.
Which statement is correct?
Higher reward-to-risk always means a better system
A 4R target that is hit 15% of the time returns 0.60 − 0.85 = −0.25R per trade before costs. The ratio is one input to expectancy; on its own it says nothing about the system.
Reward-to-risk must be evaluated with win rate, losses, and costs
Every trade must target at least 2R

The poor-reward preset in the lab is 0.8R and loses money at 58% wins; a 0.8R plan at 65% wins would make it. The minimum is whatever the win rate pays for — the first mistake this lesson names is fixing it at 2.
Break-even win rate is always 50%
50% is break-even only when the average win equals the average loss. At 2R wins against 1R losses it is 33.3%; at 0.5R wins it is 66.7%. The formula is avg loss ÷ (avg win + avg loss).
Payoff and hit rate interact. High-R systems can have low win rates, and low-R systems can work with sufficiently high win rates.
At an average win of 3R and average loss of 1R, the theoretical break-even win rate before costs is closest to:
33% is the break-even rate for 2R wins, not 3R. With 3R wins one win pays for three losses, so one in four — 1 ÷ (3 + 1) = 25% — breaks even.
50% is break-even only when wins and losses are the same size. Here a win is three times a loss, so far fewer wins are needed: 1 ÷ (3 + 1) = 25%.
75% is the loss rate at break-even, not the win rate. Three losses of 1R are paid for by one win of 3R, so the wins needed are one in four.
1 ÷ (1 + 3) = 25%. Costs raise the actual required win rate.
A target at 4R lies beyond several major resistance levels. What does the 4R calculation prove?
Only the mathematical distance, not target realism
The target will be hit
The calculation measures a distance. Whether price crosses several levels that have each stopped it before is a question about structure, and the number 4 contains no information about it.
The strategy has an edge
An edge is expectancy over a sample, which needs a win rate from Backtesting. A single planned ratio, on a target the chart argues against, is not evidence of anything.
The position size is correct
Size comes from the risk budget and the entry-to-stop distance, which the target does not enter. A 4R target on a poorly sized position is still poorly sized.
R measures planned distance. Structural realism and historical performance require separate evidence.

Place the stop beyond structural invalidation, allow appropriate execution room, and adjust position size to fit the account risk budget.
Core concepts
Use these concepts as explicit rules rather than changing them after seeing the outcome.
Invalidation first

Volatility room

Size adapts

Interactive lesson

Stop assessment

Place the stop relative to structural invalidation.
Stop-loss placement process

Mark structural failure

Place beyond failure

Measure entry-to-stop distance

What this is normally read as
The advance to 111.8 began from the 107.4 low. The correction that follows ends at 108.3, above that low, and the invalidation line sits just under it at 107.2.

Each correction so far has ended higher than the last, which is normally read as buyers acting earlier on each pullback. The 107.2 line is where that specific reading stops being available: below the 107.4 swing there is no higher-low sequence left to read, which is why the stop belongs beyond it rather than inside the correction.
Rallies end progressively lower — 107.6, then 105.0, then 103.4. Price closes at 101.5, the last close before the breakdown, then breaks down through it to 100.1 and the 99.2 entry.

The usual interpretation is that sellers keep acting at lower prices while buyers appear only after each further decline. The 101.5 line marks where that reading fails: closing back above it means the ground given up in the breakdown has been taken back, and the reason the trade was entered no longer applies.

A downtrend of lower highs — 109.4, 106.5, 103.7 — ends with a close at 104.2, the first above 103.7. The dip that follows stops at 103.4 — the higher low that makes this a reversal rather than a bounce — and the invalidation line sits just under it at 102.7, the close the break started from.

That pair is normally read as a change of character rather than another bounce: one higher high in a downtrend would not be, but the higher low after it is. The 103.4 swing is the invalidation Reversal Setups hands the plan; the line sits under it at 102.7, with room for a wick, because below that the break has been given back entirely and there is nothing left of the reading.
The stop is not on the loss side of the entry.
The stop remains inside the structure that the setup expects to hold.

The stop is beyond invalidation, but by ${buffer.toFixed(2)} — more than two ATR of ${s.atr.toFixed(2)}. Past that it is no longer buying room for normal variation; it is paying for a thesis that has already failed, and the extra distance comes straight out of position size.
The stop is beyond invalidation with a reasonable volatility buffer for this example.
A long pullback is invalid below 50. The stop is placed at 50.40 to reduce dollar risk.
Too tight; it remains inside invalidation
Valid because dollar risk is smaller

Smaller dollar risk is bought by placing the stop where the setup is still valid, so normal variation can fill it while the thesis is intact. The right way to reduce dollar risk is fewer units, not a closer stop.
Too wide would be well below 50. A stop at 50.40 is above the price that disproves the setup — it is inside invalidation, which is the opposite problem.
It is a target
A target is on the profit side of entry. 50.40 is below the entry of a long, where the stop goes; the question is only whether it is far enough.
The stop would exit before the structural condition that disproves the setup occurs.
The structural stop requires twice the distance you expected. What is the correct risk response?
Move the stop inside structure

A stop inside structure can be filled while the setup is still valid. Twice the distance at half the size is the same dollar risk with the stop where it belongs; a closer stop is a different, worse trade.
Double the risk budget

The risk budget is the account-level rule and the structure is the trade-level fact. When they disagree, size is the variable that gives — the budget was chosen precisely so that no single trade could move it.
A trade with no stop has unlimited risk and no invalidation, which means no thesis. The distance being inconvenient does not change where the setup is wrong.
Position size should adapt to the structural distance, not the reverse.
Why can a stop far beyond invalidation also be poor?
It can use unnecessary risk and reduce position efficiency
A wider stop is always better

Wider costs size: the same budget over more distance buys fewer units, so the same move pays less. Beyond invalidation plus room for noise, extra width buys nothing but a bigger loss on a thesis that has already failed.
It guarantees a win
A stop cannot make a thesis right. A very wide one only delays the moment the loss is taken and makes it larger per unit when it comes.
There is no downside
Drag the stop down on the lab and watch the unit count fall. That is the downside: reward per unit of risk shrinks with every unnecessary point of distance.
A stop should allow normal variation without remaining in the trade after the thesis is clearly wrong.
What should be determined first?
Choosing the quantity first forces the stop to fit it, which is the fourth mistake this lesson names. Quantity is the last thing computed, from the distance the structure imposes.
The target is measured after the risk is known — reward is only meaningful in units of it. Starting from the profit you want produces a stop chosen to make a ratio.
Comfort level during the trade

Comfort produces the first mistake this lesson names: a stop placed where the loss feels acceptable, which is usually inside normal variation. Where the setup is wrong is a fact about the chart, not about the trader.
Define where the setup is wrong, then calculate size from entry-to-stop distance and risk budget.

Former resistance becomes support
Resistance in a downtrend
What this is normally read as
Price has turned down twice from the same upper area — 107.0 and 107.4 — and turned back up twice from the same lower area — 99.2 and 99.7. It is rising into that upper area again.

Repeated reactions at the same two prices are normally read as both sides acting consistently in the same places: sellers meeting advances near the top, buyers meeting declines near the bottom. That describes what has already repeated — the next test is not obliged to behave like the last two, and a close well beyond either edge ends the reading.

Three attempts stall between 102.8 and 103.4. Price then closes above that area, runs to 107.2, and the pullback that follows stops at 103.6 — on the old cap, not below it. The next advance stalls at 106.9, under the 107.2 high.

The standard reading of that sequence is role reversal: the price that used to stop advances is now where a decline stopped instead. Only the behaviour has changed, not the price — which is why a close back below the old cap would end the reading. The 107.2 and 106.9 pair is the other zone this chart supports: two advances have ended there, and the second ended lower than the first.

Every rally stops lower than the one before it — 109.4, 106.7, 104.0, 101.7, 101.5, 98.9 — and each decline closes below the previous low. The last two declines, 97.8 and 97.6, are the first pair to stop at about the same price.

Read the usual way, this says sellers keep acting at lower and lower prices while buyers step in only after price has already fallen further. The cap that matters now is the most recent one, 101.7 and 101.5, where two rallies in a row were turned back; the caps above it are history. The 97.8 and 97.6 pair is support only in the weak sense that it has held twice in a falling market — enough to draw, not enough to buy. A close above the last lower high would break the sequence and end the reading.
No zones placed. Start with the most obvious repeated reactions.
Reference shown. Support is centered near ${s.support.toFixed(1)} and resistance near ${s.resistance.toFixed(1)}.
Both zones are required. Place support and resistance before evaluating.
Useful zones. Both centers fall within the reaction clusters.
Recheck the strongest reactions. Your support is ${supportError.toFixed(2)} points from the reference and resistance is ${resistanceError.toFixed(2)} points away.
Price closes above resistance, holds above it for several candles, then retests it from above.
A rejection would close back inside. This closed above, stayed above for several candles, and then held when it came back — the opposite of being rejected.
Breakout and role reversal
A sweep trades through and closes back inside on the same candle or the next. Several closes above, then a successful retest, is acceptance — the thing a sweep is not.
Price is at the old resistance, not in the middle of anything. The description is of a level being retested from the far side, which is where role reversal is decided.
Acceptance above the zone followed by a successful retest supports a breakout and potential role reversal.
Price wicks above resistance but closes back inside the range on the same candle.
Acceptance needs a close beyond the zone and trading that stays there. A wick through with the close back inside is the one pattern that rules acceptance out.
Possible sweep / failed breakout
Resistance can only become support once price has closed above it and held there. This candle never closed above it at all.
Nothing continued: the candle probed above the range and came straight back. One wick beyond a boundary is the weakest evidence on the chart, not a confirmation of anything.
Trading beyond a zone is not enough. Closing back inside suggests rejection or a sweep rather than acceptance.
A prior resistance area breaks and later repeatedly supports pullbacks.
A midpoint has no reactions at it. This area stopped advances before the break and has stopped pullbacks since — repeated reactions are what make it a level.
A level that has produced reactions on both sides is the most validated level a chart can offer. Breaking did not invalidate it; it changed which side reacts there.
A level where pullbacks keep holding is a floor under the move, not the ceiling above it. Targets come from the next opposing zone, and nothing about this one is final.
Former resistance can become support after price accepts above it.
Why should support and resistance usually be represented as zones?
Markets always reverse at exact prices
Look at the range tab: the turns came at 107.0 and 107.4, at 99.2 and 99.7. Close, never identical — which is exactly why a zone and not a line.
Orders and reactions cluster across an area
It hides incorrect analysis
A zone drawn wide enough to catch anything would hide bad analysis, and that is the failure mode, not the purpose. The width should match the spread of the reactions, no more.
It creates more trading signals
Zones exist to prioritise fewer, better-evidenced areas. More signals is what drawing a line at every pivot produces — the first mistake this lesson names.
Different participants act at nearby prices, and volatility creates a reaction area rather than a guaranteed exact tick.

Do not move the stop before +1R. At +1R, move to break-even. At +2R, reduce 50%, then trail the remainder 1R behind from the next candle.
Keep the original stop until price first closes above +1R. Then move to break-even. Reduce 50% at +2R.
Keep the original −1R stop. Do not widen it, average down, or redefine invalidation.
What this is normally read as
Each dip has ended above the one before it, and each advance has carried further than the last.
Normally read as buyers continuing to act at higher prices rather than waiting for a discount. It says nothing about where the move ends — the written plan decides that, not the reading.
Price fell back through entry to −0.45R, then recovered and closed above the +0.70R high it had made before that fall.

The usual interpretation is that the decline did not attract continuation and the ground it took was given back. Note the reading only became available after the recovery: while price sat at −0.45R the same candles were equally consistent with the setup simply failing, which is why the stop rather than the reading is what protected the trade.
Price advanced to +0.45R and has closed lower on every candle since, through entry and below it. No rally has appeared in between.

A one-way decline with no recovery attempt is normally read as nothing yet meeting the move at a higher price. The answer to that is the original stop — widening it would replace a reading that has failed with one that cannot fail.
Only the first candles are revealed.

There is not enough structure on screen to read anything yet. That is the normal condition at the start of a trade, and it is exactly why the management plan is written before the evidence arrives rather than after.

Management milestone · +2R
Candle ${st.step+1} / ${s.path.length}
Discipline ${st.correct} / ${st.total}
Reduced ${Math.round(sold*100)}% at ${st.current.toFixed(2)}R.

Simulation complete: ${st.realized>=0?"+":""}${st.realized.toFixed(2)}R. Discipline score ${st.correct}/${st.total}. ${actionNote}
The plan says move the stop to break-even only after a close above +1R. Price is currently +0.6R.
Keep the original stop
Move to break-even now

The plan says after a close above +1R, and price is at +0.6R. Run the shakeout tab and move early: the dip to −0.45R fills a break-even stop on a trade that then goes to +2.45R. That is the first mistake this lesson names.
Nothing has gone wrong — price is above entry — and widening is never a plan action anyway. The stop only tightens, at the milestones the plan wrote down.
No milestone has been reached and no invalidation has printed. An exit at +0.6R is a discretionary change to the plan, and it would be scored as one.
The predefined milestone has not occurred. Moving early changes the tested rule.
Price reaches the stop and invalidates the setup. What is prohibited?
Moving the stop farther away
Recording the loss is required, not prohibited — it is the entry Trading Journal asks for, with the plan-followed flag set to yes. The prohibited act is moving the stop so the loss is not taken.
Reviewing the setup later
Review is the point of the record. What is prohibited is changing the invalidation while the trade is open so that the review never has a loss to look at.
Accepting the planned loss
Accepting the planned loss is the plan working. The −1R was chosen before entry as the price of being wrong; the failure is refusing to pay it by widening the stop.
Widening after entry increases risk and keeps an invalid thesis alive.
One trade would have earned more without scaling out. What does that prove?
Almost nothing about the rule across many trades
Scaling is always bad

One trade that would have paid more unscaled is one path. On the shakeout path the reduce at +2R banks half before the trade ends at +2.45R; the rule’s value is the average over every path, which one trade cannot show.
Trailing is always best
Trailing looks best on the path that kept going. On a path that reverses, the trail gives back 1R of open profit that a reduce would have kept. The comparison needs a sample, not a memory.
Future trades will behave the same
The next trade is a different path, and the rule was written for the distribution of paths, not this one. Optimising management from one memorable trade is the fourth mistake this lesson names.
Management rules must be evaluated over a representative sample, not one favorable path.
What should be compared during review?
Planned actions versus actual actions and outcomes
Profit cannot tell a good decision from a lucky one. A trade managed by feel that made +2R and a trade managed to the plan that lost 1R are, on profit alone, ranked the wrong way round.
How exciting the trade felt
Excitement is usually a sign the plan was abandoned. The discipline score in the lab is the measurable version of the same question, and it does not ask how the trade felt.
An opinion is not a record of what the plan said and what was done. Review compares the written plan with the actions taken; nothing anyone else says changes either.
Execution quality and rule deviations explain whether outcomes came from the system or from inconsistent behavior.

clauses.expected: Trade Thesis
Convert market context into a conditional plan with a defined setup, trigger, invalidation, target, and no-trade condition.
Core concepts
Use these concepts as explicit rules rather than changing them after seeing the outcome.
Context
State the higher-timeframe structure and the location that makes the setup relevant.
Trigger
Define the observable event that permits entry. Directional bias alone is not a trigger.
Invalidation
Specify the price or condition that proves the thesis wrong before position size is calculated.
Interactive lesson
Change the inputs, inspect the chart, and evaluate the decision before revealing the answer.
Build the thesis
Specify direction, setup, trigger, invalidation, and target before evaluating.
A complete thesis, worked — the bullish pullback tab
Every line below is checkable against the chart at the decision candle. Read it once, then complete the other three tabs without it.
Trade thesis process
A thesis is complete only when every decision can be evaluated objectively after the trade.
Describe context
Identify structure, location, and any higher-timeframe conflict.
Name the setup
Use one defined setup such as pullback, breakout, or reversal.
Require a trigger
Write the exact close, retest, or structure event required for entry.
Define failure and objective
Set structural invalidation, target, and the no-trade condition.
Thesis completeness drill
Minimum thesis template
Common mistakes
Completion standard

Decision, setup, trigger, invalidation and target, with the evaluator agreeing — and not one line changed after the later candles are shown. On the range and conflict tabs the five lines are the no-trade condition, written out.

Daily bullish structure; price is testing prior breakout support.
Prior breakout / support
Prior high / first target
Daily bearish structure; price is compressing above range support.
Price is between established support and resistance with no edge at the midpoint.
Daily structure is bullish, but the execution timeframe remains bearish and has not shifted.
Hourly trigger not broken
What this is normally read as

Higher highs at 107.0 and 111.2, with higher lows at 102.5, 106.4 and 108.1. The correction from 111.2 ends at 108.1, on the 108.0 area price broke out from, and the 111.7 close is the first back above the whole correction.

This is normally read as buyers accepting progressively higher prices: each correction finishes above the one before it, so demand is arriving earlier each time, and sellers have not been able to return price to where the last advance began. The reading fails if price closes back under 108.1, the low the correction made; the plan’s invalidation line sits at 107.0, under that low with room for a wick, and that is the number the plan takes.
Two more closes, 113.2 and 114.4, extend the sequence. Nothing in them was available when the plan was written, and nothing in the plan should change because of them.
Rallies keep ending lower — 107.5, then 105.0, then 103.6, then 102.0 — while price compresses on top of the 101.2 range support. The 100.4 close is the first below it.

The usual interpretation is that sellers keep acting at steadily lower prices while buyers appear only after each further decline; when the floor gives way, the prices that had been defended stop being defended. One close below is the trigger this plan waits for, not proof. A close back above 103.0 would end the reading, because the last lower high would have been taken back.
Price closes 99.1, 98.3 and 96.8 — almost at the 96.0 target. Seen in advance those candles would make the plan look obvious; that is exactly why they were hidden while it was written.
Price turns down from 105.8 and again from 106.1, and turns back up from 99.6 and again from 101.6, finishing at 103.0 — the midpoint.

Read as it stands, neither side has been able to take price out of the other side of the range: sellers meet advances near the top, buyers meet declines near the bottom. At the midpoint there is nothing to read at all, because neither side has been tested here — which is why this chart supports no directional reading.

The move to 110.2 is a higher high on the slower timeframe. Price has since fallen through the 105.2 trigger and has not closed back above it, making lower highs at 104.6 and 103.2 and a lower low at 102.7.

Two readings sit on one chart and they disagree: the slower structure is normally read as buyers still in control, while the recent sequence is normally read as sellers meeting every bounce. Nothing visible resolves that — a close back above 105.2 would, and until then the honest reading is that the timeframes are saying different things.

Not evaluated. Complete the plan without using the future candles.
Direction follows the structure the reading describes, not the last candle — and on a chart with no location edge or with two timeframes disagreeing, the decision is to wait.
Name what the chart shows: a correction inside a trend, a close through a boundary, a break of the prior sequence — or no trade.
The trigger is the observable event the plan waits for; while the decision is to wait there is no trigger yet.
Invalidation sits just beyond the swing that has to hold, on the loss side of entry — read it off the red line, not off the loss you would accept.
The target is the next opposing structural level drawn on the chart, not a price that makes a ratio.

‘Daily trend is bullish, so I will buy.’ What is missing?
A trigger, invalidation, and target
An indicator would only restate the bias. What the sentence lacks is not more evidence for ‘bullish’ but the event that permits entry, the price that proves it wrong, and the level it is aiming at.
An opinion cannot be checked after the trade. A thesis is made of things that can: a trigger, an invalidation price, and a target.
‘Bullish, so I will buy’ has a direction and nothing else. It does not say when to buy, when the idea is wrong, or where it is going — so nothing about it can be evaluated afterwards.
Direction is only context. A usable thesis also defines the setup condition, invalidation, and objective.
A long thesis uses a stop above the current entry. Which component is invalid?
Context describes the structure and location; nothing in the question says it is wrong. The component that is on the wrong side of entry is the stop.
A target above entry is where a long is supposed to go. The stop above entry is the problem: a long is disproved by price falling, so its invalidation has to be below.
The setup name is not what is broken. A long with its stop above entry would be closed by the very move it wants — the invalidation is on the wrong side.
For a normal long position, invalidation must be below entry at a price that disproves the setup.
Price is in the middle of a range. What is the most defensible thesis?
Long because support exists
Support exists, but price is not at it. A long from the midpoint has its invalidation far below and resistance close above — the worst of both distances.
Short because resistance exists
Same problem in the other direction: the resistance is not here, so the short has nothing near it to be wrong at and nothing near it to aim for.
Wait for an edge or breakout
Choose the last candle direction
One candle is not context. At the midpoint neither side has been tested, so the last candle’s colour says nothing that a thesis could be built on.
At the midpoint, the nearest invalidation and target often provide poor asymmetry and no location advantage.
The setup is invalidated before the trigger occurs. What should happen?
Enter at a better price
It is a lower price, not a better one. The structure that made the entry worth taking has just failed; what is left is a fill with no thesis behind it.
There is no position yet, so there is no stop to widen — and moving invalidation to keep an idea alive is the mistake this lesson names. The price that disproved the setup has printed.
Switch timeframes until it looks valid
Choosing the timeframe after the fact is choosing the answer. The plan named its timeframe before the invalidation printed; the invalidation stands.
A pre-entry invalidation cancels the plan. Lower price is not automatically better price.

clauses.expected: Trading Journal
Record the original thesis, planned and actual execution, result in R, adherence, mistakes, and notes in a journal that can be exported for review.
Core concepts
Use these concepts as explicit rules rather than changing them after seeing the outcome.
Plan and outcome
Record what was intended separately from what happened and whether the plan was followed.
Result in R
Normalize outcomes by initial risk so trades with different prices and sizes can be compared.
Consistent tags
Use stable setup and mistake categories so patterns can be aggregated later.
Interactive lesson
Record a trade as its plan was written, score it after the exit, and export the record.
New journal entry
Journal summary
Saved entries
Trading journal process
Capture enough information to reproduce the decision and diagnose execution without rewriting history.
Record before entry
Save context, setup, trigger, entry, invalidation, target, and management plan.
Capture actual execution
Record fills, changes, partial exits, and deviations while they are factual.
Score after exit
Store result in R, plan adherence, execution score, mistake tags, and notes.
Export and review periodically
Use a consistent review interval and preserve backups outside browser storage.
Journal quality drill
What to record
Common mistakes
Completion standard
Thesis written as it was before the outcome, result in R, plan adherence, execution score, and a mistake tag wherever one applies. The simulated trade in Trade Management supplies this example.

clauses.expected: Calls and Puts
Compare long and short calls and puts by directional exposure, holder rights, writer obligations, expiration breakeven, and maximum risk.
Core concepts
Two contract types, two sides each: four positions from one strike and one premium.
Calls
A call gives its holder the right to buy the underlying at the strike under the contract terms.
Puts
A put gives its holder the right to sell the underlying at the strike under the contract terms.
Long versus short
Long positions pay premium for rights. Short positions receive premium and accept obligations.
Worked example
One strike and one premium — 100 strike, $4.00, one contract — taken through all four positions, so the arithmetic the drill asks for is done once in the open.
Interactive lesson
Choose a position and drag the expiration price; the payoff, breakeven and maximum loss follow.
Expiration scenario
Select a position and move the final stock price.
Classify a basic option position
Determine the type, side, and expiration economics before looking at a chart.
Choose call or put
Call exposure is tied to buying at the strike; put exposure is tied to selling at the strike.
Choose long or short
Long is the holder. Short is the writer who can be assigned.
Calculate breakeven
Calls use strike plus premium; puts use strike minus premium at expiration.
State maximum risk
Do not describe a position without its maximum or substantial-loss condition.
Position identification
Lesson rule
Common mistakes
Completion standard
The drill asks for the position that fits a description, a breakeven, the uncapped position, and a short put’s P/L at a price; do all four before opening the chart.

Right to buy at the strike. Bullish exposure with premium at risk.
Right to sell at the strike. Bearish exposure with premium at risk.
Obligation to sell if assigned. Uncovered loss can be theoretically unlimited.
Obligation to buy if assigned. Downside can be substantial if the stock falls.

A long call exists only because someone wrote it: the premium moved to a writer who accepted the obligation to sell at the strike. Breakeven is where the two sides come out even, so the premium is normally read as the price both agreed for the right, not as a view on direction. Below breakeven at expiration the holder paid more for that right than it turned out to be worth.

A long put exists only because someone wrote it: the premium moved to a writer who accepted the obligation to buy at the strike. The usual reading is that the premium is what both sides agreed the right to sell was worth, not a measure of how far price would fall. Above breakeven at expiration that right is worth less than it cost.

This side received the premium and, in exchange, handed the holder the right to buy at the strike. Structurally that is why the line is flat below the strike and then falls away above it: the gain is capped at the premium agreed, while the obligation above the strike is not capped at all. The reading that the premium pays for the risk stops holding once price runs far enough past the strike.

This side received the premium and handed the holder the right to sell at the strike. The line is flat above the strike and falls below it because the obligation to buy does not depend on where price ends up. Read the premium as lowering the effective purchase price, not as putting a floor under it.

Which position benefits directly from a decline and has limited premium risk?
A long call gains from a rise. Its loss is limited to the premium, but it does not benefit from a decline at all.
A short call does gain as the stock falls — but only up to the premium received — and its loss above the strike has no cap. “Limited premium risk” is false for it.
Short stock gains from a decline, but its loss has no cap as the stock rises. The premium-limited loss is the long put’s property.
A long put can gain as the underlying falls, while its maximum loss is the premium paid.
At expiration, a 100-strike long call bought for $4 begins showing profit above what stock price?
Strike minus premium is the long PUT breakeven. A call needs the stock above the strike by the premium paid: $100 + $4.
At $100 the call has no intrinsic value and the whole $4 is lost. In-the-money begins here; profit does not.
At $140 the call has $40 of intrinsic value. Profit began $36 lower, at strike plus premium.
The expiration breakeven is strike plus premium: $100 + $4 = $104.
Which basic position can have theoretically unlimited loss if uncovered?
A long call cannot lose more than the premium paid; below the strike it is simply worth nothing.
A long put cannot lose more than the premium paid.
A short put’s loss is large — down to strike minus premium if the stock goes to zero — but it is bounded, because the stock cannot fall below zero. A short call has no such floor.
An uncovered short call can lose increasingly as the stock rises without a fixed upper bound.
A 100-strike put is sold for $4 and the stock finishes at $90. What is the writer’s P/L on one contract?
The put is $10 in the money, but the $4 premium received offsets part of that: ($4 − $10) × 100 = −$600.
The premium is kept, but the put is $10 in the money: the writer buys $90 stock at $100. Net: ($4 − $10) × 100 = −$600.
$400 is the long put HOLDER’s maximum loss. The writer’s loss is intrinsic value minus the premium received: −$600.
The writer’s expiration P/L is premium minus intrinsic value: ($4 − $10) × 100 = −$600.

A short put with the purchase cash set aside: a premium now for agreeing to buy at the strike.
Position structure
A cash-secured put combines a short put with cash reserved to buy the deliverable shares at the strike.
Effective purchase price
Strike minus premium received estimates the expiration breakeven and net share basis if assigned.

Reserve sufficient cash
Use the deliverable, strike, quantity, and broker requirements.

Subtract premium from strike and include fees in real planning.

$50 is what is paid at assignment. The $2 already received lowers the effective price to $48.
Added. The premium was received, so it reduces the effective price.
$200 is the contract premium. The effective price is per share: $50 − $2.
Strike minus premium received gives a $48 effective purchase price before fees and taxes.
How much strike cash supports one 80-strike standard put?
Per share. One contract is 100 shares: $8,000.
Multiplied by 10. The multiplier is 100.
That would be ten contracts.
$80 × 100 shares = $8,000, before broker-specific treatment of premium and collateral.
What is the maximum expiration profit of a cash-secured put?
However high the stock goes, the put expires worthless and the writer keeps only the premium.
The strike is what the writer pays if assigned, not what they earn.
The stock price increase
The writer does not own the shares unless assigned; a rise in the stock earns nothing beyond the premium.
If the put expires without intrinsic value, the writer retains the premium; upside is limited to that amount.

The $300 premium received offsets part of it: (80 − 3) × 100 = $7,700.
$300 is the maximum PROFIT. The loss is the stock bought at $80 falling to $0, less the premium.
Bounded, because the stock cannot fall below zero. Unlimited loss belongs to the short call.
(strike − premium) × 100 = (80 − 3) × 100 = $7,700: substantial, and bounded only by zero.

Combine owned shares with a short call, calculate premium-adjusted breakeven and capped maximum profit, and evaluate assignment and downside exposure.
Core concepts
Long shares plus a short call: a premium now for the upside above the strike.
Position structure
A covered call combines long shares with a short call representing the same number of shares.
Income and basis
Premium received lowers the expiration breakeven by the premium amount.
Capped upside
Above the strike, further stock gains are offset by the short call, while downside in the shares remains substantial.
Interactive lesson
Set basis, strike and premium, then drag the expiration price and compare the position with the shares alone.
Covered-call position
The call is covered by owned shares. The premium reduces basis, while the short call caps upside above the strike.
Plan a covered call
The strategy is appropriate only when selling the shares at the strike is acceptable.
Confirm share coverage
Own the correct number of deliverable shares for the calls sold.
Choose an acceptable strike
The strike is a potential sale price, not merely a premium-selection input.
Calculate adjusted basis
Subtract premium from stock basis to estimate expiration breakeven.
Plan assignment and exit
Know how dividends, early assignment, and expiration can affect the stock position.

The cyan line flattens above the strike because the upside there was sold: someone paid premium for the right to buy these shares at that price. Structurally that is the trade that was agreed rather than a loss, and the purple stock-only line pulls ahead only once the move past the strike is worth more than the premium received. The reading holds only while the shares are actually held; without them the same obligation is a different position entirely.

The premium received is the price agreed for capping the upside, and it lowers the basis by exactly that amount and no more. It transfers none of the downside to anyone: the shares are still held, and the purple line shows the same decline with no premium against it. The common reading that a covered call is a conservative position fails here, because the position is long stock first.

The short call is not in the money in this scenario, so the right that was sold has no claim on the shares and the premium is retained. Structurally the two sides agreed a price for that right before the outcome was known, so retaining it is the outcome and not the reason. Above the strike the cap applies again regardless of how the shares got there.
The short call is in-the-money at expiration; assignment is likely under standard exercise procedures, though holder and broker instructions can differ.
The premium reduced the loss, but the stock decline still produces a position loss.
The short call expires out-of-the-money in this scenario and the premium is retained.

One contract represents 100 shares; one share covers one percent of it.
The standard equity multiplier is 100, not 10.
That would cover ten contracts. One is 100 shares.
One standard equity-option contract usually represents 100 shares.
Stock basis is $50 and a call is sold for $2. What is the covered-call breakeven?
The premium received lowers what the shares need to recover: $50 − $2.
Added. The premium was received, so it reduces the breakeven rather than raising it.
The strike caps the upside. Breakeven is on the downside: basis minus premium.
Expiration breakeven is stock basis minus premium received: $50 − $2 = $48.
What happens to upside above the short-call strike at expiration?
Above the strike every dollar the shares gain is a dollar the short call loses. The two cancel.
It is capped because gains on shares are offset by losses on the short call
The premium was fixed when the call was sold. Nothing about it changes with the stock.
The stock basis becomes zero
Basis is what was paid for the shares, less the premium. The strike does not touch it.
Above the strike, the short call offsets further stock gains, creating a maximum expiration profit.
Shares held at $100, a 108 call sold for $2.50, and the stock falls to $80 at expiration. What is the P/L on 100 shares?
The premium received offsets $250 of the $2,000 stock loss: −$1,750.
The premium is not the loss. The shares lost $20 each; the $2.50 offsets only that much of it.
The call expiring worthless keeps the premium, but the shares are still down $20 each. The position is long stock first.
(80 − 100) × 100 + $250 premium = −$1,750. The premium is a limited offset, not protection.

Measure first-order directional sensitivity with delta, observe how gamma changes delta, and compare linear estimates with full theoretical repricing.
Core concepts
Delta is a slope; gamma is how fast the slope changes.
Delta
Delta estimates the option-price change for a small change in the underlying, with other inputs held constant.
Position delta
Multiplying option delta by the contract multiplier and quantity estimates share-equivalent directional exposure.
Gamma
Gamma estimates how much delta changes for a $1 move in the underlying and is often greatest near the strike close to expiration.
Worked example
The 100 call, 30 DTE, IV 30%, one contract, with the stock moving from $100 to $105 — the lab’s default state, with the working shown.
Interactive lesson
Set a move and compare the delta-only estimate, the delta-plus-gamma estimate and the full repricing.
Directional sensitivity
Compare a delta-only estimate with a delta-plus-gamma estimate and the full theoretical repricing.
Use delta and gamma
Treat Greeks as changing sensitivities rather than fixed contract facts.
Read current delta
Use sign and magnitude to understand the immediate directional exposure.
Convert to position delta
Multiply by 100 and contract quantity for standard equity options.
Inspect gamma
Higher gamma means delta can change more quickly as the stock moves.
Recalculate after material changes
Stock, time, and IV changes can make the original Greeks stale.

Core concepts
Exercise is the holder’s act; assignment is what it does to a writer; expiration handling is the broker’s.
Exercise
The option holder uses the contractual right to buy or sell the underlying according to the contract terms.
Assignment
The writer is selected to fulfill the obligation created by a holder’s exercise.
Expiration handling
In-the-money standardized options may be exercised by exception, but contrary instructions and brokerage policies can change the result.

Manage expiration deliberately

Identify settlement and style
Confirm physical versus cash settlement and American versus European exercise.
Review moneyness and extrinsic value
Do not wait until the final minutes to discover an exercise or assignment exposure.
Check buying power and shares
Know the cash, margin, and deliverable requirements for every possible outcome.
Submit or close before firm deadlines
Use your broker’s actual instructions and cutoff times rather than assumptions.

With no intrinsic value the right that was sold is simply not taken up, and the premium stays where the two sides agreed it. That is normally read as the price of the possibility having been settled in advance, with this outcome resolving it to nothing. It stops holding the moment intrinsic value appears, which is why the threshold is checked rather than assumed.

Exercising is normally read as taking up the right the premium bought, and a writer on the other side is assigned and must deliver at the strike. The cash required is the strike rather than the premium, so the obligation facing this choice is its mirror image. Whether the shares are wanted is a separate question from whether the option shows a gain.

Exercising is normally read as taking up the right the premium bought, and a writer on the other side is assigned and must buy at the strike. Delivering shares is a real transfer, so this reading depends on the shares being available; without them the exercise creates a different position rather than a rounding error.

Assignment is not a fee or an administrative detail: it is the obligation the premium was received for, taken up by the holder on the other side. The choice was given away when the contract was written, so delivery happens at the strike wherever the underlying finished. If the shares are not held, the reading that this position is covered fails.

Assignment is the obligation the premium was received for, taken up by the holder on the other side. This side agreed in advance to buy at the strike, so the purchase happens at that price regardless of where the underlying finished. The premium reduces the effective basis; it does not make the purchase optional.

No; it still has 20 days
The days left matter to the holder only through extrinsic value, and here that is nearly gone. Exercising to capture the dividend costs the holder almost nothing.

In-the-money contracts are exercised by exception unless instructed otherwise; that automatic step is the reason to check what the firm does with the result.

Exercise by exception is applied after the close on expiration day. The shares are in the account before Monday’s open, along with whatever the stock does before then.
The 110 call is assigned
It is $4.50 out of the money. Nobody exercises a right to buy at $110 when the stock is $105.50.
Legs are handled one at a time: the ITM long call is exercised into 100 shares at $100, the OTM short call expires, and the account is long stock until it is sold.

Trace how a long option’s theoretical value changes as the days run out with everything else held still, separate intrinsic from extrinsic value, and explain why the daily decay is not a constant.
Core concepts
Extrinsic value is the price of time, and time runs out.
Expiration
The contract ends on its expiration date, after which the holder has no remaining option rights.
Extrinsic decay
Extrinsic value reaches zero at expiration; the path toward zero is not linear.
Theta
Theta estimates the option-value change associated with one day passing while other model inputs are held constant. It is quoted per share; a one-contract position shows it × 100.
Interactive lesson
Hold stock and volatility still and slide the days remaining; the curve is the same option priced at every day of its life.
Time remaining
Hold stock and implied volatility constant to isolate modeled time decay for a long option.
Evaluate time exposure
Time must be part of the trade thesis, not an afterthought.
Match expiration to the thesis
Allow enough time for the expected price movement and known events.
Separate intrinsic and extrinsic
Only extrinsic value is directly exposed to disappearing at expiration.
Inspect theta and DTE
Near-term options can change rapidly, especially around the strike.
Define an exit before expiration
Do not rely on automatic expiration handling as a management plan.

Core concepts
Implied volatility prices the size of movement, not its direction, and it moves on its own.
Implied volatility
IV is the volatility input consistent with an option price under a model; it does not predict direction.
Vega exposure
Long options generally gain theoretical value when IV rises and lose value when IV falls, all else equal.
Event repricing

Read current IV

Identify known events
Earnings, decisions, and other scheduled events can affect the volatility term structure.
Model IV expansion and contraction
Test whether the position remains acceptable under several IV outcomes.
Plan the exit timing

Implied volatility is the assumption backed out of the option price, so a fall in it is normally read as less uncertainty being priced than before: a repricing of the assumption, not a view on direction. That is why a favourable move in the underlying can still leave a long position worse off. Read the two contributions above as separate effects rather than as one signal.

Implied volatility is the assumption backed out of the option price, so a rise in it is normally read as more uncertainty being priced than before. It says the two sides now put a higher price on movement, and says nothing about which way that movement goes. A long position can gain from this alone even when the underlying barely moves.

Holding implied volatility still isolates the underlying move, so whatever changes in the premium here is the directional contribution on its own. The usual reading is that the price of uncertainty stayed where it was while the price of the underlying did not. Any premium change you see is therefore not evidence about what is being assumed for future movement.

The direction the stock must move

Premium tends to decrease
The strike is a contract term and never moves.
Falling IV lowers a long option’s value. Doubling would need IV to rise, and a lot.
Delta becomes exactly zero
Delta shifts a little with IV, but it does not vanish; the option still responds to the stock.
Long options generally have positive vega, so lower IV tends to reduce theoretical value.
The 100 call is bought at IV 60% for $7.03 before an event. The stock rises to $104 and IV falls to 30%. What happens to the position?
A gain of about $235; the stock went the right way
+$235 is the direction-only contribution. The IV contraction takes back −$328, and the position is worse off by about $92.
A loss of about $92: +$235 from direction, −$328 from volatility
Nothing; the two effects cancel
They do not cancel here. The volatility effect is larger than the directional one, which is why the net is a loss.
A gain; lower IV makes the option cheaper to hold
Cheaper is what you want when BUYING. Once long, lower IV lowers what you already own.
The event preset: $7.03 → $6.10, −$92 per contract. Direction added about $235; the IV fall removed about $328.
The “rough expected move” reads ±$17.20. What is that?
One standard deviation over the period under the model: roughly two chances in three the stock finishes inside it
The most the stock can move
About one outcome in three falls OUTSIDE a one-standard-deviation band. It is a typical size, not a limit.
IV has no direction, so the band is symmetric. A target would name a side.
The premium was $7.03. The move is stock × IV × √(days/365), a statement about the stock, not the option.
Stock × IV × √(days/365) is one standard deviation: 100 × 0.60 × √(30/365) ≈ $17.20.

clauses.expected: Options Trading
Read option contracts and chains, calculate expiration payoffs, interpret volatility and the Greeks, and evaluate options strategies.
Subject
Trading
Lessons
Format
Interactive
Overview
What it teaches

To read a contract line and say who owes what and what cash moves; to give any position’s breakeven and maximum loss from strike and premium; to classify a strike and split a premium into intrinsic and extrinsic value; to price the bid-ask spread on the way in and out. To say which way time and volatility move a premium and to put numbers on both — a delta into dollars and share-equivalents, theta × days and vega × points against a full repricing. To build five positions and state each one’s cost, breakeven, most it can make and most it can lose. To say what an expiring position turns into, and to write a plan that ten checks approve, exported in a published shape.
Who it is for

Anyone who can read a chart and now wants to understand the instrument that trades on top of it — including the reader who has bought a call, watched the stock go the right way, and still lost money. It starts from contract terms, so no prior options knowledge is assumed. It also suits someone who already trades options and cannot say, without guessing, which part of a premium is intrinsic and which part is the clock.
Concept dependencies

Delta, gamma, theta and vega only mean something once option premium has been split into intrinsic and extrinsic value. Options strategies assume you can price the legs. Options Trade Planning asks for a spread cost, a risk budget and an exit rule, using the calculations explained in these lessons. Planning connects knowledge of contracts and strategies to decisions about risk.
Lessons
Explanations, examples, interactive tools, and practice questions.
16 lessons

Educational use only — nothing here is trading advice. Options involve risk and are not suitable for every investor. This course is educational: it provides no personalized investment advice and no live trading signals.

Modeling scope. Every price, chain, quote, scenario and outcome in these lessons is synthetic, and theoretical values come from a simplified European Black–Scholes model. The course does not model every listed-product feature, dividend, early-exercise decision, fee, tax, margin rule or market microstructure effect. Real results can differ because of spread, slippage, commissions, gaps, liquidity, assignment, exercise, implied volatility and time decay. Verify contract specifications, brokerage procedures, costs and the current Options Disclosure Document independently before trading.
Contract basics 01–05

Lesson topics
Contract basics

What you are actually buying, before any of it has a price. The terms written into every contract and who owes what; the four positions calls and puts can take; whether a strike is in, at or out of the money; what the premium is made of; and how to read the chain it is quoted on — including the bid-ask spread you pay on the way in and again on the way out.

Why the premium moves when the stock does not. Time decay — how extrinsic value drains as expiration approaches — implied volatility on its own terms, and the sensitivities that put numbers on both: delta and gamma for direction, theta and vega for time and volatility. The Options Trade Plan lesson documents an options trade plan. It scores a complete plan and then hands it back to you as a file, so the plan can outlive the browser tab it was written in.

What comes out of it

Options Trade Planning takes the thesis, the contract, the risk budget and the exit rules you enter, scores them across ten checks, and exports the whole plan as a JSON document stamped options-trade-plan-v1 . The file records the inputs, the computed metrics — breakeven, maximum loss, spread cost, risk budget — and the score with the individual checks that produced it, so a plan you approved can be read back later against what actually happened.

Core concepts
A long option risks its premium; what it is worth before expiration is a separate question.
Long call
A long call seeks upside participation with premium at risk and no fixed maximum profit at expiration.
Long put
A long put seeks downside participation with premium at risk and substantial but limited maximum profit as stock approaches zero.
Pre-expiration value
Before expiration, option value can differ materially from intrinsic value because time and IV remain.

Choose strike and expiration

Size the position from the debit that can be lost, not from hoped-for profit.

The gap between the two curves is extrinsic value: the part of the premium that still belongs to the time remaining, priced by both sides when the contract was opened. Closing early is normally read as selling that remaining time back rather than waiting for it to be spent. The gap does not close at expiration breakeven — at that vertical the two lines are still apart by whatever extrinsic value the contract has left. It closes only at expiry itself, when nothing but intrinsic value remains.

The scenario sits on the unfavourable side of the strike for this position, so the modelled exit curve sits below the entry debit. What still separates the two curves is extrinsic value: what both sides price the remaining time at. That is the only thing between this position and the expiration line, and it reaches zero at expiration whatever the underlying does.

A 100-strike long put costs $4. What is its expiration breakeven?
At the strike the put is worthless and the whole $4 is lost. Profit needs the stock below the strike by more than the premium.
Strike plus premium is the CALL breakeven. A put profits below the strike: 100 − 4.
$400 is the contract cost. Breakeven is a stock price: $96.
Long-put expiration breakeven is strike minus premium: $100 − $4 = $96.
You bought the 100 call for $4.50 with 45 days left. Three weeks later the stock is $103, below your $104.50 breakeven. Is the position necessarily losing?
Yes; below breakeven means a loss

No; with 24 days and IV left the option is priced above intrinsic and can be sold for more than $4.50
No; the breakeven moves with the stock

Before expiration the option carries extrinsic value; the expiration breakeven says nothing about an exit three weeks early.

Only the underlying price

Classify calls and puts as in-the-money, at-the-money, or out-of-the-money and calculate intrinsic value without confusing moneyness with position profit.
Core concepts
Stock versus strike, and nothing else, decides moneyness.
In-the-money
A call is ITM when stock is above strike. A put is ITM when stock is below strike.
At-the-money
Strictly, a strike equal to the stock price, so it has no intrinsic value. A chain calls the nearest listed strike “ATM” by convention, and that strike can be a little in or out of the money.
Out-of-the-money
OTM options have no intrinsic value, though they can still have extrinsic value before expiration.
Interactive lesson
Move the stock and watch each strike’s status and intrinsic value change; click a strike to inspect it.
Move the underlying

Badges use the strict rule: a strike within 0.5% of the stock is at-the-money. The nearest listed strike is marked separately, because a chain calls that strike “ATM” by convention even when it carries a little intrinsic value.
Classify moneyness
Use only the underlying price and strike for this classification.
Read the underlying price
Use the current price of the security tied to the option.
Read the strike
Do not use the option premium as the strike.
Apply the call or put rule
Calls compare stock above strike; puts compare stock below strike.
Calculate intrinsic value
Use the appropriate max formula and never allow intrinsic value below zero.

Read a synthetic option chain, compare bid and ask prices, quantify spread friction, inspect volume and open interest, and use limit prices deliberately.
Core concepts
The quote is a bid and an ask; what you pay is the distance between them.
Bid and ask
The bid is the displayed buying price and the ask is the displayed selling price; the difference is the spread.
Volume and open interest
Volume measures contracts traded during the session; open interest measures outstanding contracts after clearing updates.
Execution quality
A directional idea can still produce a poor trade when the spread is wide or the contract is difficult to exit.
Worked example
The default row: the 100 call at 30 DTE with the stock at $100, read the way the drill will ask you to read any row.
Interactive lesson
Pick a row and an expiration, read the spread in dollars and in percent, and set a limit inside the market.
Contract selection
Evaluate direction, expiration, strike, and execution quality together.
Select from an option chain
Contract selection starts with the trade thesis and ends with execution quality.
Choose expiration
The contract must give the thesis enough time while respecting premium and event exposure.
Choose strike
Use Moneyness to match the intended exposure and cost; the sensitivities in Delta and Gamma and Theta and Vega refine the choice.
Inspect the market
Compare bid, ask, spread percentage, displayed activity, and open interest.
Use a deliberate order
Set a limit based on the displayed market and accept that it may not execute.

Completion standard
Activity columns are context; the drill asks you to price the spread and to say what a limit at the mid saves and what it risks.

Break an option premium into intrinsic and extrinsic value and observe how stock price, time to expiration, and implied volatility affect a simplified theoretical estimate.
Core concepts
A premium is intrinsic value plus everything else; the split is what the rest of the course works on.
Premium
The option premium is the market price paid by the buyer and received by the seller, quoted per share.
Intrinsic value
Intrinsic value is the amount the option is in-the-money and cannot be negative.
Extrinsic value

Extrinsic value is premium above intrinsic value. It is priced chiefly by the time remaining (Expiration and Time Decay) and by implied volatility, the model’s assumption about how much the stock might move (Implied Volatility).
Worked example
The 100 call with the stock at $108, 30 days left and IV at 30%, priced by the model this page uses.
Interactive lesson
Change stock, strike, time and volatility and watch the premium split between the two bars.
Change pricing inputs
The model isolates how stock price, strike, time, and implied volatility can affect theoretical premium.
Decompose an option premium
Separate current exercise value from all remaining value.
Calculate intrinsic value
Use the call or put intrinsic formula from the stock and strike.
Read the full premium
Use an executable quote when trading; theoretical value is only a reference.
Subtract intrinsic
Premium minus intrinsic gives extrinsic value.
Identify the drivers
Time, implied volatility, rates, dividends, and market supply and demand can affect extrinsic value.
Premium components
Lesson rule
Common mistakes
Completion standard
The drill asks for the split both ways round — an option with intrinsic value and one without — and for what is left at expiration.

Added instead of subtracted. Extrinsic value is premium minus intrinsic value.

Out-of-the-money options, and a strike exactly at the stock price
A put whose strike is above the stock is in the money and has intrinsic value of strike minus stock.
All options with more than 30 days to expiration
Time affects extrinsic value. Intrinsic value depends only on stock versus strike.
Out-of-the-money options have no intrinsic value, and neither does a strike exactly at the stock; both can still carry extrinsic value.

Nothing converts. Extrinsic value is the price of remaining possibility, and at expiration none remains.

It falls to zero

Learn the underlying, call or put type, strike, expiration, premium, contract multiplier, holder rights, writer obligations, and contract-level cash flows.
Core concepts
Terms first, then who owes what, then the multiplier that turns a quote into dollars.
Contract terms
An option specifies an underlying, option type, strike price, expiration, multiplier, exercise style, and settlement terms.
Holder and writer
The holder buys a right. The writer receives premium and accepts an obligation if assigned.
Contract multiplier
Standard equity contracts commonly represent 100 shares, while adjusted contracts can use different deliverables.
Interactive lesson
Pick a side and a type, set the strike, premium and quantity, and read the right or obligation and the dollars that move.
Decode the contract
Select the holder or writer position and calculate the contract-level result.
Read an option contract
Decode the legal and economic terms before evaluating a chart or strategy.
Identify the underlying and deliverable
Confirm the security and the exact shares, cash, or adjusted deliverable represented by one contract.
Identify call or put
A call relates to buying at the strike; a put relates to selling at the strike.
Identify long or short
Long means holder rights; short means writer obligations and assignment exposure.
Convert quotes to contract dollars
Multiply per-share premium and payoff by the contract multiplier and quantity.
Contract terms and obligations
Lesson rule
Common mistakes
Completion standard
The drill asks for the holder’s right, the writer’s obligation on assignment, and the dollar cost of a quoted premium; answer each without the multiplier being supplied.

Two sides exist here by construction: the premium was paid to a writer who accepted the obligation to sell at the strike. Structurally the premium is the price the two sides agreed for that right, not a forecast of what the underlying does. The reading fails at expiration below breakeven, where the right is worth less than what was paid for it.

The usual reading is that the premium is what both sides agreed the right to sell was worth, not a measure of how far price would fall. Above breakeven at expiration that right is worth less than its cost.

Buy the deliverable shares at the strike
Sell shares at the strike

Receive the stock for free
Assignment means paying the strike for the shares — $10,000 for one 100-strike contract — whatever the market price is at the time.
Cancel the option premium
The premium was received when the contract was written and is kept whatever happens. Assignment adds an obligation; it does not undo the premium.

Multiplied by 10. The standard equity multiplier is 100 shares, not 10.
Multiplied by 1,000 — that would be ten contracts. One standard contract is 100 shares.

A put writer is assigned to BUY at the strike. Selling at the strike is the call writer’s obligation.

Combine the underlying thesis, strategy selection, strikes, expiration, liquidity, volatility context, maximum risk, event handling, and exit conditions into one scored options plan.
Core concepts
Thesis, structure, contract, risk, exit: in that order, every time.
Underlying thesis first
The option is the instrument used to express a defined market thesis; it does not replace the thesis.
Contract and strategy fit
Direction, target, timing, IV, strike geometry, and liquidity must be internally consistent.
Predefined risk and exit
Maximum position risk, invalidation, event handling, and exit conditions must be written before entry.
Interactive lesson
Load a preset or fill the plan, evaluate it against ten checks, and export the result. Evaluate the bullish preset first: it is the worked example, and every check prints its own arithmetic.
Trade-plan inputs
Build a complete options trade plan
Use the same sequence for every candidate so weak plans are rejected before entry.
Define the underlying thesis
State direction, target, invalidation, expected duration, and no-trade conditions.
Choose the strategy
Match directional and volatility exposure to the thesis.
Select executable contracts
Verify expiration, strikes, bid-ask spread, quantity, and event timing.
Approve risk and management
Confirm maximum loss, account risk, target payoff, assignment exposure, and exit rules.
Plan quality decisions
Lesson rule
Common mistakes
Completion standard
The drill asks which figure the risk budget compares for a share-backed position; it is the one Trade Setup and Execution defined, the loss if the invalidation is hit.

A long call is premium paid to a writer who accepted the obligation to deliver at the strike, so the whole debit is at risk. Read the red invalidation line as the level that ends the plan, not as a stop the contract itself enforces.

A long put is premium paid to a writer who accepted the obligation to buy at the strike, so the whole debit is at risk. Read the red invalidation line as the level that ends the plan, not as a stop the contract itself enforces.

Two counterparties are involved: one leg was paid for, and part of its payoff was sold to the other. That is normally read as trading away the far side of the move to lower the debit, so the payoff stops at the short strike however far past it the underlying goes.

The upside beyond the short strike was sold to someone who paid premium for the right to buy the shares there. This plan is long stock first, so the red invalidation line rather than the premium is what defines where the downside thesis has failed.

This plan agrees in advance to be the buyer at the strike, and the premium is what the other side paid for the right to make that happen. The gain is fixed at that premium, so read the red invalidation line as the level where being that buyer stops matching the thesis.

The credit is the price agreed for accepting the obligation between the two strikes, and the long leg is a counterparty paid to cap what that obligation can cost. The maximum is known from the agreement in advance, so read the red invalidation line as the level that ends the plan rather than as a limit the structure imposes.

Wait or reject the contract

Enter and adjust later

Reduce size or choose a lower-risk structure
Raise the target only

Use a market order

Only ticker and direction

The premium is the cost. A plan needs what the cost buys, when it expires, and what ends it.

Combine time decay and implied-volatility sensitivity, compare linear Greek estimates with full theoretical repricing, and identify interaction effects.
Core concepts
Theta prices a day; vega prices an IV point; both are local to the current state.
Theta
Theta estimates the option-price change associated with one day passing while other inputs are unchanged.
Vega
Vega estimates the option-price change for a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility.
Local estimates
Greeks describe sensitivity at the current state and must be recalculated after meaningful changes.

Evaluate theta and vega together

That is one point. Five points is 0.12 × 5.

It applies; it is just local. It describes the next day, not every day.
Theta changes as time and other inputs change
The multiplier is always one
The multiplier scales both figures the same way and cannot create a difference between them.

The strike never changes. What changes is the sensitivity at the new state.
