Construct bull put and bear call credit spreads, calculate net credit, fixed maximum profit, defined maximum loss, breakeven, and the protection supplied by the long leg.
Core concepts
Sell one option, buy a further one: a credit now, a defined worst case.
Bull put spread
Sell a higher-strike put and buy a lower-strike put with the same expiration.
Bear call spread
Sell a lower-strike call and buy a higher-strike call with the same expiration.
Defined risk
Maximum profit is the credit; maximum loss is strike width minus credit at expiration.
Worked example
The default bull put spread: short the 100 put at $4.00, long the 90 put at $1.50, one spread, stock $103 at expiration.

Credit-spread structure
The long option limits the short option’s adverse-direction risk.
Build a credit spread
The spread receives limited premium in exchange for a larger but defined adverse outcome.
Choose direction and range
Bull put spreads require price to remain above a threshold; bear call spreads require price to remain below.
Place the short strike
The short strike defines the main obligation and breakeven relationship.
Buy the protective strike
The long leg caps loss beyond its strike.
Compare reward with maximum loss
Do not evaluate win rate without the credit-to-risk relationship and tail outcomes.

$120 is the credit, the maximum PROFIT. The loss is what the width can cost beyond it.
$500 is the width, the most the spread can cost to close. The credit already received offsets $120 of it.
Added the credit to the width. It offsets the loss; subtract it.
What is maximum profit for a credit spread?
The credit is the whole of what was received. Once both legs expire worthless there is nothing more to earn.
The net credit received
The width is the most the spread can COST. The credit is the most it can make.
The long premium was paid, not received. The net credit is short premium minus long premium.
Maximum expiration profit is the initial net credit.
Why is the long leg included?
To eliminate all assignment events
The short leg can still be assigned. The long leg limits what that costs; it does not prevent it.
To cap adverse-direction risk at the strike width less credit
To guarantee a profit
Nothing guarantees a profit. The long leg buys a ceiling on the loss, and it is paid for out of the credit.
To increase unlimited upside
A credit spread has no upside beyond the credit. The long leg is protection, not participation.
The protective long option limits loss beyond its strike, creating defined maximum risk.
Bull put spread: short the 100 put at $4.00, long the 90 put at $1.50. What is the expiration breakeven?
Used the short premium alone. The long put costs $1.50, so the credit is $2.50 and breakeven is 100 − 2.50.
Added the credit to the strike — that is the bear CALL pattern. A put spread breaks even below the short strike.
Subtracted from the long strike. The long strike marks the maximum loss; the breakeven sits on the short strike’s side.
Short strike minus net credit: 100 − (4.00 − 1.50) = $97.50.

Core concepts
Buy one option, sell a further one: lower cost, capped reward.
Bull call spread
Buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call with the same expiration.
Bear put spread
Buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put with the same expiration.
Defined outcome range
Net debit is maximum loss; strike width minus debit is maximum profit at expiration.

Choose direction

Set the long strike
The long option provides the main directional exposure.
Set the short strike
The short option reduces cost and defines the maximum-reward boundary.

Calculate +DI, −DI, and ADX; distinguish directional dominance from trend strength; adjust the lookback and threshold; and compare the indicator in trending and ranging price series.
Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
Directional movement

+DI and −DI compare smoothed positive and negative directional movement with smoothed true range — a bar’s own high-low span or its distance from the previous close, whichever is largest. Average True Range builds ATR from that same quantity.
Trend strength
ADX smooths the separation between +DI and −DI. It measures directional persistence, not bullish or bearish direction.
Threshold use
A threshold such as 20 or 25 is a rule choice, not a universal boundary. Rising and falling ADX also require context.
Interactive lesson
Change the inputs, inspect the calculation, and compare the indicator with the underlying price data.
Separate direction and strength
Change the scenario and confirm that a high ADX can occur in either an uptrend or a downtrend.
Read ADX and DI together
Use separate outputs for separate questions: direction, strength, and change in strength.
Calculate directional movement
Compare current highs and lows with the prior bar to derive positive and negative movement.
Normalize with true range
Divide smoothed directional movement by smoothed true range so +DI and −DI are percentages of the movement available, comparable across instruments.
Calculate ADX
Smooth the relative separation between the two DI lines.
Interpret all three
Use +DI versus −DI for directional dominance and ADX for strength relative to the chosen threshold.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Each rally has stalled below the one before it, and the declines have carried further than the recoveries have retraced. The usual reading is that supply is being met at progressively lower prices and that buyers appear only further down; it interprets the shape and does not measure who transacted. A close above the most recent lower high removes the evidence for it.

Price has turned back from a similar upper area and a similar lower area more than once, and neither edge has produced follow-through. Structurally this says the two sides are matched near the boundaries: sellers keep appearing near the top of the band and buyers near the bottom, and neither has held price beyond it. Acceptance outside an edge, rather than a single probe through it, would replace this reading.

The advance ends, then price gives up several times more than any pullback took during the advance, and only after that does a rally fail well below the high. Order matters here: the standard reading is a change of character, because the decline broke below the last low that had held on the way up before any lower high existed, rather than a lower high that came first. A recovery back above that failed high would return the chart to the earlier reading.

Price steps up between one close and the next open and never trades in the space between: the bar that follows opens well above the previous close and its whole range sits above it. The conventional reading is that the repricing happened while the market was closed, so no participant defended the levels inside the gap — which is exactly why the gap belongs in that bar's true range. The reading says nothing about whether the gap holds; a close back below the previous close would say it did not.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Price has crossed the same broad band repeatedly, and each move to one edge has been given back to the other. That is normally read as two-sided activity with a large amplitude rather than direction: the swing size says how far price travels between turns and says nothing about which side is prevailing. There is a slight net drift across the window, but it is small beside the swings; read the width, not the direction.

Bars are small, closes sit near the middle of each bar, and the drift across the window is gentle. This is normally read as two-sided agreement on price: neither side is pressing, so each bar's range is a fraction of what the high-volatility scenario shows. A reading of calm says nothing about the direction of the next move, only that it will start from a compressed range; a bar several times the recent size would end it.

Nothing in true range uses volume.
RSI is built from closes; true range from the high, the low and the previous close.
True range includes gap distance and uses the maximum of all three components.
ATR rises sharply during a selloff. What does ATR itself say about direction?
The decline must continue
ATR is unsigned. The same rise would appear in a sharp rally.
Nothing; ATR measures movement magnitude
A rally is guaranteed
The same problem in the other direction: ATR carries no sign.
The market is oversold
Oversold is an oscillator word. ATR has no scale of that kind.
ATR is unsigned and can rise in rallies, declines, or unstable ranges.
Why use ATR as a percentage of price?
To estimate directional momentum
Dividing by price removes scale, not sign. ATR % is still unsigned.
To compare volatility across different price scales
No earnings enter the calculation.
Gaps are already inside true range. The division does not touch them.
Normalization makes a two-dollar ATR interpretable relative to the instrument price.
Which formula defines true range?
Minimum of three range values
The minimum would hide a gap. The definition takes the maximum so the gap counts.
Maximum of high-low, |high-prev close|, and |low-prev close|
Average close over 14 bars
That is a simple moving average of closes.
High plus low plus volume
Neither a sum nor volume: true range is the largest of three distances.
The maximum captures both intrabar movement and gaps from the prior close.
Previous close 100.00; today’s high 103.00 and low 101.00. What is today’s true range?
2.00 is high minus low. The bar opened above yesterday’s close, and |high − previous close| = 3.00 is larger.
1.00 is |low − previous close|, the smallest of the three.
The three components are compared, not added.

Place the bands

For the first two thirds of the chart price stays inside a band of about four points with unusually small bars; the final third more than doubles the average bar range and leaves the band. Contraction like this is normally read as agreement on price rather than pressure building in a direction, which is why it carries no directional information on its own and the expansion has to be read separately. A return into the narrow band would make the expansion a single excursion rather than a change of regime.

Price has turned back from a similar upper area and a similar lower area more than once, and neither edge has produced follow-through. Structurally this says the two sides are matched near the boundaries: sellers keep appearing near the top of the band and buyers near the bottom, and neither has held price beyond it. Acceptance outside an edge, rather than a single probe through it, would replace this reading.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Price has crossed the same broad band repeatedly, and each move to one edge has been given back to the other. That is normally read as two-sided activity with a large amplitude rather than direction: the swing size says how far price travels between turns and says nothing about which side is prevailing. There is a slight net drift across the window, but it is small beside the swings; read the width, not the direction.

clauses.expected: Combining Indicators Without Redundancy

Group indicators by function, compare normalized outputs and correlations, build a compact set for a defined purpose, and avoid stacking multiple transformations of the same price behavior as false confirmation.
Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
Functional families
Trend, momentum, volatility, strength, and breakout indicators answer different questions.
Redundancy
Indicators built from similar inputs and smoothing can move together. Agreement may be repeated evidence rather than independent confirmation.
Purpose-first selection
Choose the minimum set needed to define regime, trigger, volatility, or another explicit function.
Interactive lesson
Change the inputs, inspect the calculation, and compare the indicator with the underlying price data.
Build a compact indicator set
Select indicators, then inspect family coverage and output similarity.
Use two to four indicators with distinct jobs.
Build an indicator set
Assign one clear job to every selected calculation.
Define the decision problem
State whether you need trend state, momentum trigger, volatility filter, breakout boundary, or another function.
Select one primary tool per job
Avoid adding a second indicator unless it answers a different question or improves robustness.
Check shared inputs and correlation
Identify calculations derived from the same close series and compare whether outputs move almost identically.
Remove unused information
If an indicator never changes a rule or decision, remove it from the system.
Indicator families and redundancy
Lesson rule
Common mistakes
Completion standard
Choose a market purpose, select a compact set, identify each family, inspect high correlations, remove redundant tools, and explain exactly how each remaining output changes a decision.

Track rolling highest highs and lowest lows, compare current-bar and prior-channel calculations, detect completed breakout events, and state which bars define the boundary a close is tested against.
Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
Rolling extremes
The upper channel is the highest high and the lower channel is the lowest low over the selected lookback.
Prior-channel signal
Using the channel calculated through the previous bar allows the current close to be tested against an already known boundary.
Stepwise updates
Channel levels can remain flat for many bars and then jump when a new extreme enters or an old extreme leaves the window.

The first stretch is a narrow band that neither side could leave; the move that follows leaves it and keeps going. Read conventionally, one side has finally been able to move price beyond the level that had been capping it. Note what is absent: there is no run of rising lows building into the break and no return to test the old band afterwards, so nothing here shows pressure accumulating first, and a sustained move back inside that band would say the break was not accepted.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Price has turned back from a similar upper area and a similar lower area more than once, and neither edge has produced follow-through. Structurally this says the two sides are matched near the boundaries: sellers keep appearing near the top of the band and buyers near the bottom, and neither has held price beyond it. Acceptance outside an edge, rather than a single probe through it, would replace this reading.

The advance ends, then price gives up several times more than any pullback took during the advance, and only after that does a rally fail well below the high. Order matters here: the standard reading is a change of character, because the decline broke below the last low that had held on the way up before any lower high existed, rather than a lower high that came first. A recovery back above that failed high would return the chart to the earlier reading.

No averaging. The channel is the extreme itself.
The highest high in the selected lookback
ATR is not an input to the channel.
RSI plays no part in it.
The channel tracks rolling price extremes.
Why use the prior channel for a breakout comparison?
To compare the current bar with a boundary known before it formed
To include future prices
The opposite: the prior channel deliberately excludes the bar being tested.
The channel is not a volatility measure.
Volume is not involved.
The current high can otherwise redefine the same upper boundary being tested.
A close above the prior upper channel establishes what?
A new rolling breakout event under the rule
In the range scenario new extremes fail more often than they run.
A new extreme says nothing about range size.
A fundamental valuation change
Price extremes carry no information about value.
It satisfies the defined price event, but continuation still requires risk and context rules.
Increasing the Donchian lookback usually does what to the channel?
Uses a broader history and often produces fewer new extremes
More bars, not fewer.
Makes it a momentum oscillator
It stays a channel of extremes.
Removes all false breaks
Fewer signals, not none.
Longer windows retain older extremes and normally require a larger move to establish a new one.
The channel is calculated including the current bar. Can a close ever be above the upper channel?
No: the close is at most the bar’s high, which is already part of the channel
Yes, on any strong up bar
The strong bar’s own high becomes the upper channel. The close cannot exceed the bar’s high.
Only when the lookback is short
Length does not matter. The current bar’s high is in every window that includes it.
Only on a gap
A gap moves the whole bar, including its high, and the high is in the channel.

A close is never above its own bar’s high, and a channel that includes the current bar is at least that high. A breakout rule written against it never fires — which is why the signal uses the prior channel.

clauses.expected: Technical Indicators
Calculate and interpret trend, momentum, and volatility indicators, and evaluate indicator rules.
Subject
Trading
Lessons
Format
Interactive
Overview
What it teaches

The transformation itself — lookback, responsiveness, warm-up, context. Trend: simple and exponential moving averages and the crossover filters built on them. What momentum and trend strength actually measure: RSI, the stochastic oscillator, MACD, and the directional-movement family. Volatility and the channels drawn from it: true range and ATR, Bollinger Bands, Keltner and Donchian channels. The reading skills that decide whether any of it helps: rate of change, divergence, redundancy, regime selection, and deterministic rules.
Who it is for

Anyone who has an indicator on their chart and could not, right now, write down its formula or say what makes it lag. It assumes you can read a chart and starts from the calculation, so no prior indicator knowledge is needed. It also suits the reader who has six indicators open and suspects — correctly — that four of them are showing the same thing twice.
Concept dependencies

Moving-average smoothing is the basis of the envelopes that use it. Indicator divergence needs the RSI, stochastic and MACD oscillators. Indicator-Based Trading Rules asks for trend, strength and volatility filters: moving-average trend filters, directional movement, ATR and the Bollinger, Keltner and Donchian channels. Reading, combining and selecting indicators connects their formulas to context.
Lessons
Explanations, examples, interactive tools, and practice questions.
16 lessons

Educational use only — nothing here is trading advice. This course teaches indicator calculation, interpretation, and rule specification. It does not provide live data, trading signals, profitability claims, or personalized investment advice. Backtesting and Trading Systems covers backtesting, costs, and robustness; Algorithmic and Automated Trading covers automation.

Calculation scope. Every price series in these lessons is a deterministic synthetic example. The course uses standard conventions — an equal-weight rolling window for the SMA, an EMA seeded with the first complete SMA, Wilder smoothing for RSI, ATR and ADX, a population standard deviation for Bollinger Bands, and a prior completed channel for Donchian breakout signals. Small differences from charting platforms can occur because of source, seed, rounding, missing-bar, adjustment, or incomplete-bar conventions. Indicators transform historical price data; they do not guarantee future direction.

Foundations

What an indicator actually is before any of them has a name: a formula applied to bars you already have. Why the lookback you pick is the whole trade-off between responsiveness and noise, why every indicator has a warm-up period during which it has nothing to say, and why the same reading means different things in different market context.

Trend

Moving-average smoothing supports the trend filters and the envelopes that use it. Two ways to average a price series and what changing the source or the lookback does to each; then the trend-state model you get by putting a fast average against a slow one — including the whipsaws it produces, and the difference between a rule that confirms late and a prediction that arrives early.

Momentum and trend strength

Four more readings of the same bars. Three of them are momentum measures — RSI, the stochastic, and MACD — and the fourth is not: the directional-movement family separates which side is dominant from how strong the move is at all. These lessons are about thresholds, and about why a level that means "stretched" in a range means "trending" a week later.

Volatility and channels

How far price moves, kept strictly separate from which way it moves. True range and the ATR built on it describe volatility measurement. The channels use distinct estimates: standard deviation around an average, an ATR envelope around an EMA, and the pure high-low channel that needs no average at all. Three envelopes, three different definitions of "outside the band".

Recommended background

Chart reading is assumed; no prior indicator knowledge is needed. Volume-derived tools belong to Volume and Order Flow. Volume and Order Flow covers relative volume, on-balance volume, accumulation/distribution, session and anchored VWAP, volume profile and value area, the tape, footprint and bid-ask delta, cumulative delta and the order book. Technical Indicators deliberately stops short of those volume-derived tools; they belong to Volume and Order Flow.
Interop
Indicator-Based Trading Rules exports a rule set

The specification lesson documents a trading system. It turns what you have learned into explicit conditions, checks them against each other, and then hands the whole rule set back to you as a file, so it can outlive the browser tab it was written in.
Format: technical-indicator-rule-v1
What comes out of it

Indicator-Based Trading Rules takes the direction, the trend, strength and volatility filters, the entry trigger, the exit and the parameters you set, marks the entry and exit events on a synthetic series, and exports the whole specification as a JSON document stamped technical-indicator-rule-v1 . The file records the data assumptions it was written against, the rule itself, and diagnostics — the clarity score, whether direction and trend agree, and the events it produced — so a rule you wrote can be read back later and reproduced exactly.

The schema linked beside this is the contract for that shape. It is worth reading if you would rather keep your rules in your own notebook or script: match the shape and the same fields carry over. Note what the export deliberately does NOT contain — any measure of profitability. The diagnostics carry performanceEvaluated: false on purpose, so a rule that is merely well specified is never mistaken for a rule that has been shown to work. Everything runs in your browser — nothing is uploaded, and there is no account anywhere in this course.

A raw price series drawn as bars across the full width, with the opening stretch shaded as a warm-up period, and a smoothed indicator line that only begins once enough bars exist to compute it.

One price series with two averages drawn over it: a simple moving average as a solid line lagging well behind the turns, and an exponential moving average as a dashed line tracking the same turns more closely.

A fast average and a slow average crossing three times: an upward cross marked in green, then a shaded stretch where the two braid together and cross twice in quick succession, marked as whipsaw, then a downward cross marked in red.

An oscillator bounded between zero and one hundred, with dashed threshold lines at seventy and thirty and a midline at fifty. The wave pushes above seventy once and below thirty once, and then stays pressed against the upper threshold without turning.

On the left, a vertical high-to-low range bar with the closing price marked near its top to show range position. On the right, the resulting percent K line with its smoothed percent D line, moving between dashed bands at eighty and twenty.

The three MACD components drawn together: a histogram of bars growing and shrinking either side of a dashed zero line, the MACD line crossing that zero line, and a slower signal line crossing the MACD line at a marked point.

Three lines on one panel: a green plus DI and a red minus DI crossing each other to show which side is dominant, and a separate ADX line that only rises above a dashed threshold once the two have separated.

Two candles with a gap between them, showing that true range is measured from the previous close rather than from the current bar's own low, with the resulting average true range plotted as a separate rising series beneath.

A price line inside a standard-deviation envelope around a moving-average basis. The bands pinch tight through a contraction in the middle of the chart and flare wide afterwards, with a marked touch of the upper band.

An exponential moving average with an evenly spaced average-true-range envelope drawn either side of it, staying far more parallel than the standard-deviation bands beside it, which are drawn faintly for comparison. A break above the upper channel is marked.

A staircase channel of rolling highest highs and lowest lows that only steps when a new extreme is made, with price breaking above the prior completed channel at a marked bar and the channel boundary stepping up only afterwards.

A price line above, and beneath it a rate-of-change oscillator that swings either side of a dashed zero line, shaded green where it is positive and red where it is negative, with the zero crossings marked.

Price making a second peak higher than the first, joined by a dashed line, while the oscillator beneath makes its second peak lower than the first, joined by a matching dashed line. The two aligned swings are marked as a divergence awaiting price confirmation.

Three small indicator panels side by side. The first two trace almost the same shape and are marked with a red cross as redundant; the third traces a different shape and is marked with a green check as the one that adds information.

Four market-regime tiles, each holding a small characteristic price shape: a trend, a range, a contraction, and a high-volatility series. The trend tile is selected and highlighted, showing that the choice of indicator follows the regime.

Three stacked condition rows for a trend filter, a strength filter and a volatility filter feeding into a price series where an entry is marked in green and an exit in red, with the whole thing exported as a braced JSON document.

clauses.expected: Indicator-Based Trading Rules

Convert indicator observations into deterministic conditions, apply trend, strength, and volatility filters, visualize entry and exit events, detect contradictory rules, and export a machine-readable specification.
Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
Boolean conditions
A rule must resolve to true or false from known bar data and explicit parameters.
Separate filter, trigger, and exit
A filter defines when a setup is allowed, a trigger defines the event, and an exit defines when the position state ends.
No performance claim
A logically complete rule can still lose money. Performance, robustness, costs, and overfitting belong to later testing courses.
Interactive lesson
Change the inputs, inspect the calculation, and compare the indicator with the underlying price data.
Build deterministic conditions
Choose a direction, filter, trigger, optional regime constraints, and exit.
Rule specification
Interpretation
Write an indicator rule specification
Every condition must be computable without subjective chart interpretation.
Define the data and timing
Specify instrument, timeframe, adjusted data policy, and completed-bar timing.
Define filters
State trend, strength, volatility, and any market-regime requirements.
Define the trigger
Use an exact crossover, threshold transition, or rolling-boundary event.
Define state and exit
Prevent duplicate entries while active and specify exact exit, reset, and invalidation behavior.
Deterministic indicator rules
Lesson rule
Common mistakes
Completion standard
Export the rule, verify that all conditions and parameters are explicit, inspect contradictory combinations, and confirm that the same bar sequence produces the same entries and exits.

Compare aligned price swings with RSI or MACD histogram swings, classify regular bullish and bearish divergence, distinguish divergence from disagreement at unrelated bars, and require price confirmation.
Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
Aligned swings
A valid comparison uses two corresponding price swing lows or highs and the oscillator values at those same bars.
Regular divergence
Bullish divergence pairs a lower price low with a higher oscillator low; bearish divergence pairs a higher price high with a lower oscillator high.
Warning, not trigger
Divergence shows that price and the selected momentum measure changed differently. It does not define entry, invalidation, or timing by itself.
Interactive lesson

Classify the relationship

Validate a divergence claim
Use aligned, meaningful swings and describe the exact relationship.
Choose two price swings
Compare low with low for bullish divergence or high with high for bearish divergence.
Align oscillator bars
Read the oscillator at the same two bars rather than selecting unrelated extrema.
Compare direction
State whether price made a higher or lower swing and whether the oscillator did the same or opposite.
Wait for confirmation
Require a predefined price-structure or entry event after the divergence observation.

Price reached a lower low while the oscillator did not. Read conventionally, the second decline carried price further but was made with less downside momentum behind it than the first, which is normally described as selling pressure weakening relative to the move it is producing. This is a condition, not a trigger: it can persist across several more lows, and a further low with a lower oscillator reading removes it.

Price reached a higher high while the oscillator did not. Read conventionally, the second advance carried price further but was made with less upside momentum behind it than the first, which is normally described as buying pressure weakening relative to the move it is producing. This is a condition, not a trigger: it can persist across several more highs, and a further high with a higher oscillator reading removes it.

Price and the oscillator moved the same way between the two marked swings, so there is no divergence to read. Aligned swings are the ordinary case: the transform is agreeing with the price move, and nothing is being contradicted. Reading a signal into this would mean treating two points that agree as though they disagreed.

Any two visually convenient oscillator points
That is the mistake the lesson names: an oscillator extreme at a different bar from the price swing is not a comparison.

Only the most recent bar
A divergence is a relation between two swings. One bar is not enough.
Volume is not part of the comparison.

Regime changes signal behavior
Trend-following calculations tend to whipsaw in ranges, while mean-reversion thresholds can remain extreme in trends.
Volatility is a separate dimension

Selection follows purpose

Reassess on regime change
Stop applying the old interpretation when price behavior no longer matches the assumptions.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Price has turned back from a similar upper area and a similar lower area more than once, and neither edge has produced follow-through. Structurally this says the two sides are matched near the boundaries: sellers keep appearing near the top of the band and buyers near the bottom, and neither has held price beyond it. Acceptance outside an edge, rather than a single probe through it, would replace this reading.

Price turns near a broad upper area and a broad lower area, but each turn comes at a slightly different level and the bars average around four and a half points. The reading is a range whose edges are not reliable: both sides are active and neither is defending a fixed boundary, so a level here is an area rather than a line. A close that holds well beyond either area, rather than another overshoot, would end the range reading.

For the first two thirds of the chart price stays inside a band of about four points with unusually small bars; the final third more than doubles the average bar range and leaves the band. Contraction like this is normally read as agreement on price rather than pressure building in a direction, which is why it carries no directional information on its own and the expansion has to be read separately. A return into the narrow band would make the expansion a single excursion rather than a change of regime.

The advance ends, then price gives up several times more than any pullback took during the advance, and only after that does a rally fail well below the high. Order matters here: the standard reading is a change of character, because the decline broke below the last low that had held on the way up before any lower high existed, rather than a lower high that came first. A recovery back above that failed high would return the chart to the earlier reading.

Construct an EMA-centered ATR envelope, change the basis and volatility settings, compare Keltner Channels with Bollinger Bands, and define channel-break conditions precisely.
Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
EMA basis
A common modern Keltner formulation centers the channel on an exponential moving average.
ATR envelope
Outer bands are placed a selected ATR multiple above and below the basis.
Different volatility input
Keltner Channels use average true range, while Bollinger Bands use standard deviation. They can contract and expand differently.
Interactive lesson
Change the inputs, inspect the calculation, and compare the indicator with the underlying price data.
Change basis and ATR settings
Period and multiplier control how quickly the center and envelope respond.
Build a Keltner Channel
Document the exact formulation because historical and platform variants exist.
Choose the centerline
Select the EMA source and period.
Calculate ATR
Choose the true-range smoothing period and convention.
Set the multiplier
Place the upper and lower bands at a fixed ATR multiple from the EMA.
Define the event
Use an exact close, intrabar touch, re-entry, slope, or width condition rather than the word breakout alone.

The first stretch is a narrow band that neither side could leave; the move that follows leaves it and keeps going. For the first two thirds of the chart price stays inside a band of about four points with unusually small bars; the final third more than doubles the average bar range and leaves the band. Contraction like this is normally read as agreement on price rather than pressure building in a direction, which is why it carries no directional information on its own and the expansion has to be read separately. A return into the narrow band would make the expansion a single excursion rather than a change of regime.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. Price has crossed the same broad band repeatedly, and each move to one edge has been given back to the other. That is normally read as two-sided activity with a large amplitude rather than direction: the swing size says how far price travels between turns and says nothing about which side is prevailing. There is a slight net drift across the window, but it is small beside the swings; read the width, not the direction.

Separate the MACD line, signal line, and histogram; change the three periods; identify zero-line and signal-line events; and name what each component measures.
Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
MACD line
The MACD line is the difference between a fast EMA and a slow EMA.
Signal line
The signal line is an EMA of the MACD line, adding another layer of smoothing.
Histogram
The histogram is MACD minus signal. It shows the distance between the two lines, not trading volume.
Interactive lesson
Change the inputs, inspect the calculation, and compare the indicator with the underlying price data.
Change all three periods
Keep the fast period below the slow period and observe how shorter settings increase event frequency.
Interpret MACD components
Do not collapse three different calculations into a single vague bullish or bearish label.
Compare fast and slow EMAs
The sign of the MACD line reflects which EMA is higher.
Compare MACD with signal
A crossover shows that MACD changed relative to its own smoothed average.
Read histogram direction
Histogram expansion or contraction describes changing separation between MACD and signal.
Use price context
Confirm whether the event occurs in a trend, a range, near a structural level, or after a large delayed move.

The advance ends, then price gives up several times more than any pullback took during the advance, and only after that does a rally fail well below the high. Order matters here: the standard reading is a change of character, because the decline broke below the last low that had held on the way up before any lower high existed, rather than a lower high that came first. A recovery back above that failed high would return the chart to the earlier reading.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Price has turned back from a similar upper area and a similar lower area more than once, and neither edge has produced follow-through. Structurally this says the two sides are matched near the boundaries: sellers keep appearing near the top of the band and buyers near the bottom, and neither has held price beyond it. Acceptance outside an edge, rather than a single probe through it, would replace this reading.

Read conventionally, one side has finally been able to move price beyond the level that had been capping it. What is the MACD line?
Fast EMA minus slow EMA
No volume enters MACD anywhere.
Both are oscillators, but neither is an input to MACD.
That is the bar’s range, the first true-range component.
The main line is the difference between two exponential moving averages.
What does the MACD histogram measure?
The bars look like volume and this is the most common misreading. They are MACD minus signal.
MACD line minus signal line
Price minus strike price
That is an option’s intrinsic value.
ATR divided by price
That is ATR %. The histogram has no volatility input.
Its sign and size show the separation between MACD and its signal average.
MACD is above zero. What does that mean?
Fast EMA is above slow EMA
The fast EMA can sit above the slow one for many bars while price falls toward both.
Signal line is always positive
The signal is an EMA of MACD and lags it. MACD can cross zero before the signal does.
The sign of MACD says which EMA is higher. It says nothing about range size.
A positive fast-minus-slow difference means the fast EMA is higher.
Why are very short MACD settings usually more active?
They include future data
No setting sees ahead. Shorter EMAs simply react sooner to the closes they already have.
Their EMAs react more quickly to recent price changes
They remove all smoothing
An EMA of period 3 still smooths; it just weights the newest close heavily.
They use order flow
MACD is computed from closes only.
Shorter exponential windows respond faster and create more frequent state changes.

MACD 1.50, histogram 0.50
MACD 0.50, histogram 1.50
Reversed. MACD is fast − slow = 1.50; the histogram is MACD − signal = 0.50.
MACD 1.50, histogram 1.00
1.00 is the signal line itself. The histogram is the gap between MACD and signal: 1.50 − 1.00.

MACD is a difference, not a sum: 101.50 − 100.00 = 1.50.

Trend state
Fast above slow defines one state; fast below slow defines the opposite state. The rule is explicit but delayed.
Crossover event
A crossover occurs only when the relative order changes, not on every bar that remains above or below.
Whipsaw risk
Sideways or rapidly alternating price can produce repeated crossings without a durable trend.

Define a crossover rule

Set fast and slow periods

Choose SMA or EMA
Do not mix calculation methods unless the rule explicitly requires it.
Define the event
Use the first completed bar where fast moves from one side of slow to the other.

Count rapid opposite crosses and evaluate the rule separately in trending and ranging conditions.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

The band is about as wide as an ordinary range, but price crosses it more than twice as often and turns quickly at both edges. The usual reading is that neither side is holding what it takes: each push is met and reversed within a few bars, so an extreme here is a test rather than a resolution. A move that leaves one edge and stays away longer than the previous swings would break the pattern.

The advance ends, then price gives up several times more than any pullback took during the advance, and only after that does a rally fail well below the high. Order matters here: the standard reading is a change of character, because the decline broke below the last low that had held on the way up before any lower high existed, rather than a lower high that came first. A recovery back above that failed high would return the chart to the earlier reading.

The first stretch is a narrow band that neither side could leave; the move that follows leaves it and keeps going. Read conventionally, one side has finally been able to move price beyond the level that had been capping it. Note what is absent: there is no run of rising lows building into the break and no return to test the old band afterwards, so nothing here shows pressure accumulating first, and a sustained move back inside that band would say the break was not accepted.

The fast average crossed above the slow average yesterday and remains above today. How many bullish crossover events occurred?
The transition happened yesterday: fast moved from at-or-below to above. That is one event.
Today is the same state continuing. A state that persists is not a second event.
One on every bar above
That is the mistake the lesson names: counting state as signal. The event is the change of order, once.
The crossover is the single transition from fast at or below slow to fast above slow.
Why do crossover systems often struggle in ranges?
Ranges remove historical data
The data is all there. The problem is that both averages sit inside the range and price keeps crossing them.
Price repeatedly moves around both averages
They calculate on every bar. In a range they converge, so small moves flip their order.
The slow average becomes volume weighted
Neither average uses volume. The formula does not change with the regime; only its behaviour does.
Alternating price can repeatedly reverse the relative order and create whipsaws.
A bullish crossover usually occurs after price has already risen. What does that illustrate?
Look-ahead is using information that was not available at the time. A late signal is the opposite problem.
The lag says the move began earlier. It says nothing about whether it continues.
Lag is a property of averaging past closes. It happens at any volatility.
Both moving averages summarize historical prices, so the confirmation commonly follows the initial turn.
Which rule is most precise?
Buy when the averages look good
“Look good” cannot be computed. Two people would fire on different bars.
Buy on a completed bar where EMA 10 crosses above EMA 30
Buy near the blue line
A colour is not a calculation, and “near” has no number.
Buy whenever price feels strong
Nothing in that sentence resolves to true or false from bar data.
It specifies calculation method, periods, direction, and bar-completion condition.
In this lesson’s lab, which event is counted as a whipsaw?
Any bar where the fast average is above the slow one
That is a state, and it is the thing the lesson tells you not to count.
A crossover followed by an opposite crossover within eight bars
A bearish crossover in a downtrend is the rule working. It becomes a whipsaw only if it is reversed almost at once.
Any crossover in a range
The count is defined by spacing, not by the regime. The range only makes such pairs common.
The lab counts a whipsaw when an opposite crossover arrives within eight bars of the previous one — a signal reversed before it could have been used.

Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
Simple moving average
The SMA gives equal weight to every observation in its window and changes when a new value enters and the oldest value leaves.
Exponential moving average
The EMA applies more weight to recent observations while retaining a decaying influence from earlier data.
Parameter tradeoff
Short periods follow price closely and generate more changes. Long periods smooth noise but respond later to turns and shocks.

Choose the horizon

The first stretch is a narrow band that neither side could leave; the move that follows leaves it and keeps going. Read conventionally, one side has finally been able to move price beyond the level that had been capping it. Note what is absent: there is no run of rising lows building into the break and no return to test the old band afterwards, so nothing here shows pressure accumulating first, and a sustained move back inside that band would say the break was not accepted.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Price has turned back from a similar upper area and a similar lower area more than once, and neither edge has produced follow-through. Structurally this says the two sides are matched near the boundaries: sellers keep appearing near the top of the band and buyers near the bottom, and neither has held price beyond it. Acceptance outside an edge, rather than a single probe through it, would replace this reading.

The advance ends, then price gives up several times more than any pullback took during the advance, and only after that does a rally fail well below the high. Order matters here: the standard reading is a change of character, because the decline broke below the last low that had held on the way up before any lower high existed, rather than a lower high that came first. A recovery back above that failed high would return the chart to the earlier reading.

For the same period and input series, why does an EMA usually react faster than an SMA?
It uses future prices
No average uses a bar that has not closed. Both are computed from the same past closes; only the weights differ.
It places more weight on recent observations
It ignores the current bar
The opposite: the current bar gets the largest single weight, α = 2 ÷ (period + 1).
It always uses fewer bars
An EMA’s weights never reach zero, so it carries more history than an SMA, not less. It reacts faster because the newest bars weigh most.
The exponential weighting gives recent changes a larger effect while older observations decay gradually.
What does a 20-period moving average describe without a timeframe?
Only on a daily chart. On an hourly chart the same setting covers less than three sessions.
Twenty daily bars is roughly a month of trading, but the setting says nothing about the bar size.
Nothing about a fixed duration
Only on an hourly chart.
The duration depends on the chart interval: 20 daily bars, hourly bars, or five-minute bars are different horizons.
Which is a valid reason to choose a longer moving-average period?
To eliminate all false signals
A longer window reduces how often the line turns. It cannot remove false turns, and it pays for the ones it removes with later confirmation.
To smooth more short-term variation
To make the indicator predict earnings
Averaging closes cannot see earnings. Length changes responsiveness, not what the input contains.
To remove the need for a stop
No lookback changes where a trade is wrong. Invalidation is set from price structure, separately.
Longer windows smooth more observations but generally respond later.
Price is above a rising EMA. What can you conclude by itself?
A profitable long trade is guaranteed
It is an observation about two lines. Entry, invalidation and target still have to come from somewhere.
The selected trend reference is rising and price is above it
The market cannot enter a range
Price sits above a rising average at the top of every range, right before it turns back.
The average says nothing about range size. ATR and band width measure that.
That is a defined trend observation, not a complete setup or guarantee.
What is the EMA smoothing factor α for a 9-period EMA in this course?
0.10 is α for a 19-period EMA: 2 ÷ 20. For period 9 it is 2 ÷ (9 + 1).
1 ÷ 9 is the weight each close gets in a 9-bar SMA. The EMA’s factor is 2 ÷ (period + 1) = 0.20.
0.90 would give the newest close almost all of the weight. 1 − α = 0.80 is the weight carried forward from the previous EMA; α itself is 0.20.
α = 2 ÷ (period + 1) = 2 ÷ 10 = 0.20; each new EMA is 0.20 × close + 0.80 × the previous EMA.

clauses.expected: Rate of Change and Momentum
Measure price change over a fixed lookback in percentage and absolute terms, compare zero-line crossings, adjust sensitivity, and distinguish momentum from trend direction and volatility.
Core concepts
Understand what the indicator calculates, how its parameters affect it, and what it cannot establish by itself.
Rate of change
ROC expresses the percentage change from the price a selected number of bars earlier.
Absolute momentum
Simple momentum subtracts the earlier price from the current price and retains price-unit scale.
Zero line
Positive values mean the current price is above the comparison price; negative values mean it is below. The crossing timing depends directly on lookback.
Interactive lesson
Change the inputs, inspect the calculation, and compare the indicator with the underlying price data.
Change the comparison horizon
Short lookbacks react quickly; long lookbacks compare price with a more distant reference.
Use a fixed-horizon momentum measure
Know exactly which prior price forms the comparison.
Choose the lookback
Define how many completed bars separate current and comparison prices.
Choose absolute or percentage form
Use momentum for price-unit change or ROC for normalized percentage change.
Interpret the zero line
Positive and negative values describe position relative to the lookback price.
Define the event
Specify a zero cross, threshold, slope change, or divergence rather than using momentum as a vague adjective.
Fixed-horizon price change

Common mistakes
Completion standard
Identify current and lookback prices, calculate absolute and percentage change, explain the zero-line state, and compare signal timing under short and long lookbacks.

Price has turned back from a similar upper area and a similar lower area more than once, and neither edge has produced follow-through. Structurally this says the two sides are matched near the boundaries: sellers keep appearing near the top of the band and buyers near the bottom, and neither has held price beyond it. Acceptance outside an edge, rather than a single probe through it, would replace this reading.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Each rally has stalled below the one before it, and the declines have carried further than the recoveries have retraced. The usual reading is that supply is being met at progressively lower prices and that buyers appear only further down; it interprets the shape and does not measure who transacted. A close above the most recent lower high removes the evidence for it.

The band is about as wide as an ordinary range, but price crosses it more than twice as often and turns quickly at both edges. The usual reading is that neither side is holding what it takes: each push is met and reversed within a few bars, so an extreme here is a test rather than a resolution. A move that leaves one edge and stays away longer than the previous swings would break the pattern.

The calculation locates the close between the recent lowest low and highest high.
What does %D usually represent?
A moving average of %K
The day count to expiration
That is an options term. Nothing in the stochastic knows about expiry.
It is a smoothed position within the range. ATR and band width measure size.
The highest high is an input to %K, not a line of its own.
%D is the slower signal line derived by smoothing %K.
Why can stochastic remain above 80 in an uptrend?
The formula stops working
It works exactly as written: each new close is near the top of a range that keeps rising.
Closes repeatedly occur near the upper part of the rolling range
The range has no highs
The range always has a highest high. In an uptrend it is usually the latest one.
The %D smoothing is too short
Smoothing changes timing slightly. The reading stays high because of where the closes are, not because of the smoothing.
Persistent strength can keep each new close near the recent range high.
Increasing %K smoothing usually has what effect?
More smoothing removes variation; that is what smoothing does.
Fewer and slower changes
Only a smoothing of 1 leaves raw %K unchanged.
Future data enters the formula
The smoothing averages past %K values. Nothing ahead of the current bar is used.
Additional smoothing reduces short-term variation and delays some crossings.
Lowest low 100, highest high 110, close 108. What is raw %K?
8 is the distance from the low in price units. Divide by the range and scale: 8 ÷ 10 × 100.
98 would be close ÷ highest high. %K measures position inside the range: (close − low) ÷ (high − low).
20 is the distance from the high as a share of the range. %K measures from the low.

Rising highs with rising lows is conventionally read as buyers stepping in earlier on each pullback: every decline has stopped above the low the previous advance began from, so nothing has been fully given back. That is a reading of what has already happened, not a forecast of the next bar. A close below the most recent higher low ends it.

Price has turned back from a similar upper area and a similar lower area more than once, and neither edge has produced follow-through. Structurally this says the two sides are matched near the boundaries: sellers keep appearing near the top of the band and buyers near the bottom, and neither has held price beyond it. Acceptance outside an edge, rather than a single probe through it, would replace this reading.

The first stretch is a narrow band that neither side could leave; the move that follows leaves it and keeps going. Read conventionally, one side has finally been able to move price beyond the level that had been capping it. Note what is absent: there is no run of rising lows building into the break and no return to test the old band afterwards, so nothing here shows pressure accumulating first, and a sustained move back inside that band would say the break was not accepted.

Price has crossed the same broad band repeatedly, and each move to one edge has been given back to the other. That is normally read as two-sided activity with a large amplitude rather than direction: the swing size says how far price travels between turns and says nothing about which side is prevailing. There is a slight net drift across the window, but it is small beside the swings; read the width, not the direction.

A 20-bar indicator requires 20 valid observations before its first complete value. What are the preceding bars called?
Confirmation is a rule word: a bar that satisfies a separately defined condition. It is not the name for bars the calculation cannot yet use.
A breakout window is a lookback used to set a boundary, such as a Donchian channel. It is a parameter, not the bars before the first value exists.
Execution is about when an order is filled. It has nothing to do with whether a calculation has enough observations yet.
The implementation needs enough observations to seed or complete the first calculation; until then the indicator has no value.
What is the usual effect of reducing a moving-average lookback from 30 bars to 5 bars?
It reacts faster and becomes noisier
It becomes slower and smoother
That is the effect of lengthening the window. With five observations each new bar carries a fifth of the weight, so the line moves sooner and turns more often.
A 5-bar average still averages five bars that have already closed. It lags less than a 30-bar average, not zero.
It predicts more accurately
No lookback makes an average predictive. A shorter one only tracks what has already happened more closely, and pays for it with more false turns.
A shorter window weights recent changes more heavily but also responds to more short-term noise.
Two platforms show slightly different RSI values with the same period. What should you verify first?
That one platform has a bug
Possible, but not first. Different seeds, price sources and rounding produce small differences routinely, and each of those can be checked in a minute.
Input source and smoothing convention
The question says the period already matches. The next candidates are the price source, the smoothing seed and the rounding.
The timeframe of the trade you plan
The timeframe changes what the value means to you. It does not explain why two calculations of the same bars disagree.
Source price, smoothing, seeding, rounding, and missing-bar handling can change exact values even when the nominal period matches.
Which statement best describes a technical indicator?
A guarantee of future price direction
Nothing in the formula sees a bar that has not closed. The output summarises what has already happened.
A transformation of historical market data
A replacement for risk management
An indicator says nothing about position size or where a trade is wrong. Those are decided separately, and every lesson in this course says so.
A direct measure of company value
The inputs are price and range data, not earnings or assets. The calculation cannot see value.
Indicators summarize historical data according to a formula; interpretation and risk controls remain separate.
The last five closes are 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18. What is the 5-bar simple moving average?
16 is the second most recent close. An SMA gives the newest close no more weight than the oldest, so it sits at the centre of this window: 70 ÷ 5 = 14.
18 is the latest close. The average of five closes can only equal the highest of them if all five are equal.
70 is the sum of the window. Divide by the lookback: 70 ÷ 5 = 14.
Sum the window and divide by the lookback: (10 + 12 + 14 + 16 + 18) ÷ 5 = 70 ÷ 5 = 14.

Measure where price closes inside each bar’s range and weight that location by volume.
Closing near the high suggests buying pressure; closing near the low suggests selling pressure.
A/D and CMF infer pressure from close location and volume. They do not directly observe whether each trade hit the bid or lifted the ask.
What to understand
Keep the interpretation direct: participation, aggressive side, and actual price progress.
Money Flow Multiplier
Places the close from −1 near the low to +1 near the high of the bar.
A/D Line
Cumulatively adds the multiplier multiplied by volume.
Chaikin Money Flow
Sums money-flow volume over a lookback and divides by total volume.
Change the market conditions
Use the controls and read the “What the market is doing” explanation after each change.

Weight by volume

Compare with price

Zero is the multiplier for a close exactly at the bar's midpoint; a close near the high is well above it.
Near zero describes closing location, not price structure; trending bars that close mid-range give the same reading.
