Price finishes about 13% above where the window opened while the last fourteen bars average close to twice the volume of the first fourteen. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices with more contracts changing hands as they do — though the volume half is participation only, since every one of those contracts had a seller on the other side. The direction in this reading is carried by the price progress; a close back under the lows the advance started from would leave the same volume with none of it.

Price finishes about 13% lower with the same expansion in participation, roughly 1.9 times the opening bars by the close of the window. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices while more contracts trade. Expanding volume is not bearish by itself — it counts trades, both sides of each — so a reclaim of the highs the decline began from would end the reading without the volume changing at all.

Participation rises through the window while price ends within half a percent of where it started, rotating in a band of roughly two and a half points. The usual interpretation is that both sides are active at these prices and neither is making the other give ground; heavy volume here is evidence of a contest, not of a result. It stops reading as balance when a close holds outside the band rather than turning back into it.

Volume in the closing stretch runs about three and a half times the earlier bars while price gains about half a point across that stretch and a little over a point across the whole window. Normally read as absorption: aggressive orders arriving into resting size that is willing to take the other side at these prices. It is a reading about what has happened so far and nothing more — it fails as a description the moment price begins making sustained progress on that same volume.

Price gains about 15% and the last fourteen bars average roughly 83% more volume than the first fourteen. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices with participation expanding behind them. The volume is the count of contracts, not a net side, so it is the price progress that makes this directional; a close back under the level the advance began from would end the reading with the volume unchanged.

Price gains about 14% while the last fourteen bars average roughly 39% less volume than the first fourteen. Normally read as an advance fewer participants are taking part in: buyers are still accepting higher prices, but the evidence behind each new high is thinner than it was. The usual caution is that this weakens the case for the trend rather than reversing it; volume expanding again on a down close is the first thing that would change the reading.

Price loses about 11% while volume in the closing bars runs about 84% above the opening bars. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices with participation expanding. Expanding volume is not itself bearish — every one of those trades had a buyer — and the reading ends where price stops making downward progress on the same activity.

Price falls about 12% while the last fourteen bars average roughly 40% less volume than the first fourteen. Normally read as a decline fewer participants are taking part in: the usual caution is that a move on contracting participation has less evidence behind it, not that it must turn. Volume expanding again without price making a new low would be the first thing to break the reading.

The marked bar trades about 4.7 times the twenty-bar baseline and the sixteen bars after it carry price roughly four and a half points higher. Normally read as a burst of participation the market then followed through on — and it is the follow-through, not the height of the bar, that makes it readable. A stall or a return back under the spike bar would leave the same 4.7x print saying nothing in particular.

Participation keeps expanding after the marked bar, reaching close to six times baseline on the final bars, while price stops advancing and gives back about a point. Normally read as a climax: the heaviest activity of the window arriving where price can no longer make progress on it. The failure to advance is the whole reading — price simply resuming higher on that same volume is what would remove it.

The marked bar trades about seven times baseline and price ends the following sixteen bars roughly where it started them, inside a one and a half point band. Normally read as absorption, aggressive orders meeting resting size content to take the other side here. The spike itself says nothing directional; sustained progress away from this area on comparable volume is what would end the reading.

About four times baseline volume prints inside a range price never leaves, and the sixteen bars after it close within roughly seven tenths of a point of one another. Normally read as heavy two-way trade at an agreed price rather than a directional event. It stops reading that way when a close holds outside the range this activity has been contained in.

The bar that closes above 101.10 carries about 1.6 times the prior eighteen-bar average, and all five of the most recent closes are still above the level. Normally read as acceptance rather than a probe: the level stopped capping price and the bars since have held above it without needing to retest whether it does. A close back under 101.10 is what would return this to a failed break.

The break bar carries only about 1.2 times the prior baseline, and that baseline had itself been thinning into the break, yet price holds above 101.10 on all five recent closes. The usual reading is that the level gave way with thin evidence of participation behind it, so acceptance is being shown by price alone — the weaker of the two. Volume expanding on a pullback that then closes back inside would settle it the other way.

Price closes above 101.10 on about 1.8 times the prior baseline, reaches 103.41, then closes below the level for the rest of the window and finishes near 95.35 — under the range it broke out of. Normally read as a failed break: participation at the level did not convert into acceptance above it. Reclaiming 101.10 and holding there is what would break this reading in turn.

No bar in the window closes above 101.10; the highest high reaches 100.96. Structurally this says the level has not been tested to completion, so the volume trading inside the range is participation with no decision attached to it. The reading begins when a close appears on the other side of the level, not before.

Price finishes about 14% higher and OBV ends at its high for the window, having risen through nearly all of it. Normally read as up-closing bars carrying the larger share of the volume — but OBV is built from these same closes and these same volumes, so it restates the chart above it rather than adding evidence to it. OBV turning down while price keeps making highs is the condition that would make it worth a second look.

Price finishes about 15% lower and OBV falls with it to its low for the window. Normally read as down-closing bars carrying the larger share of the volume. The caveat is in the construction: OBV assigns a bar's entire volume to the direction of its close, so a bar that closed a cent lower after trading both ways counts wholly as selling, and OBV flattening while price keeps making lows is what would put the reading in question.

Price finishes about 17% higher with its high on the last bar, while OBV peaks a little past the halfway point and ends near -14,200, more than 20,000 below that peak. Normally read as a bearish non-confirmation: the bars that closed down carried more volume than the bars that closed up, so the advance is being made on the lighter side of the tape. It is a warning about the evidence, not a signal; OBV turning back up through its prior swing high, or price simply continuing on rising OBV, would end it.

Price finishes about 11% lower with its low on the last bar, while OBV bottoms about a third of the way through the window and ends around +8,900, rising through the whole second half. The usual interpretation is a bullish non-confirmation: the up-closing bars are carrying more of the volume even as price makes lower lows. As with the mirror case it describes the evidence behind the trend, not the next bar, and price confirmation is still required before anyone is called in control.

Every bar closes in the upper part of its own range, averaging near 78% of the bar, which holds CMF around +0.55 at any lookback the slider offers. Normally read as persistent buying pressure; what is actually measured is closing location weighted by that bar's volume, not who transacted. CMF cannot contradict this chart — it is computed from the same highs, lows, closes and volumes drawn above it.

Every bar closes in the lower part of its range, averaging near 21% of the bar, and CMF stays around -0.6 for every available lookback. The usual interpretation is persistent selling pressure. The measurement behind it is closing location weighted by volume, so a bar dragged to its low by one late print counts the same as one that spent the whole period there.

Closes average right at the midpoint of their bars and price ends the window within a quarter of a percent of where it began, which keeps CMF within about 0.08 of zero at every lookback the slider offers. Normally read as no persistent closing pressure either way: the positive and negative money-flow contributions are offsetting. This is also where the indicator's limit shows, since a reading near zero can mean balance or two opposite halves cancelling out, and only the bars themselves say which.

All sixty-four bars close above session VWAP and the line is never crossed. Normally read as the session's business being done above its own volume-weighted average price — a statement about where trade has occurred, since VWAP is an average of this same series rather than an independent level. The first close back below it is what would end the reading.

No bar in the window closes above VWAP and the line falls throughout. Normally read as the session's trade taking place entirely below its own volume-weighted average, with each attempt back toward the line turned away before a close prints above it. A close above VWAP that holds is what would break it.

Price crosses VWAP thirteen times and finishes twenty-seven of sixty-four bars above it, with the line moving about a tenth of a point over the last ten bars. Normally read as trade rotating around an agreed average rather than either side holding an edge: the line is being used as a pivot, not defended. It stops reading that way when closes stop returning through it.

Price spends the first two thirds of the window below VWAP, crosses once near bar forty-five, then closes above it for all nineteen remaining bars while the line itself turns from falling to rising. Normally read as a reclaim rather than a bounce — a single cross is an event, but a volume-weighted average changes direction only when enough trade occurs at the higher prices. A close back below VWAP, particularly one that flattens the line again, is what would undo it.

Price is above the anchored average and the average is rising, so trade since the chosen event has on balance occurred below where price is now. Normally read as favourable location for anything initiated after that event — a claim about one anchor, not about the market, since moving the anchor moves the line and the reading with it. A close below the anchored line, with the line flattening, is what would end it.

Price is below the anchored average and the average is falling, so trade since the chosen event has on balance occurred above where price is now. The usual interpretation is favourable location for the other side, and it is tied entirely to the anchor — which is why the anchor is chosen before the reading rather than moved until one appears. A close back above the line, with the line turning up, is what would end it.

The heaviest bins sit in the middle of the window and the outermost bins hold no volume at all, with roughly 70% of the traded volume fitting into about a point and a quarter around the POC. Structurally this says where trade concentrated, not where price is meant to go — a POC is a record of agreement, not a target. It stops describing the market when volume starts building outside the value area instead of returning into it.

The busiest bins sit near the top of the window: the POC prints around 111.7 in a 99.4 to 115.8 range, so volume built at the higher prices rather than at the ones price left behind. Normally read as higher prices being accepted rather than merely visited, since time and volume followed the move instead of staying where it began. Volume rebuilding down at the old prices is what would take that reading away.

About 53% of the window's volume trades after price leaves the old range at bar 43, and instead of spreading out it settles: the last fifteen bars rotate inside about a point around 104.9 at breakout volume, so the profile shows two nodes — one at the old range near 99.5 to 100.0, one at the new near 104.5 to 105.0 — with thin bins between them. Normally read as acceptance after the breakout, since a second distribution has formed where price went rather than price merely visiting. Two cautions travel with it: a single value area drawn across both nodes spans the thin middle too, which is why a double distribution is usually read as two profiles; and volume rebuilding in that thin middle is what would begin to undo the reading.

The current line sits between the value-area low and high, in the band that took about 70% of the window's volume. Normally read as trade at an agreed price: both sides are transacting where they have been transacting, so location alone is not saying that anyone is giving way. The reading changes when price starts spending time outside the area rather than passing through it.

The line is above the value-area high, but the profile behind it has not changed: every bin above the area still holds less than half the volume of the busiest one. Normally read as an excursion above value, and what would make it acceptance is volume building up there — a second node forming above the old area, not a line drawn above it. Price returning inside is what ends an excursion without it ever becoming acceptance.

The line sits just under the value-area high, back inside the band holding most of the window's volume, while the bins above it are among the thinnest on the profile. Structurally this says the higher prices exist on the chart but attracted little trade. Normally read as those prices being rejected rather than a level being defended, and it stops reading that way if trade starts filling those bins in.

The line is below the value-area low, in bins holding a fraction of the volume the busiest band holds. Normally read as an excursion below value, with the same test as the upside case: acceptance would mean volume beginning to build down there, not price merely visiting. A return into the value area leaves the excursion as an excursion.

The line sits below the value-area low, in the thinnest bin of trade beneath it — one holding a small fraction of what the busiest bin took. Normally read as a transition area — prices the market moved through rather than settled at, which is why movement across them is often quick. Quick is not the same as certain: a thin area can equally be traded back through, and a low-volume node describes the past rather than a speed to come.

The two sides show comparable displayed size, about 3,940 bid against 4,070 offered across five levels, with a two-cent spread. Normally read as an orderly book: a 700-lot market buy fills at roughly 100.015 against a 100.01 best offer, so the cost of demanding immediacy here is about half a tick. None of that displayed size is a commitment — it is what is currently shown, and any line of it can be pulled before a trade reaches it.

Every level holds roughly a quarter of the size it did in the normal book while the quoted spread stays at two cents. Structurally this says spread and depth are separate things: the same 700-lot market buy now walks four levels for an average near 100.029, and 3,000 would exhaust the displayed offers entirely. The reading is about impact, not direction — a thin book says nothing about which way price goes next.

A single displayed bid of 4,200 sits one cent under the best bid, more size than the entire offer side of the book. Normally read as support, which is exactly the inference this subject warns about: a resting order is an intention, cancellable at no cost, and nothing is committed until size trades against it. Note also what it does to execution rather than to price — it changes nothing about the cost of buying, because a buyer never touches it.

A displayed offer of 4,300 sits one cent above the best offer, nearly doubling the ask side of the book. Normally read as resistance, but to anyone buying it is the opposite of an obstacle: a 3,000-lot market buy averages about 100.019 here against roughly 100.030 in the normal book, because that size is liquidity to consume. It can also simply be cancelled, at which point the level it appeared to defend was never tested.

Twenty-five of the forty-two prints classify at the ask, carrying 8,110 shares against 5,139 at the bid, and price walks from 100.01 to 100.17, with small pullbacks along the way but none that undoes the advance. Normally read as buyers paying the offer and the offer moving up to meet them — with the caveat that at-bid and at-ask describe where a print landed relative to the quote, not who initiated it. The price progress is what carries the reading: the same split with price unchanged would say the opposite.

Twenty-six prints classify at the bid, carrying 6,665 shares against 4,798 at the ask, and price works from 100.00 down to 99.79. Normally read as sellers hitting the bid and the bid stepping lower each time it is taken. It would stop reading that way the moment the same bid-side flow arrived without price following it.

Thirty-three of forty-two prints land at the ask and ask-classified volume runs about 2.7 times the bid side, yet price covers four cents across the entire tape. Normally read as absorption: resting size is willing to keep selling at these prices for as long as the buying keeps arriving. What would break the reading is simply price starting to travel on the same flow, which so far it has not.

Bid-classified volume runs about five and a half times the ask side over forty-two prints while price falls four cents. The usual interpretation is that resting buyers are taking the other side of everything being sold here. To be precise about it, those 10,452 shares are not net selling — every one of them was bought by someone — and it reads as absorption only while price refuses to move.

The print count is nearly even but the size is not: 7,714 shares classify at the bid against 5,800 at the ask, and the whole tape stays inside a six-cent band. Normally read as two-way trade at an agreed price, and it is a useful demonstration that a thirty percent classification imbalance can produce essentially no movement. Classification imbalance is not direction; price progress is what would make it directional.

Every candle in the window carries positive delta and closes above its open, with the selected one showing delta at a little over a third of its own volume and the others between a tenth and a third. Normally read as ask-side aggression that price is following. Delta is an inference from where each print landed against the quote rather than a measurement of who initiated, so a positive-delta candle that closes at or below its open is what would separate the aggression from the result.

Every candle carries negative delta and closes below its open. Normally read as bid-side aggression that price is following down, with the same caveat: the classification describes prints against the quote and can be wrong on any individual one. The reading holds only while the two agree.

All six candles carry positive delta — the largest is nearly half its own candle's volume — and every one closes at or below its open. Normally read as absorption at the ask: buying is arriving and being met by resting size without price being pushed. This is the case that makes the point about delta, since a strongly positive number and a lower close belong to the same candle, and it is the close that shows the aggression did not work.

All six candles carry negative delta while closing at or above their opens. Normally read as absorption at the bid: the selling is being taken by resting size and is not moving price. As in the mirror case the delta figure alone would have read as one-sided; only the close shows that what was resting on the other side was enough.

Price gains 14.09 points and cumulative delta rises from zero to about +14,000 without ever turning negative. Normally read as ask-classified aggression and price progress agreeing — the least surprising case, since both are driven by the same up-closing bars. CVD is a running sum of an estimate: classification, venue, aggregation and the reset bar all move the line without a single trade changing.

Price loses 14.08 points and cumulative delta falls to about -14,100, never turning positive. Normally read as bid-classified aggression tracking the decline. Because the two agree, this chart says little on its own; the informative cases are the ones where they do not.

Cumulative delta climbs to roughly +18,400, the largest reading of any case here, while price finishes 0.82 points higher inside a three-point range. Normally read as absorption: the ask-classified aggression is arriving into resting size that is taking it at these prices. The invalidation is direct — price beginning to travel on that same slope would make it an ordinary advance instead.

Cumulative delta falls to about -17,400 while price ends the window six hundredths of a point below where it started. Normally read as absorption on the bid side, the aggression being taken without price being moved. Note what the number is not: -17,400 is not net selling, since every one of those contracts was bought by someone, it is an estimate of which side crossed the spread.

Price rises 16.39 points while cumulative delta ends near -7,700 and never turns positive. Normally read as price advancing without the ask-classified aggression usually seen alongside it — which is as much a reason to distrust the estimate as the move, since passive buying does not register as positive delta at all. It is a divergence to note rather than a signal: the two can re-converge in either direction.

Price falls 16.10 points while cumulative delta ends near +7,600 and never turns negative. The usual interpretation is that the decline is happening without matching bid-classified aggression, either because the selling is passive and sitting on the offer rather than crossing the spread, or because the classification is missing it. A divergence describes a disagreement between a price and an estimate; it does not settle which of them is wrong.

Little of this book has been tested yet. Structurally that is the whole content of the state: displayed size is what participants are currently willing to show, and until an order arrives there is no way to separate showing from meaning it. Everything readable about depth comes from what happens next — whether the size is executed, replenished, or cancelled.

Eight hundred lots trade against the 4,200 displayed at 99.98, and the level is back to 4,500 by the next event and 4,600 after that, larger than before it was hit. Normally read as a bid being defended, since size that replenishes after being taken is doing something a cancelled order cannot. The invalidation is the one that matters for depth: the level can be withdrawn rather than taken, and a bid that is cancelled was never support.

Nine hundred lots are lifted from the 4,300 displayed at 100.02, and the level returns to 4,600 and then 4,700 with the best offer never moving. Normally read as an offer being defended, replenishment being the part that distinguishes it from resting size nobody has tested. The same caution applies in reverse: it can be pulled instead of traded, and an offer that is cancelled never resisted anything.

The large level is gone. It absorbed real executions and replenished twice before it withdrew, and then near-touch depth drops from about 6,000 to 2,300 between events. Structurally this says what displayed size is: an intention, revocable at no cost, and therefore not evidence of anything until it is executed. It is the reason depth is read as available liquidity rather than as support or resistance.

The order eats through the front of a book holding roughly a quarter of the normal size per level, and the best offer walks from 100.01 to 100.03 while the spread widens from two cents to four. Normally read as price impact rather than as a move: nothing about the market changed, one order simply cost more because there was less to trade against. Depth returning at the new prices would leave the impact temporary; it not returning is what turns impact into a repricing.

The 99.99 bid was added to, then sold into, then finished: the best bid is now 99.98 and the spread has widened to three cents. Normally read as a level consumed rather than withdrawn — the version of the story where displayed size did mean something, because it was there, it traded, and it is gone. What it does not say is where price goes next, only that the price at which buying was resting has moved down a cent.

clauses.expected: Order Book and Market Depth
Inspect resting liquidity, queue changes, spread, depth, and the difference between displayed intent and executed trades.
The order book shows available intentions, not completed control.
A large displayed bid can support price only if it remains and absorbs selling. A large ask can cap price only if it remains and absorbs buying. Orders can be added, moved, or canceled.
What to understand
Keep the interpretation direct: participation, aggressive side, and actual price progress.
Depth
Displayed resting quantity at multiple bid and ask prices.
Queue
Orders at the same price wait according to venue priority rules.
Events
Adds, executions, modifications, and cancellations change the book.
Change the market conditions
Use the controls and read the “What the market is doing” explanation after each change.
Order Book and Market Depth Lab
Synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Follow the reading steps
Do not jump from one number to a trade. Describe the evidence first.
Read spread and depth
How much quantity is displayed near the market?
Track changes
Does liquidity remain, replenish, get consumed, or disappear?
Require execution evidence
Displayed size matters only through its behavior when tested.
Check your interpretation
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. A large bid is repeatedly hit but price does not fall. What may be happening?
2. A large ask disappears before price reaches it. What happened?
3. Why is depth alone an incomplete liquidity measure?
4. Bids: 420 at 99.99 and 690 at 99.98. Asks: 380 at 100.01 and 610 at 100.02. What are the near-touch depth (two levels each side) and the spread?
Practical rules
Depth is one liquidity dimension, not the whole picture.
Displayed orders can be canceled.
Use executions and price response to validate a wall.
Common mistakes
Trading every large displayed order.
Assuming all liquidity is visible.
Ignoring order-book speed and queue position.

Price finishes about 13% above where the window opened while the last fourteen bars average close to twice the volume of the first fourteen. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices with more contracts changing hands as they do — though the volume half is participation only, since every one of those contracts had a seller on the other side. The direction in this reading is carried by the price progress; a close back under the lows the advance started from would leave the same volume with none of it.

Price finishes about 13% lower with the same expansion in participation, roughly 1.9 times the opening bars by the close of the window. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices while more contracts trade. Expanding volume is not bearish by itself — it counts trades, both sides of each — so a reclaim of the highs the decline began from would end the reading without the volume changing at all.

Participation rises through the window while price ends within half a percent of where it started, rotating in a band of roughly two and a half points. The usual interpretation is that both sides are active at these prices and neither is making the other give ground; heavy volume here is evidence of a contest, not of a result. It stops reading as balance when a close holds outside the band rather than turning back into it.

Volume in the closing stretch runs about three and a half times the earlier bars while price gains about half a point across that stretch and a little over a point across the whole window. Normally read as absorption: aggressive orders arriving into resting size that is willing to take the other side at these prices. It is a reading about what has happened so far and nothing more — it fails as a description the moment price begins making sustained progress on that same volume.

Price gains about 15% and the last fourteen bars average roughly 83% more volume than the first fourteen. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices with participation expanding behind them. The volume is the count of contracts, not a net side, so it is the price progress that makes this directional; a close back under the level the advance began from would end the reading with the volume unchanged.

Price gains about 14% while the last fourteen bars average roughly 39% less volume than the first fourteen. Normally read as an advance fewer participants are taking part in: buyers are still accepting higher prices, but the evidence behind each new high is thinner than it was. The usual caution is that this weakens the case for the trend rather than reversing it; volume expanding again on a down close is the first thing that would change the reading.

Price loses about 11% while volume in the closing bars runs about 84% above the opening bars. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices with participation expanding. Expanding volume is not itself bearish — every one of those trades had a buyer — and the reading ends where price stops making downward progress on the same activity.

Price falls about 12% while the last fourteen bars average roughly 40% less volume than the first fourteen. Normally read as a decline fewer participants are taking part in: the usual caution is that a move on contracting participation has less evidence behind it, not that it must turn. Volume expanding again without price making a new low would be the first thing to break the reading.

The marked bar trades about 4.7 times the twenty-bar baseline and the sixteen bars after it carry price roughly four and a half points higher. Normally read as a burst of participation the market then followed through on — and it is the follow-through, not the height of the bar, that makes it readable. A stall or a return back under the spike bar would leave the same 4.7x print saying nothing in particular.

Participation keeps expanding after the marked bar, reaching close to six times baseline on the final bars, while price stops advancing and gives back about a point. Normally read as a climax: the heaviest activity of the window arriving where price can no longer make progress on it. The failure to advance is the whole reading — price simply resuming higher on that same volume is what would remove it.

The marked bar trades about seven times baseline and price ends the following sixteen bars roughly where it started them, inside a one and a half point band. Normally read as absorption, aggressive orders meeting resting size content to take the other side here. The spike itself says nothing directional; sustained progress away from this area on comparable volume is what would end the reading.

About four times baseline volume prints inside a range price never leaves, and the sixteen bars after it close within roughly seven tenths of a point of one another. Normally read as heavy two-way trade at an agreed price rather than a directional event. It stops reading that way when a close holds outside the range this activity has been contained in.

The bar that closes above 101.10 carries about 1.6 times the prior eighteen-bar average, and all five of the most recent closes are still above the level. Normally read as acceptance rather than a probe: the level stopped capping price and the bars since have held above it without needing to retest whether it does. A close back under 101.10 is what would return this to a failed break.

The break bar carries only about 1.2 times the prior baseline, and that baseline had itself been thinning into the break, yet price holds above 101.10 on all five recent closes. The usual reading is that the level gave way with thin evidence of participation behind it, so acceptance is being shown by price alone — the weaker of the two. Volume expanding on a pullback that then closes back inside would settle it the other way.

Price closes above 101.10 on about 1.8 times the prior baseline, reaches 103.41, then closes below the level for the rest of the window and finishes near 95.35 — under the range it broke out of. Normally read as a failed break: participation at the level did not convert into acceptance above it. Reclaiming 101.10 and holding there is what would break this reading in turn.

No bar in the window closes above 101.10; the highest high reaches 100.96. Structurally this says the level has not been tested to completion, so the volume trading inside the range is participation with no decision attached to it. The reading begins when a close appears on the other side of the level, not before.

Price finishes about 14% higher and OBV ends at its high for the window, having risen through nearly all of it. Normally read as up-closing bars carrying the larger share of the volume — but OBV is built from these same closes and these same volumes, so it restates the chart above it rather than adding evidence to it. OBV turning down while price keeps making highs is the condition that would make it worth a second look.

Price finishes about 15% lower and OBV falls with it to its low for the window. Normally read as down-closing bars carrying the larger share of the volume. The caveat is in the construction: OBV assigns a bar's entire volume to the direction of its close, so a bar that closed a cent lower after trading both ways counts wholly as selling, and OBV flattening while price keeps making lows is what would put the reading in question.

Price finishes about 17% higher with its high on the last bar, while OBV peaks a little past the halfway point and ends near -14,200, more than 20,000 below that peak. Normally read as a bearish non-confirmation: the bars that closed down carried more volume than the bars that closed up, so the advance is being made on the lighter side of the tape. It is a warning about the evidence, not a signal; OBV turning back up through its prior swing high, or price simply continuing on rising OBV, would end it.

Price finishes about 11% lower with its low on the last bar, while OBV bottoms about a third of the way through the window and ends around +8,900, rising through the whole second half. The usual interpretation is a bullish non-confirmation: the up-closing bars are carrying more of the volume even as price makes lower lows. As with the mirror case it describes the evidence behind the trend, not the next bar, and price confirmation is still required before anyone is called in control.

Every bar closes in the upper part of its own range, averaging near 78% of the bar, which holds CMF around +0.55 at any lookback the slider offers. Normally read as persistent buying pressure; what is actually measured is closing location weighted by that bar's volume, not who transacted. CMF cannot contradict this chart — it is computed from the same highs, lows, closes and volumes drawn above it.

Every bar closes in the lower part of its range, averaging near 21% of the bar, and CMF stays around -0.6 for every available lookback. The usual interpretation is persistent selling pressure. The measurement behind it is closing location weighted by volume, so a bar dragged to its low by one late print counts the same as one that spent the whole period there.

Closes average right at the midpoint of their bars and price ends the window within a quarter of a percent of where it began, which keeps CMF within about 0.08 of zero at every lookback the slider offers. Normally read as no persistent closing pressure either way: the positive and negative money-flow contributions are offsetting. This is also where the indicator's limit shows, since a reading near zero can mean balance or two opposite halves cancelling out, and only the bars themselves say which.

All sixty-four bars close above session VWAP and the line is never crossed. Normally read as the session's business being done above its own volume-weighted average price — a statement about where trade has occurred, since VWAP is an average of this same series rather than an independent level. The first close back below it is what would end the reading.

No bar in the window closes above VWAP and the line falls throughout. Normally read as the session's trade taking place entirely below its own volume-weighted average, with each attempt back toward the line turned away before a close prints above it. A close above VWAP that holds is what would break it.

Price crosses VWAP thirteen times and finishes twenty-seven of sixty-four bars above it, with the line moving about a tenth of a point over the last ten bars. Normally read as trade rotating around an agreed average rather than either side holding an edge: the line is being used as a pivot, not defended. It stops reading that way when closes stop returning through it.

Price spends the first two thirds of the window below VWAP, crosses once near bar forty-five, then closes above it for all nineteen remaining bars while the line itself turns from falling to rising. Normally read as a reclaim rather than a bounce — a single cross is an event, but a volume-weighted average changes direction only when enough trade occurs at the higher prices. A close back below VWAP, particularly one that flattens the line again, is what would undo it.

Price is above the anchored average and the average is rising, so trade since the chosen event has on balance occurred below where price is now. Normally read as favourable location for anything initiated after that event — a claim about one anchor, not about the market, since moving the anchor moves the line and the reading with it. A close below the anchored line, with the line flattening, is what would end it.

Price is below the anchored average and the average is falling, so trade since the chosen event has on balance occurred above where price is now. The usual interpretation is favourable location for the other side, and it is tied entirely to the anchor — which is why the anchor is chosen before the reading rather than moved until one appears. A close back above the line, with the line turning up, is what would end it.

The heaviest bins sit in the middle of the window and the outermost bins hold no volume at all, with roughly 70% of the traded volume fitting into about a point and a quarter around the POC. Structurally this says where trade concentrated, not where price is meant to go — a POC is a record of agreement, not a target. It stops describing the market when volume starts building outside the value area instead of returning into it.

The busiest bins sit near the top of the window: the POC prints around 111.7 in a 99.4 to 115.8 range, so volume built at the higher prices rather than at the ones price left behind. Normally read as higher prices being accepted rather than merely visited, since time and volume followed the move instead of staying where it began. Volume rebuilding down at the old prices is what would take that reading away.

About 53% of the window's volume trades after price leaves the old range at bar 43, and instead of spreading out it settles: the last fifteen bars rotate inside about a point around 104.9 at breakout volume, so the profile shows two nodes — one at the old range near 99.5 to 100.0, one at the new near 104.5 to 105.0 — with thin bins between them. Normally read as acceptance after the breakout, since a second distribution has formed where price went rather than price merely visiting. Two cautions travel with it: a single value area drawn across both nodes spans the thin middle too, which is why a double distribution is usually read as two profiles; and volume rebuilding in that thin middle is what would begin to undo the reading.

The current line sits between the value-area low and high, in the band that took about 70% of the window's volume. Normally read as trade at an agreed price: both sides are transacting where they have been transacting, so location alone is not saying that anyone is giving way. The reading changes when price starts spending time outside the area rather than passing through it.

The line is above the value-area high, but the profile behind it has not changed: every bin above the area still holds less than half the volume of the busiest one. Normally read as an excursion above value, and what would make it acceptance is volume building up there — a second node forming above the old area, not a line drawn above it. Price returning inside is what ends an excursion without it ever becoming acceptance.

The line sits just under the value-area high, back inside the band holding most of the window's volume, while the bins above it are among the thinnest on the profile. Structurally this says the higher prices exist on the chart but attracted little trade. Normally read as those prices being rejected rather than a level being defended, and it stops reading that way if trade starts filling those bins in.

The line is below the value-area low, in bins holding a fraction of the volume the busiest band holds. Normally read as an excursion below value, with the same test as the upside case: acceptance would mean volume beginning to build down there, not price merely visiting. A return into the value area leaves the excursion as an excursion.

The line sits below the value-area low, in the thinnest bin of trade beneath it — one holding a small fraction of what the busiest bin took. Normally read as a transition area — prices the market moved through rather than settled at, which is why movement across them is often quick. Quick is not the same as certain: a thin area can equally be traded back through, and a low-volume node describes the past rather than a speed to come.

The two sides show comparable displayed size, about 3,940 bid against 4,070 offered across five levels, with a two-cent spread. Normally read as an orderly book: a 700-lot market buy fills at roughly 100.015 against a 100.01 best offer, so the cost of demanding immediacy here is about half a tick. None of that displayed size is a commitment — it is what is currently shown, and any line of it can be pulled before a trade reaches it.

Every level holds roughly a quarter of the size it did in the normal book while the quoted spread stays at two cents. Structurally this says spread and depth are separate things: the same 700-lot market buy now walks four levels for an average near 100.029, and 3,000 would exhaust the displayed offers entirely. The reading is about impact, not direction — a thin book says nothing about which way price goes next.

A single displayed bid of 4,200 sits one cent under the best bid, more size than the entire offer side of the book. Normally read as support, which is exactly the inference this subject warns about: a resting order is an intention, cancellable at no cost, and nothing is committed until size trades against it. Note also what it does to execution rather than to price — it changes nothing about the cost of buying, because a buyer never touches it.

A displayed offer of 4,300 sits one cent above the best offer, nearly doubling the ask side of the book. Normally read as resistance, but to anyone buying it is the opposite of an obstacle: a 3,000-lot market buy averages about 100.019 here against roughly 100.030 in the normal book, because that size is liquidity to consume. It can also simply be cancelled, at which point the level it appeared to defend was never tested.

Twenty-five of the forty-two prints classify at the ask, carrying 8,110 shares against 5,139 at the bid, and price walks from 100.01 to 100.17, with small pullbacks along the way but none that undoes the advance. Normally read as buyers paying the offer and the offer moving up to meet them — with the caveat that at-bid and at-ask describe where a print landed relative to the quote, not who initiated it. The price progress is what carries the reading: the same split with price unchanged would say the opposite.

Twenty-six prints classify at the bid, carrying 6,665 shares against 4,798 at the ask, and price works from 100.00 down to 99.79. Normally read as sellers hitting the bid and the bid stepping lower each time it is taken. It would stop reading that way the moment the same bid-side flow arrived without price following it.

Thirty-three of forty-two prints land at the ask and ask-classified volume runs about 2.7 times the bid side, yet price covers four cents across the entire tape. Normally read as absorption: resting size is willing to keep selling at these prices for as long as the buying keeps arriving. What would break the reading is simply price starting to travel on the same flow, which so far it has not.

Bid-classified volume runs about five and a half times the ask side over forty-two prints while price falls four cents. The usual interpretation is that resting buyers are taking the other side of everything being sold here. To be precise about it, those 10,452 shares are not net selling — every one of them was bought by someone — and it reads as absorption only while price refuses to move.

The print count is nearly even but the size is not: 7,714 shares classify at the bid against 5,800 at the ask, and the whole tape stays inside a six-cent band. Normally read as two-way trade at an agreed price, and it is a useful demonstration that a thirty percent classification imbalance can produce essentially no movement. Classification imbalance is not direction; price progress is what would make it directional.

Every candle in the window carries positive delta and closes above its open, with the selected one showing delta at a little over a third of its own volume and the others between a tenth and a third. Normally read as ask-side aggression that price is following. Delta is an inference from where each print landed against the quote rather than a measurement of who initiated, so a positive-delta candle that closes at or below its open is what would separate the aggression from the result.

Every candle carries negative delta and closes below its open. Normally read as bid-side aggression that price is following down, with the same caveat: the classification describes prints against the quote and can be wrong on any individual one. The reading holds only while the two agree.

All six candles carry positive delta — the largest is nearly half its own candle's volume — and every one closes at or below its open. Normally read as absorption at the ask: buying is arriving and being met by resting size without price being pushed. This is the case that makes the point about delta, since a strongly positive number and a lower close belong to the same candle, and it is the close that shows the aggression did not work.

All six candles carry negative delta while closing at or above their opens. Normally read as absorption at the bid: the selling is being taken by resting size and is not moving price. As in the mirror case the delta figure alone would have read as one-sided; only the close shows that what was resting on the other side was enough.

Price gains 14.09 points and cumulative delta rises from zero to about +14,000 without ever turning negative. Normally read as ask-classified aggression and price progress agreeing — the least surprising case, since both are driven by the same up-closing bars. CVD is a running sum of an estimate: classification, venue, aggregation and the reset bar all move the line without a single trade changing.

Price loses 14.08 points and cumulative delta falls to about -14,100, never turning positive. Normally read as bid-classified aggression tracking the decline. Because the two agree, this chart says little on its own; the informative cases are the ones where they do not.

Cumulative delta climbs to roughly +18,400, the largest reading of any case here, while price finishes 0.82 points higher inside a three-point range. Normally read as absorption: the ask-classified aggression is arriving into resting size that is taking it at these prices. The invalidation is direct — price beginning to travel on that same slope would make it an ordinary advance instead.

Cumulative delta falls to about -17,400 while price ends the window six hundredths of a point below where it started. Normally read as absorption on the bid side, the aggression being taken without price being moved. Note what the number is not: -17,400 is not net selling, since every one of those contracts was bought by someone, it is an estimate of which side crossed the spread.

Price rises 16.39 points while cumulative delta ends near -7,700 and never turns positive. Normally read as price advancing without the ask-classified aggression usually seen alongside it — which is as much a reason to distrust the estimate as the move, since passive buying does not register as positive delta at all. It is a divergence to note rather than a signal: the two can re-converge in either direction.

Price falls 16.10 points while cumulative delta ends near +7,600 and never turns negative. The usual interpretation is that the decline is happening without matching bid-classified aggression, either because the selling is passive and sitting on the offer rather than crossing the spread, or because the classification is missing it. A divergence describes a disagreement between a price and an estimate; it does not settle which of them is wrong.

Little of this book has been tested yet. Structurally that is the whole content of the state: displayed size is what participants are currently willing to show, and until an order arrives there is no way to separate showing from meaning it. Everything readable about depth comes from what happens next — whether the size is executed, replenished, or cancelled.

Eight hundred lots trade against the 4,200 displayed at 99.98, and the level is back to 4,500 by the next event and 4,600 after that, larger than before it was hit. Normally read as a bid being defended, since size that replenishes after being taken is doing something a cancelled order cannot. The invalidation is the one that matters for depth: the level can be withdrawn rather than taken, and a bid that is cancelled was never support.

Nine hundred lots are lifted from the 4,300 displayed at 100.02, and the level returns to 4,600 and then 4,700 with the best offer never moving. Normally read as an offer being defended, replenishment being the part that distinguishes it from resting size nobody has tested. The same caution applies in reverse: it can be pulled instead of traded, and an offer that is cancelled never resisted anything.

The large level is gone. It absorbed real executions and replenished twice before it withdrew, and then near-touch depth drops from about 6,000 to 2,300 between events. Structurally this says what displayed size is: an intention, revocable at no cost, and therefore not evidence of anything until it is executed. It is the reason depth is read as available liquidity rather than as support or resistance.

The order eats through the front of a book holding roughly a quarter of the normal size per level, and the best offer walks from 100.01 to 100.03 while the spread widens from two cents to four. Normally read as price impact rather than as a move: nothing about the market changed, one order simply cost more because there was less to trade against. Depth returning at the new prices would leave the impact temporary; it not returning is what turns impact into a repricing.

The 99.99 bid was added to, then sold into, then finished: the best bid is now 99.98 and the spread has widened to three cents. Normally read as a level consumed rather than withdrawn — the version of the story where displayed size did mean something, because it was there, it traded, and it is gone. What it does not say is where price goes next, only that the price at which buying was resting has moved down a cent.

Note: this rule is countertrend relative to the selected uptrend context. That is a choice rather than a contradiction, but the rule should say why the trend is expected to fail.
Note: this rule is countertrend relative to the selected downtrend context. That is a choice rather than a contradiction, but the rule should say why the trend is expected to fail.
Rule is internally consistent under this simplified model.
The rule asks the market to show conflicting behavior.
Revise the conditions before backtesting.
The rule requires buyers to show participation, aggression, and upward price confirmation.
A long trigger appears only after buyers make measurable progress in the selected context.
The rule requires sellers to show participation, aggression, and downward price confirmation.
A short trigger appears only after sellers make measurable progress in the selected context.

clauses.expected: Price and Volume Relationships
Interpret the four basic combinations of price direction and changing participation.
Direction comes from price; conviction comes from participation.
Rising price means buyers are making progress. Falling price means sellers are making progress. Volume shows whether participation is expanding or contracting.
What to understand
Keep the interpretation direct: participation, aggressive side, and actual price progress.
Price up + volume up
Buyers keep accepting higher prices while participation expands.
Price down + volume up
Sellers keep accepting lower prices while participation expands.
Price move + volume down
Price is progressing, but fewer participants are supporting the move.
Change the market conditions
Use the controls and read the “What the market is doing” explanation after each change.
Price and Volume Relationships Lab
Synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Follow the reading steps
Do not jump from one number to a trade. Describe the evidence first.
Choose direction
Identify whether closing prices are rising or falling.
Measure participation
Compare recent volume with its baseline.
Avoid certainty
Strong participation confirms activity, not guaranteed continuation.
Check your interpretation
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. Price falls while volume expands. What is happening?
2. Price rises while volume contracts. What is the best description?
3. Which variable establishes direction?
4. The last fourteen bars average 1,250 contracts; the first fourteen averaged 1,000. What volume trend does the lab report?
Practical rules
Describe price first and volume second.
Falling volume weakens evidence; it does not automatically reverse the trend.
Treat mixed evidence as mixed, not as a forced signal.
Common mistakes
Equating green candles with buyer-initiated volume.
Assuming low-volume trends must immediately reverse.
Using one bar instead of a sequence.

Falling price is sellers accepting lower bids; the buyers in those trades are the passive side, not the side making progress.
Balance means price ends near where it began; a falling price on rising participation is a decided move, not a contest.
Confirmation is expanding participation behind the move; contracting volume is the weaker of the two cases, not the stronger.
Thin participation lowers the evidence for the trend; it does not reverse it, and trends on falling volume can persist for a long time.
Volume has no sign: every contract was bought and sold. Direction is what price did while it traded.
