The stop sits at 109.40, 1.05 above the protected low that defines this swing — and two bars inside that swing printed lows of 109.25 and 108.50 without breaking it. Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. Normally read as the ordinary case, in which a price exists at the level and the half-spread is the visible cost of taking it. That one window contains both outcomes is the point: the reading holds only while there is a price to fill against.

Each of these positions has sold a right to someone who paid for it, and that is where the ceiling on this line comes from: beyond it the position stops taking part in the move. Normally read as a defined outcome, and the geometry is defined — but the curve is the payoff at expiration, so an assignment before then leaves the underlying obligation rather than a point on this line. The premium received is the price agreed for that ceiling, not a bound on what the position can lose.

The debit has already been paid to the other side of these contracts, which is why the flat lower section of the line is the whole of it. Normally read as the favourable case when the underlying moves as required — the qualification being that this curve is the expiration payoff, while the modelled result above it also applies the implied-volatility change and the days elapsed. Direction alone does not settle it.

The flat lower section is the full debit, and it is the maximum loss because it has already been paid to the other side of these contracts. Normally read as risk that is defined, which is not the same as risk that is small: the entire amount is lost at every underlying price along that flat section. The line is the expiration payoff, and time and implied volatility move the result before then in either direction.

clauses.expected: Reward-to-Risk and R-Multiples
Express trade outcomes in units of initial risk, compare targets consistently, and avoid confusing a large target with a high-quality setup.
One R is the distance from entry to the original invalidation.
When price moves one initial-risk distance in your favor, the trade is at +1R. A target only matters if market structure provides a realistic path to it.
What to understand
Keep the process direct: define the risk, calculate it, and enforce the limit.
Initial risk
The planned loss from entry to the original stop, including position size.
R-multiple
Realized or unrealized profit and loss divided by initial risk.
Target feasibility
Reward-to-risk is meaningful only when the target aligns with market structure and liquidity.
Change the risk conditions
Adjust the controls and read the market behavior and account impact after each change.
Reward-to-Risk and R-Multiples Lab
Synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Apply it in order
Risk calculations should happen before the order is submitted.
Mark entry and stop
This distance defines 1R.
Locate the structural target
Use prior highs, lows, range boundaries, or tested value areas.
Compare without forcing
Reject trades whose realistic target does not provide acceptable reward relative to risk.
Check your understanding
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. A trade risks $200 and gains $400. What is the outcome?
2. Does a 5R target make a setup automatically better?
3. Which risk defines R after the stop is moved?
4. Initial risk $300. Half the position exits at +2R and the other half is stopped at −1R. Realized result?
Practical rules
Define 1R from the original entry and stop.
Use structural targets before calculating reward-to-risk.
Record realized outcomes in R for cross-trade comparison.
Common mistakes
Moving the stop closer only to improve the ratio.
Calling an unrealized maximum excursion the realized result.
Ignoring partial exits when calculating R.

+1R would be a $200 gain, the same size as the risk; $400 is twice it.
+4R would be $800; the R-multiple is the result divided by the initial risk, $400 ÷ $200 = 2.

A target is a hope until structure supplies a path to it; a 5R target price never reaches is worth nothing, and Win Rate, Average Win/Loss, and Expectancy shows that a large average win only helps if it actually happens.
Tightening the stop to inflate the ratio moves it inside the noise (Stop-Loss and Structural Invalidation), so the trade is stopped before the target is ever tested.
Re-basing R to the trailed stop makes every trade look small: a +3R winner becomes +0.5R once the stop is trailed to +2.5R. The unit is fixed at entry.
The account balance sets the dollars behind 1R (Risk Per Trade); it is not the unit itself.
+1R adds the two halves’ R-multiples without weighting them; each half is half the position, so each counts half.
+2R is what the first half earned on its share; the second half gave back 1R on its share. Weighted: 0.5 × 2 − 0.5 × 1 = +0.5R.

The stop sits at 109.40, 1.05 above the protected low that defines this swing — and two bars inside that swing printed lows of 109.25 and 108.50 without breaking it. Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. clauses.expected: Risk Management Fundamentals
Sort a trade's variables into the ones you set and the ones you absorb, state the planned loss in dollars before entry, and separate market uncertainty from account damage.
The market outcome is uncertain. Your exposure is the controlled variable.
A valid setup can still lose. Risk management limits the account damage when price does not follow the thesis.
What to understand
Keep the process direct: define the risk, calculate it, and enforce the limit.
Controllable risk
You can control position size, planned exit, total exposure, and whether a trade is taken.
Uncontrollable outcome
You cannot control the next price move, gaps, news, or the order in which wins and losses arrive.
Survival first
A strategy can only produce long-term results if normal losses do not remove the ability to continue.
Change the risk conditions
Adjust the controls and read the market behavior and account impact after each change.

Check total exposure

2. A strong setup loses. What does that prove?

Practical rules
Define maximum loss before entry.
Calculate position size from the stop distance.
Treat unexpected gaps and slippage as additional risk.
Common mistakes
Assuming confidence should increase position size.
Moving the stop because the trade is losing.
Measuring risk only after the position is open.

The stop sits at 109.40, 1.05 above the protected low that defines this swing — and two bars inside that swing printed lows of 109.25 and 108.50 without breaking it. Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. Normally read as the ordinary case, in which a price exists at the level and the half-spread is the visible cost of taking it. That one window contains both outcomes is the point: the reading holds only while there is a price to fill against.

Each of these positions has sold a right to someone who paid for it, and that is where the ceiling on this line comes from: beyond it the position stops taking part in the move. Normally read as a defined outcome, and the geometry is defined — but the curve is the payoff at expiration, so an assignment before then leaves the underlying obligation rather than a point on this line. The premium received is the price agreed for that ceiling, not a bound on what the position can lose.

The debit has already been paid to the other side of these contracts, which is why the flat lower section of the line is the whole of it. Normally read as the favourable case when the underlying moves as required — the qualification being that this curve is the expiration payoff, while the modelled result above it also applies the implied-volatility change and the days elapsed. Direction alone does not settle it.

The flat lower section is the full debit, and it is the maximum loss because it has already been paid to the other side of these contracts. Normally read as risk that is defined, which is not the same as risk that is small: the entire amount is lost at every underlying price along that flat section. The line is the expiration payoff, and time and implied volatility move the result before then in either direction.

clauses.expected: Risk of Ruin
Estimate how strategy expectancy, payoff, risk per trade, and sequence variance affect the probability of crossing a failure threshold.
Large risk per trade makes ordinary variance more likely to cross the failure threshold.
Positive expectancy does not eliminate severe paths. Risk of ruin asks whether a losing sequence can reduce the account below the level required to continue.
What to understand
Keep the process direct: define the risk, calculate it, and enforce the limit.
Ruin threshold
The equity level at which the strategy can no longer be traded as intended.
Path dependency
Outcome order affects whether the account reaches the threshold.
Simulation estimate
Monte Carlo results are scenario estimates, not guarantees or exact future probabilities.
Change the risk conditions
Adjust the controls and read the market behavior and account impact after each change.
Risk of Ruin Lab
Synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Apply it in order
Risk calculations should happen before the order is submitted.
Define ruin practically
Use the minimum equity needed for strategy size, margin, or personal tolerance.
Model realistic outcomes
Use net win rate, payoff, costs, gaps, and occasional larger losses.
Stress the assumptions
Increase loss clustering and reduce expectancy to test robustness.
Check your understanding
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. What generally increases risk of ruin most directly?
2. Does positive expectancy guarantee zero ruin risk?
3. What is a Monte Carlo result?
4. Risk 5% of current equity per trade, ruin defined as a 50% drawdown. How many consecutive full losses reach it?
Practical rules
Use conservative expectancy assumptions.
Include rare losses larger than the planned stop.
Set risk low enough that bad sequences remain survivable.
Common mistakes
Treating simulation output as certainty.
Using gross backtest results without costs.
Defining ruin only as a zero balance.
Official reading
The labs use simplified synthetic examples. These sources cover the underlying risk and execution concepts.

Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. Normally read as the ordinary case, in which a price exists at the level and the half-spread is the visible cost of taking it. That one window contains both outcomes is the point: the reading holds only while there is a price to fill against.

Each of these positions has sold a right to someone who paid for it, and that is where the ceiling on this line comes from: beyond it the position stops taking part in the move. Normally read as a defined outcome, and the geometry is defined — but the curve is the payoff at expiration, so an assignment before then leaves the underlying obligation rather than a point on this line. The premium received is the price agreed for that ceiling, not a bound on what the position can lose.

The debit has already been paid to the other side of these contracts, which is why the flat lower section of the line is the whole of it. Normally read as the favourable case when the underlying moves as required — the qualification being that this curve is the expiration payoff, while the modelled result above it also applies the implied-volatility change and the days elapsed. Direction alone does not settle it.

The flat lower section is the full debit, and it is the maximum loss because it has already been paid to the other side of these contracts. Normally read as risk that is defined, which is not the same as risk that is small: the entire amount is lost at every underlying price along that flat section. The line is the expiration payoff, and time and implied volatility move the result before then in either direction.

Increasing risk after a loss is the recovery escalation the lesson warns against; the percentage rule does the opposite automatically.
That is fixed-dollar sizing. At a fixed percentage the amount is recomputed from the smaller balance, so it falls.
50% of the remaining half is only a quarter of the original; the recovery is measured from the reduced balance, not from the peak.
75% of the remaining half brings the account to 87.5% of its peak. Only doubling, 100%, gets back to it.
Fewer trades slows everything down but does not change the depth of a streak of a given length; the size of each loss does.
A written stop bounds each loss; it is the control, not the damage.

6.0% is the fixed-dollar answer, three losses of the same $1,000 on $50,000. At a fixed percentage the second and third losses are taken on a smaller balance: 0.98 × 0.98 × 0.98 = 0.9412, a 5.9% drawdown.
8% would take four 2% losses at a fixed dollar amount; three at a fixed percentage compound to 0.98³ = 0.9412, a 5.9% drawdown.

The stop sits at 109.40, 1.05 above the protected low that defines this swing — and two bars inside that swing printed lows of 109.25 and 108.50 without breaking it. Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. Normally read as the ordinary case, in which a price exists at the level and the half-spread is the visible cost of taking it. That one window contains both outcomes is the point: the reading holds only while there is a price to fill against.

Each of these positions has sold a right to someone who paid for it, and that is where the ceiling on this line comes from: beyond it the position stops taking part in the move. Normally read as a defined outcome, and the geometry is defined — but the curve is the payoff at expiration, so an assignment before then leaves the underlying obligation rather than a point on this line. The premium received is the price agreed for that ceiling, not a bound on what the position can lose.

The debit has already been paid to the other side of these contracts, which is why the flat lower section of the line is the whole of it. Normally read as the favourable case when the underlying moves as required — the qualification being that this curve is the expiration payoff, while the modelled result above it also applies the implied-volatility change and the days elapsed. Direction alone does not settle it.

The flat lower section is the full debit, and it is the maximum loss because it has already been paid to the other side of these contracts. Normally read as risk that is defined, which is not the same as risk that is small: the entire amount is lost at every underlying price along that flat section. The line is the expiration payoff, and time and implied volatility move the result before then in either direction.

In a bullish setup, buyers remain in control while the protected low holds.
A break below the protected low shows that buyers failed to defend the structure. The stop belongs beyond invalidation, not at an arbitrary dollar loss.
What to understand
Keep the process direct: define the risk, calculate it, and enforce the limit.
Structural stop
Placed beyond the level whose break invalidates the setup.
Noise risk
A stop inside normal price movement may exit while the thesis remains valid.
Size adjustment
A wider valid stop requires a smaller position, not a forced tighter stop.
Change the risk conditions
Adjust the controls and read the market behavior and account impact after each change.
Stop-Loss and Structural Invalidation Lab
Synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Apply it in order
Risk calculations should happen before the order is submitted.
Identify the protected level
Use the swing or range boundary that must hold for the thesis.
Allow for normal movement
Place the exit beyond invalidation rather than directly inside common wick activity.
Size from the distance
Calculate quantity only after entry and stop are known.
Check your understanding
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. Where should a structural stop be based?
2. A valid stop is wider than expected. What should usually change?
3. Price wicks below a minor low but holds the protected low. What happened?
4. Entry 113.80, protected low 108.50, stop placed 0.15 beneath it, dollar risk $500. How many shares?
Practical rules
Define invalidation before calculating quantity.
Use candle-close or wick rules consistently.
Include possible slippage beyond the trigger.
Common mistakes
Placing stops where the loss feels comfortable.
Moving a stop farther after entry.
Using the same percentage-distance stop for every chart.

Stop-Loss and Structural Invalidation

The stop sits at 109.40, 1.05 above the protected low that defines this swing — and two bars inside that swing printed lows of 109.25 and 108.50 without breaking it. Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. Normally read as the ordinary case, in which a price exists at the level and the half-spread is the visible cost of taking it. That one window contains both outcomes is the point: the reading holds only while there is a price to fill against.

Each of these positions has sold a right to someone who paid for it, and that is where the ceiling on this line comes from: beyond it the position stops taking part in the move. Normally read as a defined outcome, and the geometry is defined — but the curve is the payoff at expiration, so an assignment before then leaves the underlying obligation rather than a point on this line. The premium received is the price agreed for that ceiling, not a bound on what the position can lose.

The debit has already been paid to the other side of these contracts, which is why the flat lower section of the line is the whole of it. Normally read as the favourable case when the underlying moves as required — the qualification being that this curve is the expiration payoff, while the modelled result above it also applies the implied-volatility change and the days elapsed. Direction alone does not settle it.

The flat lower section is the full debit, and it is the maximum loss because it has already been paid to the other side of these contracts. Normally read as risk that is defined, which is not the same as risk that is small: the entire amount is lost at every underlying price along that flat section. The line is the expiration payoff, and time and implied volatility move the result before then in either direction.

clauses.expected: Trading Risk Plan
Combine account limits, position sizing, execution constraints, portfolio exposure, options rules, and review triggers into one testable risk specification.
A risk plan defines the response before market pressure changes the decision.
The plan states how much can be lost, when trading stops, how exposure is calculated, and which conditions prohibit a trade.
What to understand
Keep the process direct: define the risk, calculate it, and enforce the limit.
Numeric limits
Risk per trade, portfolio heat, leverage, daily loss, and weekly loss must be measurable.
Decision rules
Specify when to reduce size, reject a trade, or stop trading.
Review triggers
Define when results require investigation, simulation, or strategy suspension.
Change the risk conditions
Adjust the controls and read the market behavior and account impact after each change.
Trading Risk Plan Lab
Synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Apply it in order
Risk calculations should happen before the order is submitted.
Write the limits
Use exact percentages, dollars, and conditions.
Check contradictions
Open-risk limits must be compatible with per-trade risk and maximum concurrent positions.
Export and enforce
Use the same specification in journals, backtests, alerts, and future automation.
Check your understanding
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. A risk plan should be written:
2. What makes a risk rule testable?
3. What should happen when plan limits conflict?
4. Risk per trade 1%, maximum positions 4, maximum open risk 5%. What does the validator in this lesson’s lab say?
Practical rules
Use measurable limits and explicit actions.
Validate portfolio, leverage, and options rules together.
Version the plan and record every change.
Common mistakes
Using vague terms such as “small risk.”
Allowing exceptions without predefined criteria.
Changing multiple limits after a short losing sample.
Official reading
The labs use simplified synthetic examples. These sources cover the underlying risk and execution concepts.
CME Group · Trading Strategies in Your Trade Plan Write exact entry, exit, stop, target, and portfolio-risk conditions.
FINRA · Risk Risk tolerance and risk types should be understood before investing.

The stop sits at 109.40, 1.05 above the protected low that defines this swing — and two bars inside that swing printed lows of 109.25 and 108.50 without breaking it. Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. Normally read as the ordinary case, in which a price exists at the level and the half-spread is the visible cost of taking it. That one window contains both outcomes is the point: the reading holds only while there is a price to fill against.

Each of these positions has sold a right to someone who paid for it, and that is where the ceiling on this line comes from: beyond it the position stops taking part in the move. Normally read as a defined outcome, and the geometry is defined — but the curve is the payoff at expiration, so an assignment before then leaves the underlying obligation rather than a point on this line. The premium received is the price agreed for that ceiling, not a bound on what the position can lose.

The debit has already been paid to the other side of these contracts, which is why the flat lower section of the line is the whole of it. Normally read as the favourable case when the underlying moves as required — the qualification being that this curve is the expiration payoff, while the modelled result above it also applies the implied-volatility change and the days elapsed. Direction alone does not settle it.

The flat lower section is the full debit, and it is the maximum loss because it has already been paid to the other side of these contracts. Normally read as risk that is defined, which is not the same as risk that is small: the entire amount is lost at every underlying price along that flat section. The line is the expiration payoff, and time and implied volatility move the result before then in either direction.

The stop sits at 109.40, 1.05 above the protected low that defines this swing — and two bars inside that swing printed lows of 109.25 and 108.50 without breaking it. Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. Normally read as the ordinary case, in which a price exists at the level and the half-spread is the visible cost of taking it. That one window contains both outcomes is the point: the reading holds only while there is a price to fill against.

Each of these positions has sold a right to someone who paid for it, and that is where the ceiling on this line comes from: beyond it the position stops taking part in the move. Normally read as a defined outcome, and the geometry is defined — but the curve is the payoff at expiration, so an assignment before then leaves the underlying obligation rather than a point on this line. The premium received is the price agreed for that ceiling, not a bound on what the position can lose.

The debit has already been paid to the other side of these contracts, which is why the flat lower section of the line is the whole of it. Normally read as the favourable case when the underlying moves as required — the qualification being that this curve is the expiration payoff, while the modelled result above it also applies the implied-volatility change and the days elapsed. Direction alone does not settle it.

The flat lower section is the full debit, and it is the maximum loss because it has already been paid to the other side of these contracts. Normally read as risk that is defined, which is not the same as risk that is small: the entire amount is lost at every underlying price along that flat section. The line is the expiration payoff, and time and implied volatility move the result before then in either direction.

clauses.expected: Win Rate, Average Win/Loss, and Expectancy
Combine win rate, average win, average loss, and trading costs to estimate the average outcome per trade.
The market produces a distribution of wins and losses, not certainty on each trade.
A lower win rate can still be profitable when average wins are sufficiently larger than average losses. Expectancy combines both sides.
What to understand
Keep the process direct: define the risk, calculate it, and enforce the limit.
Win rate
Winning trades divided by total trades.
Payoff ratio
Average win divided by average loss.
Expectancy
Expected average R or dollars per trade after losses and costs.
Change the risk conditions
Adjust the controls and read the market behavior and account impact after each change.
Win Rate, Average Win/Loss, and Expectancy Lab
Synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Apply it in order
Risk calculations should happen before the order is submitted.
Use enough trades
A small sample can produce unstable win-rate and payoff estimates.
Include all costs
Commissions, spread, slippage, and assignment effects reduce expectancy.
Evaluate the combination
Never judge a system from win rate alone.
Check your understanding
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. A strategy wins 40% with +2R wins and -1R losses. Expectancy before costs is:
2. Why is win rate alone incomplete?
3. What do trading costs do to expectancy?
4. Average win 1.5R, average loss 1R, no costs. What is the breakeven win rate?
Practical rules
Measure win rate and payoff together.
Use net results after all known costs.
Track expectancy by setup, timeframe, and regime.
Common mistakes
Optimizing only for win rate.
Using best-case targets instead of realized exits.
Treating a 10-trade sample as stable evidence.

The labs use simplified synthetic examples. These sources cover the underlying risk and execution concepts.

The stop sits at 109.40, 1.05 above the protected low that defines this swing — and two bars inside that swing printed lows of 109.25 and 108.50 without breaking it. Normally read as a level ordinary movement inside the pattern can reach, so an exit there ends the trade before the structure has said anything. The reading itself ends only at a close below 108.35.

Lows rise from 108.50 at bar 30 to 112.27 at bar 41, and the entry prints at 113.80 above all of them. Normally read as an advance whose most recent higher low is still intact; the stop at 108.35 sits 0.15 under that low, so the level that ends the trade and the level that ends the reading are the same one. Nothing here says the sequence continues, only that it has not yet been contradicted.

At 106.35 the stop is 2.00 below the level whose break would invalidate this structure, at a price the series last traded twenty-nine bars before the entry. Normally read as distance the pattern is not asking for: the reading has already failed by the time price arrives there, so the extra 2.00 is carried without being part of the invalidation. It buys nothing against a gap either, which jumps a far stop and a near one alike.

The drawn series makes higher lows into the entry: across its last thirty bars the deepest is 5.86 under the entry price and the most recent is 0.33 under it. A stop within six points of entry therefore sits inside the band those bars have already travelled, which is normally read as a level ordinary movement can reach without the advance being contradicted. The calculator cannot see that — it divides the budget by whatever distance it is handed, and the size it returns bounds the loss on one trade at a normal fill, which is the assumption the slippage reserve exists to qualify.

More than six points under the entry puts the stop below every low this series has printed in its last thirty-one bars. Normally read as more distance than the recent structure is asking for; the arithmetic accepts it either way and simply returns fewer units for the same budget. Fewer units do not remove the exposure to a gap through the level — that is what the slippage reserve prices, not the stop distance.

After the entry bar this series never trades more than 0.62 below it, reaches 7.30 above at its highest and closes 6.64 above at the end of the window. Normally read as an advance that was never handed back to the entry — but the four levels drawn here come from the inputs rather than from these bars, so a target or an exit can sit where the series never went. The one distance the chart does fix is entry to stop; that is 1R, and it stays 1R whatever happens afterwards.

The same rising series is drawn: at its worst it is 0.62 below the entry, at its best 7.30 above. Normally read as a favourable path, which is exactly why a result under +1R is worth separating from it — the exit input decides where the trade came out, not these bars. R was fixed by the entry-to-stop distance before any of this, and nothing later in the window changes the unit the result is measured in.

In this state the series is drawn falling: from the entry bar on it reaches 10.08 below the entry, never trades more than 0.82 above it (0.31 once the entry bar itself is past), and closes 9.34 below. Normally read as an entry that was wrong almost immediately — with the caveat that the chart follows the exit input rather than producing it, so it shows the sign of the result and not the path that produced it. The stop distance set before entry is still the unit: a 1R loss and a 3R loss are different sizes of the same plan failing.

Sixty-five bars run from 100.40 to 107.74 and true range averages about 1.2 at every lookback the period slider offers, putting a 2× ATR distance at 2.36. Normally read as an orderly advance rather than a strong one: 26 of the 65 bars still close below their own open, and no bar in the last thirty printed a low more than 2× ATR under the previous close. ATR measures range and not direction, so the smaller distance permits more size without making the direction any more certain.

True range here averages about 2.4 at any lookback the slider offers, twice the quiet regime, and the window ends at 95.27 — 5.49 below where it started, after reaching 105.73. Normally read as a market whose bar-to-bar range has doubled, which is why the same dollar budget supports roughly half the size at a 2× ATR distance; that is arithmetic rather than a forecast. Wider ranges also widen the distance a stop can be jumped by, so what the sizing holds constant is the planned loss, not the realized one.

The bar after the gap opens 5.00 under the previous close with no print anywhere between the two, so the trigger is a price at which nothing traded. Normally read as the difference between a price and a fill — a limit protects the price it names and for that reason cannot execute inside a range where no transaction occurred. The position is still open here, so what the chart shows is not yet what the account has realized.

The bar after the gap carries a true range of 5.72 against a median near 1.15 for this window, almost all of it the 5.00 opening jump. Normally read as a repricing rather than a move through the level: an order resting at the trigger could only be filled on the far side of it, which is why the realized loss is larger than the distance drawn between entry and stop. The chart distance is the plan and the fill is the outcome; the two separate exactly where no trade occurred in between.

The gap bar is still on this chart — 5.00 below the previous close on a 5.72 true range against a median near 1.15 — even in the scenario where the exit fills close to the trigger. Normally read as the ordinary case, in which a price exists at the level and the half-spread is the visible cost of taking it. That one window contains both outcomes is the point: the reading holds only while there is a price to fill against.

Each of these positions has sold a right to someone who paid for it, and that is where the ceiling on this line comes from: beyond it the position stops taking part in the move. Normally read as a defined outcome, and the geometry is defined — but the curve is the payoff at expiration, so an assignment before then leaves the underlying obligation rather than a point on this line. The premium received is the price agreed for that ceiling, not a bound on what the position can lose.

The debit has already been paid to the other side of these contracts, which is why the flat lower section of the line is the whole of it. Normally read as the favourable case when the underlying moves as required — the qualification being that this curve is the expiration payoff, while the modelled result above it also applies the implied-volatility change and the days elapsed. Direction alone does not settle it.

The flat lower section is the full debit, and it is the maximum loss because it has already been paid to the other side of these contracts. Normally read as risk that is defined, which is not the same as risk that is small: the entire amount is lost at every underlying price along that flat section. The line is the expiration payoff, and time and implied volatility move the result before then in either direction.

clauses.expected: Backtesting Fundamentals
Use historical data to simulate a defined strategy, separate assumptions from results, and state what a backtest can and cannot establish.
A backtest measures how fixed rules behaved in selected historical conditions.
It does not prove that the same behavior will continue. The result depends on data, execution assumptions, costs, and market regimes.
What to understand
Keep each definition operational so it can be implemented and tested.
Rules before results
Define entries, exits, sizing, costs, and timing before inspecting performance.
Historical simulation
Apply the same rules consistently across every eligible bar or event.
Evidence, not certainty
Use the result to reject weak ideas and estimate behavior, not to guarantee future profit.
Backtesting Assumptions Lab
Change the market regime, rule parameters, and costs. Compare the strategy result with the market behavior that produced it.
Backtesting Assumptions Lab
Deterministic synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Backtest in a fixed order
Do not optimize the conclusion before the test is defined.
Define
Write the hypothesis and exact rules.
Simulate
Apply realistic timing, fills, costs, and accounting.
Evaluate
Review returns, drawdown, trade count, regimes, and stability.
Check your understanding
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. What does a backtest directly measure?
2. Which item must be defined before reviewing results?
3. A strong historical result is best treated as:
4. A rule completes two trades, +7.5% and −1.1%. Its net return is:
Practical rules
Write the hypothesis before running the test.
Include realistic costs and execution timing.
Review performance by market regime, not only overall return.
Common mistakes
Treating historical profit as a prediction.
Changing rules after seeing every losing period.
Ignoring how assumptions created the result.
Official reading
The labs are simplified simulations. These sources cover historical performance, data, costs, or execution limitations.
FINRA · Smart Beta—What You Need to Know Explains that historical backtesting is hypothetical and does not predict future performance.
