Price finishes about 29% above where the sample opens and the deepest setback from a running high is roughly 3.5%. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices for the whole window, each pullback ending above the one before it. A close back under 123.4, the low the final third has held, would end that reading — and a rule scored only here has been measured against a market that never made it necessary.

Price ends about 16% lower, with the sample high of 103.82 at bar 48 never revisited and the low of 81.36 arriving at bar 186. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices, each rally stopping under the previous one. A close back above 94.18, the highest price of the last third, would break it; a long-only rule scored on this sample is being measured mostly on how well it stays out.

Price ends about 1% from where it started after rotating between 95.72 and 106.11 for all 190 bars. The usual interpretation is that neither side is making the other give ground at these prices. It stops reading as balance when a close holds outside that band instead of turning back into it — and a trend rule scored only here is being measured on a market that never offered one.

Price advances about 19% into bar 53, gives it back through the middle of the sample, and finishes about 3% below where it opened after reaching 93.36 near bar 186. Normally read as three conditions inside one window rather than one condition. That is what makes the sample useful: a single net return over these 190 bars averages an advance, a rotation and a decline into one number that describes none of them.

Price runs about 30% higher into bar 90, then loses roughly 19% from its high of 132.94 and finishes at 112.70. Normally read as both sides moving price in size, with bar ranges wide enough that the distance between a signal and its fill stops being a rounding error. Direction is the least of it here — the same rule run on this sample and on the trending one is being asked two different questions.

Price opens at 100.00 and closes at 139.14, higher in each of its three thirds (105.3, 113.2 and 130.0 on average), with the sample low of 99.10 at bar 2 and the high of 140.28 at bar 148. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices for the whole window, each setback ending above the last; the deepest, 4.3% from bar 45 to bar 65, is regained inside twenty bars. A close back under 121.73, the lowest low of the final third, would end that reading — and the default long breakout rule scored here (seven trades, every one a time exit) is being measured on a market that never made its stop necessary.

The first seventy-two bars stay between 94.67 and 100.60; price then leaves that area and the remaining fifty-seven bars hold above 101.70. Normally read as acceptance above the old range rather than a probe through it, since the level that used to cap price became the floor of everything after it. A close back inside the old band would end the reading — and the rule you are composing knows none of this, because it fires on its own arithmetic and not on the shape.

Price rotates between 93.25 and 101.52 for all 150 bars and finishes about 2.6% below where it started. The usual interpretation is two-way trade at an agreed area with neither side holding the other's ground. It stops reading that way when a close holds outside the band; until then a breakout rule scored here is being measured almost entirely on how it treats signals that do not follow through.

Price holds between about 91.9 and 101.68 for the first seventy-two bars, then closes below that area and declines to 65.83, printing the lowest low of the sample on the final bar. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices with no rally reaching back to the area price left. A close above 89.07, the highest price of the final sixty-three bars, would be the first thing to break it — the sample simply ends before anything of the kind is tested.

Repaired, the series tracks the clean reference: 100.00 at the open to 127.56 at the close, higher in each third (103.6, 110.8 and 121.0 on average), with its low of 99.10 at bar 2 and its highest close, 127.94, at bar 118; the deepest setback is 4.3%, from bar 45 to bar 65. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices throughout. Be precise about what validation established: that the flagged bars are now consistent with their neighbours — a statement about the data, and no evidence about the market it was drawn to resemble.

Every flagged bar closes about 28% above the bar before it, and the bar after prints straight back at the old level. A single bar like that is normally read as a violent repricing, which is exactly the trap: no trade produced it, the value was multiplied in. The tell is on the chart rather than in the number — a real repricing leaves the bars after it somewhere new, and these leave them where they were.

The flagged bars carry no price at all, so the line stops and restarts around them. There is nothing to read as market behaviour, which makes this the least misleading defect to look at and the most misleading to compute on: every hole disqualifies the twelve bars that follow it, so the breakout count on the raw series is a fraction of the validated one — the signal difference in the row above is that gap. Absent data does not announce itself as absent in a result.

The flagged bars repeat the previous bar's open, high, low and close exactly. Two identical bars are normally read as a pause, an area where price stopped making progress, and here they are one bar recorded twice. It moves the level by about a percent or less and leaves the breakout count essentially where it was, which is why it survives review: the damage is to the time axis and to anything that counts bars, not to the price.

The flagged bars print the previous close as their open, high, low and close, so they have no range at all. A zero-range bar is normally read as a period nobody contested. Here it is a feed that stopped updating, and the distinction matters to anything measuring range or volatility: the level stays within about a percent of the clean series while the bar's range is understated all the way to zero.

The defects arrive in a fixed order as the count rises: a bar 28% above its neighbour, then a bar with no data, then a bar copied from the one before it, then a bar with no range. Only the first is readable as market behaviour at all, and it is the one that would be read as a violent repricing. The other three are not readable, which is where the quieter damage sits — they move the breakout count without ever looking like anything on the chart.

Repaired, the line tracks the clean reference: price rotates between about 93.5 and 101.7 and ends within half a percent of where it began. Normally read as two-way trade with neither side holding ground. Be precise about what has been established, though — the series is now consistent with the reference, which is a statement about the data and not evidence about the market.

Repaired, the series rises to about 107.8 near bar 54 and then declines to finish about 9% below where it opened. Normally read as one condition replacing another inside a single sample. Validation changed none of that; it removed the bars that were not measurements, which is the whole of what cleaning can claim.

All eight names are carried for the whole window and the line ends 1.8% above where it began, having fallen from 108.1 to 97.2 in the single period FAIL loses 82% of its value. Normally read as a market that went almost nowhere. What the line cannot show is that seven of the eight names ended higher — VALUE among them once its cash distribution is counted, SPLT once its split is — and the eighth was enough to take the window back: a breadth reading rather than a direction one, and the only version of this chart in which the failure is still counted.

The same eighty-three periods, with the one name that failed removed, end 16.2% higher and never set back more than 0.3%. Normally read as a broad and orderly advance, produced without a single price on the chart changing. The reading is made by the universe rather than by the market: excluding FAIL is a decision available only after period 55, and the test claims to have started at period 1.

Four of the eight names are held, chosen by their change across the whole window, and the line ends 22.5% higher with a deepest setback of 0.5%. Normally read as selection that worked. The smoothness is the giveaway: the ranking used each series' final value to decide what to hold from the first period, and an advance this clean is what sorting on an outcome produces, not what choosing under uncertainty produces.

The line drops from 104.7 to 98.5 in one period at 42 and ends 5.0% below where it started. A six-point fall across an entire equal-weight universe is normally read as a broad sell-off. Nothing sold off: SPLT's quoted price halved in a two-for-one split and the holder's value did not move. Twelve periods earlier, at 30, VALUE's quoted price fell 4.3% going ex-distribution and the cash was booked nowhere — a smaller version of the same error, hidden inside an up step. The split is the one defect here that a chart cannot tell from a real decline without the corporate-action record beside it.

At sixty minutes the regular session becomes seven bars and the average bar covers 2.12% of price, against 0.38% for that same session at five minutes. Take the bar beginning at minute 360: it opens at 110.04, trades between 109.99 and 112.25 and closes at 111.43, which is normally read as an up bar with a small tail — and it is exactly that. What it cannot say is order: a stop at 110 and a target at 112 both sit inside it, and the bar records that each was reached, not which was reached first.

The added bars carry the minutes before 60 and after 449, which average 337 in volume against 1,994 during the session. Including them moves the last close on the chart from 110.34 to 106.19 — normally read as the market giving four points back, and it did trade there. The reading that matters is a different one: those prices are on the chart whether or not the system could act at them, and at the default interval and lookback they take the breakout count from 10 to 13.

The regular session opens at 99.95 and closes at 110.34, with its low of 99.88 in the first minutes and its high of 112.25 late. Between them, minutes 115 to 299 hold between 102.66 and 104.54. Normally read as higher prices being accepted in two legs with an acceptance area between them; a close back under that shelf would end the reading, and finer bars are what let a test place a signal or a fill inside it at all.

Seven entry markers, each one bar after a close exceeded the previous eighteen closes. Three sit inside the advance from 97.84 at bar 26 to 108.17 at bar 57 — entries at bars 36, 46 and 56 — and win; four sit in the rotation between 106.76 and 110.92 that follows and in the decline to 102.56 at bar 148 — bars 73, 96, 122 and 157 — and lose. Normally read as a breakout rule that works while buyers are accepting higher prices and stops working when they are not, which is what a breakout rule is. Every marker sits one bar after its signal, and that is the whole of what this chart claims: the rule acted on bars that had already printed, and it finished at −0.9%.

Each marker has moved onto the bar whose own close produced the signal — bar 35 instead of 36, bar 44 instead of 46 — and there are still seven. In this gapless synthetic series the next open is the signal close, so the fill price did not change; the clock did. Every exit arrives one bar earlier and the result is −2.8% instead of −0.9%, while the market underneath still reads as an advance to bar 57, a rotation to bar 105 and a decline after it. What changed is not the reading but the claim behind it: the fill is booked at a close that was not knowable until that bar had finished.

Three of the seven entries survive, at bars 36, 46 and 56, all inside the advance, and the four that lost are gone. Normally read as a rule that found the breakouts which continued. It found nothing: the filter read the open of the bar each trade would exit on and kept the signal only when that price was higher, so the markers are placed by information that did not exist when the signal fired. At the default settings the selected return is +5.4% against −0.9% for the causal baseline — a weak rule made to look precise by choosing its trades after the fact.

Both errors are on together: three markers, at bars 35, 44 and 55, each on the bar whose close created the signal, each kept because the exit bar said it would win. The market is the same one every other state on this page shows — an advance to bar 57, a rotation to bar 105, a decline after it — so nothing about the chart's structure distinguishes this run from the honest one at −0.9%; this one reads +5.0%. Only the selection differs, which is the point: there is no shape on a price chart that reveals a test which knew too much.

The order level sits outside everything price does after bar 21: the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 from there, the short path 94.37 to 103.65. There is no entry or exit on the chart to read, and that is the reading — a resting order is a request, and a level price never reaches is a level that never traded. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level did.

No entry or exit is on the chart because the order was withdrawn before price reached its level. From bar 21 the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 and the short path 94.37 to 103.65, so a level outside that range was never going to fill, and a level inside it was reached, if at all, only after the order's life had run out. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level and the chosen lifetime did — and a test that leaves resting orders open forever is claiming fills at prices from a market the signal never saw.

From bar 21 price works from 99.80 up to a high of 110.78 at bar 37 and closes the sample at 109.49, with the deepest close-to-close setback along the way about 2.61 points. Normally read as higher prices being accepted once the order is active. Bar 26 is where the reading has to slow down: it opens at 102.87 and closes at 106.70, so any level inside that bar is credited or missed on an assumption about a path the bar itself does not record.

Bar 22 opens at 103.80 after bar 21 closed at 99.80, and its lowest trade is 103.51. Normally read as a four-point repricing between bars, which is what it is. The part to read carefully is the space it left behind: at the default stop and target the target level, 103.09, never traded on that bar, so the exit is booked at the first price that did, the open at 103.80 — 2.36R instead of the 2.00R the level promised. A gap through a target is a gift; the same gap through a stop, one bar later at 100.41, is the −1.72R the stop-market order shows.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range across that stretch from 1.81 points to 4.61 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. Be precise about what expanded: anything computed from closes sees an identical market, and only the touches change — the same target is reached a bar earlier here purely because a high was extended to it.

From bar 21 price first works against the short, reaching 103.65 at bar 26, before declining to 94.37 at bar 49 and closing the sample at 96.09. Normally read as an advance that fails and gives way to lower prices being accepted. The order of events is the reading: about three points of adverse movement arrive before any of the eight the decline eventually offers, so a stop placed inside that first stretch settles the trade before the market does anything the label describes.

Bar 22 opens at 95.73 after bar 21 closed at 99.73, and its lowest trade is 95.43. Normally read as a four-point repricing in the short's favour. It is also where a gap stops being a gift: at the default target of 94.80 the move is not enough to close the trade, bar 23 trades back up to 101.77, and the same gap that would have been read as confirmation is followed by the stop.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range there from 1.68 points to 4.48 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. What expanded is the recorded extreme and not the path: a stop above the entry is touched by a high that was stretched to it, and a test reading closes alone would report the same market with a different outcome.

The benchmark ends 6.7% above where it started, having reached 113.7 and traded as low as 96.3, with a deepest setback of 11.0%. Normally read as a market that ended higher; the word the line does not support is continued, since the index spent part of the window below its own opening level. That is what the comparison beside it runs against: a strategy is being scored on a path, not on the 6.7%.

The benchmark ends 10.6% lower, reaching 106.9 early and 87.6 late, with a deepest setback of 18.1%. Normally read as lower prices being accepted across the whole market. Worth being exact about what carries that: 137 of the 252 steps close up, so the direction comes from the size of the down steps rather than their count, and a majority of up days under a falling index is not a contradiction.

The benchmark rotates between 93.1 and 107.5 and finishes 3.1% below where it began. Normally read as a market with no sustained direction to lend a strategy or to take away from it. Note also that a 13.4% setback still occurs here with no trend to attribute it to, which is what makes this the sample where an independent return is easiest to see as independent.

The benchmark covers 85.6 to 114.5 and ends 8.2% lower, with annualised volatility of 26.8% against 14.2% in the other samples and a largest single step of 3.89%. Normally read as both sides moving price in size without either holding it. The drift underneath is identical to the balanced sample and only the step size differs, which is precisely why return alone cannot separate the two and a risk-adjusted comparison exists at all.

Build a point-in-time universe, include failed and delisted instruments, and adjust splits and distributions without using information learned later.
A historical universe must contain what was actually available at each point in time.
Keeping only today’s survivors removes failures. Selecting assets after seeing returns makes the test know the future.
What to understand
Keep each definition operational so it can be implemented and tested.
Survivorship bias
Exclude failed instruments and historical performance usually looks stronger.
Selection bias
Choosing markets or periods after reviewing results changes the question being tested.
Corporate actions
Splits, dividends, mergers, and delistings must be handled consistently with the strategy.

Slippage is the difference between the planned and the actual fill, the subject of Transaction Costs, Spread, Slippage, and Liquidity; it has nothing to do with which names are in the test.
Spreading exposure across time is a portfolio idea; a universe that contains only today's survivors is a data defect, not a diversification.
A holder of one share at $110 holds two at $55 after the split; nothing about the value changed.
A split moves the quoted price and the share count in opposite directions; the position is worth what it was.
Costs are charged at each fill from the execution model; universe membership does not enter them.
Drawdown is read off the equity curve; the universe decides what is in the curve, not whether it can be measured.
That is the unadjusted figure, and it books a loss no holder took; twice the shares at half the price is the same value.
The share count doubled and the price halved; counting only one side of that gives a return in either direction, and both are wrong.

Price finishes about 29% above where the sample opens and the deepest setback from a running high is roughly 3.5%. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices for the whole window, each pullback ending above the one before it. A close back under 123.4, the low the final third has held, would end that reading — and a rule scored only here has been measured against a market that never made it necessary.

Price ends about 16% lower, with the sample high of 103.82 at bar 48 never revisited and the low of 81.36 arriving at bar 186. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices, each rally stopping under the previous one. A close back above 94.18, the highest price of the last third, would break it; a long-only rule scored on this sample is being measured mostly on how well it stays out.

Price ends about 1% from where it started after rotating between 95.72 and 106.11 for all 190 bars. The usual interpretation is that neither side is making the other give ground at these prices. It stops reading as balance when a close holds outside that band instead of turning back into it — and a trend rule scored only here is being measured on a market that never offered one.

Price advances about 19% into bar 53, gives it back through the middle of the sample, and finishes about 3% below where it opened after reaching 93.36 near bar 186. Normally read as three conditions inside one window rather than one condition. That is what makes the sample useful: a single net return over these 190 bars averages an advance, a rotation and a decline into one number that describes none of them.

Price runs about 30% higher into bar 90, then loses roughly 19% from its high of 132.94 and finishes at 112.70. Normally read as both sides moving price in size, with bar ranges wide enough that the distance between a signal and its fill stops being a rounding error. Direction is the least of it here — the same rule run on this sample and on the trending one is being asked two different questions.

Price opens at 100.00 and closes at 139.14, higher in each of its three thirds (105.3, 113.2 and 130.0 on average), with the sample low of 99.10 at bar 2 and the high of 140.28 at bar 148. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices for the whole window, each setback ending above the last; the deepest, 4.3% from bar 45 to bar 65, is regained inside twenty bars. A close back under 121.73, the lowest low of the final third, would end that reading — and the default long breakout rule scored here (seven trades, every one a time exit) is being measured on a market that never made its stop necessary.

The first seventy-two bars stay between 94.67 and 100.60; price then leaves that area and the remaining fifty-seven bars hold above 101.70. Normally read as acceptance above the old range rather than a probe through it, since the level that used to cap price became the floor of everything after it. A close back inside the old band would end the reading — and the rule you are composing knows none of this, because it fires on its own arithmetic and not on the shape.

Price rotates between 93.25 and 101.52 for all 150 bars and finishes about 2.6% below where it started. The usual interpretation is two-way trade at an agreed area with neither side holding the other's ground. It stops reading that way when a close holds outside the band; until then a breakout rule scored here is being measured almost entirely on how it treats signals that do not follow through.

Price holds between about 91.9 and 101.68 for the first seventy-two bars, then closes below that area and declines to 65.83, printing the lowest low of the sample on the final bar. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices with no rally reaching back to the area price left. A close above 89.07, the highest price of the final sixty-three bars, would be the first thing to break it — the sample simply ends before anything of the kind is tested.

Repaired, the series tracks the clean reference: 100.00 at the open to 127.56 at the close, higher in each third (103.6, 110.8 and 121.0 on average), with its low of 99.10 at bar 2 and its highest close, 127.94, at bar 118; the deepest setback is 4.3%, from bar 45 to bar 65. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices throughout. Be precise about what validation established: that the flagged bars are now consistent with their neighbours — a statement about the data, and no evidence about the market it was drawn to resemble.

Every flagged bar closes about 28% above the bar before it, and the bar after prints straight back at the old level. A single bar like that is normally read as a violent repricing, which is exactly the trap: no trade produced it, the value was multiplied in. The tell is on the chart rather than in the number — a real repricing leaves the bars after it somewhere new, and these leave them where they were.

The flagged bars carry no price at all, so the line stops and restarts around them. There is nothing to read as market behaviour, which makes this the least misleading defect to look at and the most misleading to compute on: every hole disqualifies the twelve bars that follow it, so the breakout count on the raw series is a fraction of the validated one — the signal difference in the row above is that gap. Absent data does not announce itself as absent in a result.

The flagged bars repeat the previous bar's open, high, low and close exactly. Two identical bars are normally read as a pause, an area where price stopped making progress, and here they are one bar recorded twice. It moves the level by about a percent or less and leaves the breakout count essentially where it was, which is why it survives review: the damage is to the time axis and to anything that counts bars, not to the price.

The flagged bars print the previous close as their open, high, low and close, so they have no range at all. A zero-range bar is normally read as a period nobody contested. Here it is a feed that stopped updating, and the distinction matters to anything measuring range or volatility: the level stays within about a percent of the clean series while the bar's range is understated all the way to zero.

The defects arrive in a fixed order as the count rises: a bar 28% above its neighbour, then a bar with no data, then a bar copied from the one before it, then a bar with no range. Only the first is readable as market behaviour at all, and it is the one that would be read as a violent repricing. The other three are not readable, which is where the quieter damage sits — they move the breakout count without ever looking like anything on the chart.

Repaired, the line tracks the clean reference: price rotates between about 93.5 and 101.7 and ends within half a percent of where it began. Normally read as two-way trade with neither side holding ground. Be precise about what has been established, though — the series is now consistent with the reference, which is a statement about the data and not evidence about the market.

Repaired, the series rises to about 107.8 near bar 54 and then declines to finish about 9% below where it opened. Normally read as one condition replacing another inside a single sample. Validation changed none of that; it removed the bars that were not measurements, which is the whole of what cleaning can claim.

All eight names are carried for the whole window and the line ends 1.8% above where it began, having fallen from 108.1 to 97.2 in the single period FAIL loses 82% of its value. Normally read as a market that went almost nowhere. What the line cannot show is that seven of the eight names ended higher — VALUE among them once its cash distribution is counted, SPLT once its split is — and the eighth was enough to take the window back: a breadth reading rather than a direction one, and the only version of this chart in which the failure is still counted.

The same eighty-three periods, with the one name that failed removed, end 16.2% higher and never set back more than 0.3%. Normally read as a broad and orderly advance, produced without a single price on the chart changing. The reading is made by the universe rather than by the market: excluding FAIL is a decision available only after period 55, and the test claims to have started at period 1.

Four of the eight names are held, chosen by their change across the whole window, and the line ends 22.5% higher with a deepest setback of 0.5%. Normally read as selection that worked. The smoothness is the giveaway: the ranking used each series' final value to decide what to hold from the first period, and an advance this clean is what sorting on an outcome produces, not what choosing under uncertainty produces.

The line drops from 104.7 to 98.5 in one period at 42 and ends 5.0% below where it started. A six-point fall across an entire equal-weight universe is normally read as a broad sell-off. Nothing sold off: SPLT's quoted price halved in a two-for-one split and the holder's value did not move. Twelve periods earlier, at 30, VALUE's quoted price fell 4.3% going ex-distribution and the cash was booked nowhere — a smaller version of the same error, hidden inside an up step. The split is the one defect here that a chart cannot tell from a real decline without the corporate-action record beside it.

At sixty minutes the regular session becomes seven bars and the average bar covers 2.12% of price, against 0.38% for that same session at five minutes. Take the bar beginning at minute 360: it opens at 110.04, trades between 109.99 and 112.25 and closes at 111.43, which is normally read as an up bar with a small tail — and it is exactly that. What it cannot say is order: a stop at 110 and a target at 112 both sit inside it, and the bar records that each was reached, not which was reached first.

The added bars carry the minutes before 60 and after 449, which average 337 in volume against 1,994 during the session. Including them moves the last close on the chart from 110.34 to 106.19 — normally read as the market giving four points back, and it did trade there. The reading that matters is a different one: those prices are on the chart whether or not the system could act at them, and at the default interval and lookback they take the breakout count from 10 to 13.

The regular session opens at 99.95 and closes at 110.34, with its low of 99.88 in the first minutes and its high of 112.25 late. Between them, minutes 115 to 299 hold between 102.66 and 104.54. Normally read as higher prices being accepted in two legs with an acceptance area between them; a close back under that shelf would end the reading, and finer bars are what let a test place a signal or a fill inside it at all.

Seven entry markers, each one bar after a close exceeded the previous eighteen closes. Three sit inside the advance from 97.84 at bar 26 to 108.17 at bar 57 — entries at bars 36, 46 and 56 — and win; four sit in the rotation between 106.76 and 110.92 that follows and in the decline to 102.56 at bar 148 — bars 73, 96, 122 and 157 — and lose. Normally read as a breakout rule that works while buyers are accepting higher prices and stops working when they are not, which is what a breakout rule is. Every marker sits one bar after its signal, and that is the whole of what this chart claims: the rule acted on bars that had already printed, and it finished at −0.9%.

Each marker has moved onto the bar whose own close produced the signal — bar 35 instead of 36, bar 44 instead of 46 — and there are still seven. In this gapless synthetic series the next open is the signal close, so the fill price did not change; the clock did. Every exit arrives one bar earlier and the result is −2.8% instead of −0.9%, while the market underneath still reads as an advance to bar 57, a rotation to bar 105 and a decline after it. What changed is not the reading but the claim behind it: the fill is booked at a close that was not knowable until that bar had finished.

Three of the seven entries survive, at bars 36, 46 and 56, all inside the advance, and the four that lost are gone. Normally read as a rule that found the breakouts which continued. It found nothing: the filter read the open of the bar each trade would exit on and kept the signal only when that price was higher, so the markers are placed by information that did not exist when the signal fired. At the default settings the selected return is +5.4% against −0.9% for the causal baseline — a weak rule made to look precise by choosing its trades after the fact.

Both errors are on together: three markers, at bars 35, 44 and 55, each on the bar whose close created the signal, each kept because the exit bar said it would win. The market is the same one every other state on this page shows — an advance to bar 57, a rotation to bar 105, a decline after it — so nothing about the chart's structure distinguishes this run from the honest one at −0.9%; this one reads +5.0%. Only the selection differs, which is the point: there is no shape on a price chart that reveals a test which knew too much.

The order level sits outside everything price does after bar 21: the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 from there, the short path 94.37 to 103.65. There is no entry or exit on the chart to read, and that is the reading — a resting order is a request, and a level price never reaches is a level that never traded. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level did.

No entry or exit is on the chart because the order was withdrawn before price reached its level. From bar 21 the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 and the short path 94.37 to 103.65, so a level outside that range was never going to fill, and a level inside it was reached, if at all, only after the order's life had run out. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level and the chosen lifetime did — and a test that leaves resting orders open forever is claiming fills at prices from a market the signal never saw.

From bar 21 price works from 99.80 up to a high of 110.78 at bar 37 and closes the sample at 109.49, with the deepest close-to-close setback along the way about 2.61 points. Normally read as higher prices being accepted once the order is active. Bar 26 is where the reading has to slow down: it opens at 102.87 and closes at 106.70, so any level inside that bar is credited or missed on an assumption about a path the bar itself does not record.

Bar 22 opens at 103.80 after bar 21 closed at 99.80, and its lowest trade is 103.51. Normally read as a four-point repricing between bars, which is what it is. The part to read carefully is the space it left behind: at the default stop and target the target level, 103.09, never traded on that bar, so the exit is booked at the first price that did, the open at 103.80 — 2.36R instead of the 2.00R the level promised. A gap through a target is a gift; the same gap through a stop, one bar later at 100.41, is the −1.72R the stop-market order shows.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range across that stretch from 1.81 points to 4.61 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. Be precise about what expanded: anything computed from closes sees an identical market, and only the touches change — the same target is reached a bar earlier here purely because a high was extended to it.

From bar 21 price first works against the short, reaching 103.65 at bar 26, before declining to 94.37 at bar 49 and closing the sample at 96.09. Normally read as an advance that fails and gives way to lower prices being accepted. The order of events is the reading: about three points of adverse movement arrive before any of the eight the decline eventually offers, so a stop placed inside that first stretch settles the trade before the market does anything the label describes.

Bar 22 opens at 95.73 after bar 21 closed at 99.73, and its lowest trade is 95.43. Normally read as a four-point repricing in the short's favour. It is also where a gap stops being a gift: at the default target of 94.80 the move is not enough to close the trade, bar 23 trades back up to 101.77, and the same gap that would have been read as confirmation is followed by the stop.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range there from 1.68 points to 4.48 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. What expanded is the recorded extreme and not the path: a stop above the entry is touched by a high that was stretched to it, and a test reading closes alone would report the same market with a different outcome.

The benchmark ends 6.7% above where it started, having reached 113.7 and traded as low as 96.3, with a deepest setback of 11.0%. Normally read as a market that ended higher; the word the line does not support is continued, since the index spent part of the window below its own opening level. That is what the comparison beside it runs against: a strategy is being scored on a path, not on the 6.7%.

The benchmark ends 10.6% lower, reaching 106.9 early and 87.6 late, with a deepest setback of 18.1%. Normally read as lower prices being accepted across the whole market. Worth being exact about what carries that: 137 of the 252 steps close up, so the direction comes from the size of the down steps rather than their count, and a majority of up days under a falling index is not a contradiction.

The benchmark rotates between 93.1 and 107.5 and finishes 3.1% below where it began. Normally read as a market with no sustained direction to lend a strategy or to take away from it. Note also that a 13.4% setback still occurs here with no trend to attribute it to, which is what makes this the sample where an independent return is easiest to see as independent.

The benchmark covers 85.6 to 114.5 and ends 8.2% lower, with annualised volatility of 26.8% against 14.2% in the other samples and a largest single step of 3.89%. Normally read as both sides moving price in size without either holding it. The drift underneath is identical to the balanced sample and only the step size differs, which is precisely why return alone cannot separate the two and a risk-adjusted comparison exists at all.

clauses.expected: Testable Trading Rules and Hypotheses
Convert a market idea into deterministic entry, exit, sizing, and invalidation rules that produce the same decision from the same data.
A trading idea becomes testable only when every decision has an explicit condition.
“Buy strong stocks” is not a rule. A valid system states the data, threshold, timing, order, size, exit, and no-trade conditions.
What to understand
Keep each definition operational so it can be implemented and tested.
Hypothesis
State why a repeatable market behavior may produce an edge.
Deterministic rule
The same inputs must always produce the same signal.
Complete lifecycle
Define no-trade, entry, sizing, management, exit, and invalidation conditions.
Trading Rule Builder
Build a long or short rule, inspect its generated signals, and verify that the rule is complete enough to test.
Trading Rule Builder
Deterministic synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Convert observations into conditions
Use exact values and event timing.
Observe
Describe the price and volume behavior.
Specify
Translate it into measurable conditions.
Reject ambiguity
Remove discretionary words that cannot be calculated.
Check your understanding
Select one answer for each question. Feedback appears immediately.
1. Which statement is directly testable?
2. What should a complete rule include?
3. Why define the hypothesis first?
4. A rule reads: buy when the close exceeds the prior 20-bar high. Today's close is 104.20 and the prior 20-bar high is 104.00. The earliest price the rule can fill at is:
Practical rules
Use exact thresholds and time references.
Specify when the signal is known and when the order is placed.
Define conditions that prevent a trade.
Common mistakes
Using words such as strong, weak, or near without values.
Testing entry rules without exits.
Allowing manual exceptions during the test.
Official reading
The labs are simplified simulations. These sources cover historical performance, data, costs, or execution limitations.
FINRA · Smart Beta—What You Need to Know Explains that historical backtesting is hypothetical and does not predict future performance.
FINRA Rule 2210 · Communications with the Public Includes restrictions on performance projections and misleading performance claims.

"Looks strong" has no threshold; two people reading the same chart make different trades, so the rule is not deterministic.
A feeling has no data field, no value and no timestamp; nothing can be computed from it.
An entry with no exit is not a trade, and a test of it has no outcomes to measure.
A return is what the test produces, not what the rule states; a rule is the set of conditions that generate decisions.
A hypothesis is a claim to be tested, and most are rejected; it guarantees nothing.
The hypothesis says what data to look at and why; it cannot replace the data.
The signal exists only once the close is known, and by then that price has gone; Signal Timing, Look-Ahead Bias, and Data Leakage calls this a same-close fill.
104.00 is the level the close was compared with, not a price available after the comparison was made.

Price rotates between 93.25 and 101.52 for all 150 bars and finishes about 2.6% below where it started. The usual interpretation is two-way trade at an agreed area with neither side holding the other's ground. It stops reading that way when a close holds outside the band; until then a breakout rule scored here is being measured almost entirely on how it treats signals that do not follow through.

Price holds between about 91.9 and 101.68 for the first seventy-two bars, then closes below that area and declines to 65.83, printing the lowest low of the sample on the final bar. Normally read as sellers accepting lower prices with no rally reaching back to the area price left. A close above 89.07, the highest price of the final sixty-three bars, would be the first thing to break it — the sample simply ends before anything of the kind is tested.

Repaired, the series tracks the clean reference: 100.00 at the open to 127.56 at the close, higher in each third (103.6, 110.8 and 121.0 on average), with its low of 99.10 at bar 2 and its highest close, 127.94, at bar 118; the deepest setback is 4.3%, from bar 45 to bar 65. Normally read as buyers accepting higher prices throughout. Be precise about what validation established: that the flagged bars are now consistent with their neighbours — a statement about the data, and no evidence about the market it was drawn to resemble.

Every flagged bar closes about 28% above the bar before it, and the bar after prints straight back at the old level. A single bar like that is normally read as a violent repricing, which is exactly the trap: no trade produced it, the value was multiplied in. The tell is on the chart rather than in the number — a real repricing leaves the bars after it somewhere new, and these leave them where they were.

The flagged bars carry no price at all, so the line stops and restarts around them. There is nothing to read as market behaviour, which makes this the least misleading defect to look at and the most misleading to compute on: every hole disqualifies the twelve bars that follow it, so the breakout count on the raw series is a fraction of the validated one — the signal difference in the row above is that gap. Absent data does not announce itself as absent in a result.

The flagged bars repeat the previous bar's open, high, low and close exactly. Two identical bars are normally read as a pause, an area where price stopped making progress, and here they are one bar recorded twice. It moves the level by about a percent or less and leaves the breakout count essentially where it was, which is why it survives review: the damage is to the time axis and to anything that counts bars, not to the price.

The flagged bars print the previous close as their open, high, low and close, so they have no range at all. A zero-range bar is normally read as a period nobody contested. Here it is a feed that stopped updating, and the distinction matters to anything measuring range or volatility: the level stays within about a percent of the clean series while the bar's range is understated all the way to zero.

The defects arrive in a fixed order as the count rises: a bar 28% above its neighbour, then a bar with no data, then a bar copied from the one before it, then a bar with no range. Only the first is readable as market behaviour at all, and it is the one that would be read as a violent repricing. The other three are not readable, which is where the quieter damage sits — they move the breakout count without ever looking like anything on the chart.

Repaired, the line tracks the clean reference: price rotates between about 93.5 and 101.7 and ends within half a percent of where it began. Normally read as two-way trade with neither side holding ground. Be precise about what has been established, though — the series is now consistent with the reference, which is a statement about the data and not evidence about the market.

Repaired, the series rises to about 107.8 near bar 54 and then declines to finish about 9% below where it opened. Normally read as one condition replacing another inside a single sample. Validation changed none of that; it removed the bars that were not measurements, which is the whole of what cleaning can claim.

All eight names are carried for the whole window and the line ends 1.8% above where it began, having fallen from 108.1 to 97.2 in the single period FAIL loses 82% of its value. Normally read as a market that went almost nowhere. What the line cannot show is that seven of the eight names ended higher — VALUE among them once its cash distribution is counted, SPLT once its split is — and the eighth was enough to take the window back: a breadth reading rather than a direction one, and the only version of this chart in which the failure is still counted.

The same eighty-three periods, with the one name that failed removed, end 16.2% higher and never set back more than 0.3%. Normally read as a broad and orderly advance, produced without a single price on the chart changing. The reading is made by the universe rather than by the market: excluding FAIL is a decision available only after period 55, and the test claims to have started at period 1.

Four of the eight names are held, chosen by their change across the whole window, and the line ends 22.5% higher with a deepest setback of 0.5%. Normally read as selection that worked. The smoothness is the giveaway: the ranking used each series' final value to decide what to hold from the first period, and an advance this clean is what sorting on an outcome produces, not what choosing under uncertainty produces.

The line drops from 104.7 to 98.5 in one period at 42 and ends 5.0% below where it started. A six-point fall across an entire equal-weight universe is normally read as a broad sell-off. Nothing sold off: SPLT's quoted price halved in a two-for-one split and the holder's value did not move. Twelve periods earlier, at 30, VALUE's quoted price fell 4.3% going ex-distribution and the cash was booked nowhere — a smaller version of the same error, hidden inside an up step. The split is the one defect here that a chart cannot tell from a real decline without the corporate-action record beside it.

Take the bar beginning at minute 360: it opens at 110.04, trades between 109.99 and 112.25 and closes at 111.43, which is normally read as an up bar with a small tail — and it is exactly that. What it cannot say is order: a stop at 110 and a target at 112 both sit inside it, and the bar records that each was reached, not which was reached first.

The added bars carry the minutes before 60 and after 449, which average 337 in volume against 1,994 during the session. Including them moves the last close on the chart from 110.34 to 106.19 — normally read as the market giving four points back, and it did trade there. The reading that matters is a different one: those prices are on the chart whether or not the system could act at them, and at the default interval and lookback they take the breakout count from 10 to 13.

The regular session opens at 99.95 and closes at 110.34, with its low of 99.88 in the first minutes and its high of 112.25 late. Between them, minutes 115 to 299 hold between 102.66 and 104.54. Normally read as higher prices being accepted in two legs with an acceptance area between them; a close back under that shelf would end the reading, and finer bars are what let a test place a signal or a fill inside it at all.

Normally read as a breakout rule that works while buyers are accepting higher prices and stops working when they are not, which is what a breakout rule is. Every marker sits one bar after its signal, and that is the whole of what this chart claims: the rule acted on bars that had already printed, and it finished at −0.9%.

Each marker has moved onto the bar whose own close produced the signal — bar 35 instead of 36, bar 44 instead of 46 — and there are still seven. In this gapless synthetic series the next open is the signal close, so the fill price did not change; the clock did. Every exit arrives one bar earlier and the result is −2.8% instead of −0.9%, while the market underneath still reads as an advance to bar 57, a rotation to bar 105 and a decline after it. What changed is not the reading but the claim behind it: the fill is booked at a close that was not knowable until that bar had finished.

Three of the seven entries survive, at bars 36, 46 and 56, all inside the advance, and the four that lost are gone. Normally read as a rule that found the breakouts which continued. Both errors are on together: three markers, at bars 35, 44 and 55, each on the bar whose close created the signal, each kept because the exit bar said it would win. The market is the same one every other state on this page shows — an advance to bar 57, a rotation to bar 105, a decline after it — so nothing about the chart's structure distinguishes this run from the honest one at −0.9%; this one reads +5.0%. Only the selection differs, which is the point: there is no shape on a price chart that reveals a test which knew too much.

The order level sits outside everything price does after bar 21: the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 from there, the short path 94.37 to 103.65. There is no entry or exit on the chart to read, and that is the reading — a resting order is a request, and a level price never reaches is a level that never traded. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level did.

No entry or exit is on the chart because the order was withdrawn before price reached its level. From bar 21 the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 and the short path 94.37 to 103.65, so a level outside that range was never going to fill, and a level inside it was reached, if at all, only after the order's life had run out. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level and the chosen lifetime did — and a test that leaves resting orders open forever is claiming fills at prices from a market the signal never saw.

From bar 21 price works from 99.80 up to a high of 110.78 at bar 37 and closes the sample at 109.49, with the deepest close-to-close setback along the way about 2.61 points. Normally read as higher prices being accepted once the order is active. Bar 26 is where the reading has to slow down: it opens at 102.87 and closes at 106.70, so any level inside that bar is credited or missed on an assumption about a path the bar itself does not record.

Bar 22 opens at 103.80 after bar 21 closed at 99.80, and its lowest trade is 103.51. Normally read as a four-point repricing between bars, which is what it is. The part to read carefully is the space it left behind: at the default stop and target the target level, 103.09, never traded on that bar, so the exit is booked at the first price that did, the open at 103.80 — 2.36R instead of the 2.00R the level promised. Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range across that stretch from 1.81 points to 4.61 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. From bar 21 price first works against the short, reaching 103.65 at bar 26, before declining to 94.37 at bar 49 and closing the sample at 96.09. Normally read as an advance that fails and gives way to lower prices being accepted. The order of events is the reading: about three points of adverse movement arrive before any of the eight the decline eventually offers, so a stop placed inside that first stretch settles the trade before the market does anything the label describes.

Bar 22 opens at 95.73 after bar 21 closed at 99.73, and its lowest trade is 95.43. Normally read as a four-point repricing in the short's favour. It is also where a gap stops being a gift: at the default target of 94.80 the move is not enough to close the trade, bar 23 trades back up to 101.77, and the same gap that would have been read as confirmation is followed by the stop.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range there from 1.68 points to 4.48 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. What expanded is the recorded extreme and not the path: a stop above the entry is touched by a high that was stretched to it, and a test reading closes alone would report the same market with a different outcome.

The benchmark ends 6.7% above where it started, having reached 113.7 and traded as low as 96.3, with a deepest setback of 11.0%. Normally read as a market that ended higher; the word the line does not support is continued, since the index spent part of the window below its own opening level. The benchmark ends 10.6% lower, reaching 106.9 early and 87.6 late, with a deepest setback of 18.1%. Normally read as lower prices being accepted across the whole market. The benchmark rotates between 93.1 and 107.5 and finishes 3.1% below where it began. Normally read as a market with no sustained direction to lend a strategy or to take away from it. Normally read as both sides moving price in size without either holding it. Define how raw trades or quotes become bars, which sessions are eligible, and how timeframe choices change indicators, signals, and fills.
A timeframe does not merely change the chart view; it changes the information available to the system.
A 60-minute bar hides the sequence inside twelve 5-minute bars. Extended-hours data can create signals that regular-session rules never see.
What to understand
Keep each definition operational so it can be implemented and tested.
Bar interval
Open, high, low, close, and volume depend on the aggregation window.
Session rule
Regular, extended, overnight, and exchange-specific sessions produce different datasets.
Decision clock
Define the exact timestamp when indicators update and orders become eligible.
Timeframe and Session Lab
Aggregate the same intraday sequence into different bars and sessions. Observe how signals and market interpretation change.
Timeframe and Session Lab
Deterministic synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Define the market clock
Bar boundaries and sessions must be fixed before testing.
Choose source frequency
Use data granular enough for the execution assumptions.
Define sessions
Include only times the system is allowed to observe and trade.
Aggregate consistently
Use one timezone, calendar, and boundary rule.

Practical rules
Store timestamps in a clear canonical timezone.
Use exchange calendars and session definitions.
Use lower-frequency bars only when their information supports the fill model.
Common mistakes
Assuming all daily bars close at the same time.
Mixing extended-hours signals with regular-hours fills without rules.
Using daily OHLC to infer an exact intraday sequence.

The same eighty-three periods, with the one name that failed removed, end 16.2% higher and never set back more than 0.3%. Normally read as a broad and orderly advance, produced without a single price on the chart changing. The reading is made by the universe rather than by the market: excluding FAIL is a decision available only after period 55, and the test claims to have started at period 1.

Four of the eight names are held, chosen by their change across the whole window, and the line ends 22.5% higher with a deepest setback of 0.5%. Normally read as selection that worked. The smoothness is the giveaway: the ranking used each series' final value to decide what to hold from the first period, and an advance this clean is what sorting on an outcome produces, not what choosing under uncertainty produces.

The line drops from 104.7 to 98.5 in one period at 42 and ends 5.0% below where it started. A six-point fall across an entire equal-weight universe is normally read as a broad sell-off. Nothing sold off: SPLT's quoted price halved in a two-for-one split and the holder's value did not move. Twelve periods earlier, at 30, VALUE's quoted price fell 4.3% going ex-distribution and the cash was booked nowhere — a smaller version of the same error, hidden inside an up step. The split is the one defect here that a chart cannot tell from a real decline without the corporate-action record beside it.

At sixty minutes the regular session becomes seven bars and the average bar covers 2.12% of price, against 0.38% for that same session at five minutes. Take the bar beginning at minute 360: it opens at 110.04, trades between 109.99 and 112.25 and closes at 111.43, which is normally read as an up bar with a small tail — and it is exactly that. What it cannot say is order: a stop at 110 and a target at 112 both sit inside it, and the bar records that each was reached, not which was reached first.

The added bars carry the minutes before 60 and after 449, which average 337 in volume against 1,994 during the session. Including them moves the last close on the chart from 110.34 to 106.19 — normally read as the market giving four points back, and it did trade there. The reading that matters is a different one: those prices are on the chart whether or not the system could act at them, and at the default interval and lookback they take the breakout count from 10 to 13.

The regular session opens at 99.95 and closes at 110.34, with its low of 99.88 in the first minutes and its high of 112.25 late. Between them, minutes 115 to 299 hold between 102.66 and 104.54. Normally read as higher prices being accepted in two legs with an acceptance area between them; a close back under that shelf would end the reading, and finer bars are what let a test place a signal or a fill inside it at all.

Seven entry markers, each one bar after a close exceeded the previous eighteen closes. Three sit inside the advance from 97.84 at bar 26 to 108.17 at bar 57 — entries at bars 36, 46 and 56 — and win; four sit in the rotation between 106.76 and 110.92 that follows and in the decline to 102.56 at bar 148 — bars 73, 96, 122 and 157 — and lose. Normally read as a breakout rule that works while buyers are accepting higher prices and stops working when they are not, which is what a breakout rule is. Every marker sits one bar after its signal, and that is the whole of what this chart claims: the rule acted on bars that had already printed, and it finished at −0.9%.

Each marker has moved onto the bar whose own close produced the signal — bar 35 instead of 36, bar 44 instead of 46 — and there are still seven. In this gapless synthetic series the next open is the signal close, so the fill price did not change; the clock did. Every exit arrives one bar earlier and the result is −2.8% instead of −0.9%, while the market underneath still reads as an advance to bar 57, a rotation to bar 105 and a decline after it. What changed is not the reading but the claim behind it: the fill is booked at a close that was not knowable until that bar had finished.

Three of the seven entries survive, at bars 36, 46 and 56, all inside the advance, and the four that lost are gone. Normally read as a rule that found the breakouts which continued. It found nothing: the filter read the open of the bar each trade would exit on and kept the signal only when that price was higher, so the markers are placed by information that did not exist when the signal fired. At the default settings the selected return is +5.4% against −0.9% for the causal baseline — a weak rule made to look precise by choosing its trades after the fact.

Both errors are on together: three markers, at bars 35, 44 and 55, each on the bar whose close created the signal, each kept because the exit bar said it would win. The market is the same one every other state on this page shows — an advance to bar 57, a rotation to bar 105, a decline after it — so nothing about the chart's structure distinguishes this run from the honest one at −0.9%; this one reads +5.0%. Only the selection differs, which is the point: there is no shape on a price chart that reveals a test which knew too much.

The order level sits outside everything price does after bar 21: the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 from there, the short path 94.37 to 103.65. There is no entry or exit on the chart to read, and that is the reading — a resting order is a request, and a level price never reaches is a level that never traded. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level did.

No entry or exit is on the chart because the order was withdrawn before price reached its level. From bar 21 the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 and the short path 94.37 to 103.65, so a level outside that range was never going to fill, and a level inside it was reached, if at all, only after the order's life had run out. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level and the chosen lifetime did — and a test that leaves resting orders open forever is claiming fills at prices from a market the signal never saw.

From bar 21 price works from 99.80 up to a high of 110.78 at bar 37 and closes the sample at 109.49, with the deepest close-to-close setback along the way about 2.61 points. Normally read as higher prices being accepted once the order is active. Bar 26 is where the reading has to slow down: it opens at 102.87 and closes at 106.70, so any level inside that bar is credited or missed on an assumption about a path the bar itself does not record.

Bar 22 opens at 103.80 after bar 21 closed at 99.80, and its lowest trade is 103.51. Normally read as a four-point repricing between bars, which is what it is. The part to read carefully is the space it left behind: at the default stop and target the target level, 103.09, never traded on that bar, so the exit is booked at the first price that did, the open at 103.80 — 2.36R instead of the 2.00R the level promised. A gap through a target is a gift; the same gap through a stop, one bar later at 100.41, is the −1.72R the stop-market order shows.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range across that stretch from 1.81 points to 4.61 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. Be precise about what expanded: anything computed from closes sees an identical market, and only the touches change — the same target is reached a bar earlier here purely because a high was extended to it.

From bar 21 price first works against the short, reaching 103.65 at bar 26, before declining to 94.37 at bar 49 and closing the sample at 96.09. Normally read as an advance that fails and gives way to lower prices being accepted. The order of events is the reading: about three points of adverse movement arrive before any of the eight the decline eventually offers, so a stop placed inside that first stretch settles the trade before the market does anything the label describes.

Bar 22 opens at 95.73 after bar 21 closed at 99.73, and its lowest trade is 95.43. Normally read as a four-point repricing in the short's favour. It is also where a gap stops being a gift: at the default target of 94.80 the move is not enough to close the trade, bar 23 trades back up to 101.77, and the same gap that would have been read as confirmation is followed by the stop.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range there from 1.68 points to 4.48 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. What expanded is the recorded extreme and not the path: a stop above the entry is touched by a high that was stretched to it, and a test reading closes alone would report the same market with a different outcome.

The benchmark ends 6.7% above where it started, having reached 113.7 and traded as low as 96.3, with a deepest setback of 11.0%. Normally read as a market that ended higher; the word the line does not support is continued, since the index spent part of the window below its own opening level. That is what the comparison beside it runs against: a strategy is being scored on a path, not on the 6.7%.

The benchmark ends 10.6% lower, reaching 106.9 early and 87.6 late, with a deepest setback of 18.1%. Normally read as lower prices being accepted across the whole market. Worth being exact about what carries that: 137 of the 252 steps close up, so the direction comes from the size of the down steps rather than their count, and a majority of up days under a falling index is not a contradiction.

The benchmark rotates between 93.1 and 107.5 and finishes 3.1% below where it began. Normally read as a market with no sustained direction to lend a strategy or to take away from it. Note also that a 13.4% setback still occurs here with no trend to attribute it to, which is what makes this the sample where an independent return is easiest to see as independent.

The benchmark covers 85.6 to 114.5 and ends 8.2% lower, with annualised volatility of 26.8% against 14.2% in the other samples and a largest single step of 3.89%. Normally read as both sides moving price in size without either holding it. The drift underneath is identical to the balanced sample and only the step size differs, which is precisely why return alone cannot separate the two and a risk-adjusted comparison exists at all.

Model market, limit, stop, stop-limit, target, and cancellation behavior using prices that could realistically execute in the tested sequence.
A signal is not a trade until the order model produces a valid fill.
Market orders prioritize execution, limit orders prioritize price, and gaps can move the fill beyond the planned level.
What to understand
Keep each definition operational so it can be implemented and tested.
Order eligibility
The order becomes active only after its submission event.
Fill condition
Price touching a level does not always prove the full order could execute there.
Intrabar ambiguity
When stop and target are both inside one bar, the sequence is unknown without finer data.
Order and Fill Simulation Lab
Select an order type, gap condition, and intrabar assumption. Inspect the simulated fill, exit, and R-multiple.
Order and Fill Simulation Lab
Deterministic synthetic educational data · no live market connection
Separate signal from execution

Submit

Match
Apply eligible prices, spread, liquidity, and queue assumptions.
Resolve
Fill, partially fill, cancel, expire, stop, or target the order.
Check your understanding

Use order-specific fill logic.
Use conservative handling for unresolved intrabar order.

Allowing orders to fill before submission.

Price advances about 19% into bar 53, gives it back through the middle of the sample, and finishes about 3% below where it opened after reaching 93.36 near bar 186. Price runs about 30% higher into bar 90, then loses roughly 19% from its high of 132.94 and finishes at 112.70. Price rotates between 93.25 and 101.52 for all 150 bars and finishes about 2.6% below where it started. Every flagged bar closes about 28% above the bar before it, and the bar after prints straight back at the old level. The flagged bars carry no price at all, so the line stops and restarts around them. There is nothing to read as market behaviour, which makes this the least misleading defect to look at and the most misleading to compute on: every hole disqualifies the twelve bars that follow it, so the breakout count on the raw series is a fraction of the validated one — the signal difference in the row above is that gap. Absent data does not announce itself as absent in a result.

The flagged bars repeat the previous bar's open, high, low and close exactly. It moves the level by about a percent or less and leaves the breakout count essentially where it was, which is why it survives review: the damage is to the time axis and to anything that counts bars, not to the price.

The flagged bars print the previous close as their open, high, low and close, so they have no range at all. A zero-range bar is normally read as a period nobody contested. The defects arrive in a fixed order as the count rises: a bar 28% above its neighbour, then a bar with no data, then a bar copied from the one before it, then a bar with no range. The order level sits outside everything price does after bar 21: the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 from there, the short path 94.37 to 103.65. There is no entry or exit on the chart to read, and that is the reading — a resting order is a request, and a level price never reaches is a level that never traded. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level did.

No entry or exit is on the chart because the order was withdrawn before price reached its level. From bar 21 the long path covers 98.66 to 110.78 and the short path 94.37 to 103.65, so a level outside that range was never going to fill, and a level inside it was reached, if at all, only after the order's life had run out. Nothing about the market produced this outcome; the chosen level and the chosen lifetime did — and a test that leaves resting orders open forever is claiming fills at prices from a market the signal never saw.

From bar 21 price works from 99.80 up to a high of 110.78 at bar 37 and closes the sample at 109.49, with the deepest close-to-close setback along the way about 2.61 points. Normally read as higher prices being accepted once the order is active. Bar 26 is where the reading has to slow down: it opens at 102.87 and closes at 106.70, so any level inside that bar is credited or missed on an assumption about a path the bar itself does not record.

Bar 22 opens at 103.80 after bar 21 closed at 99.80, and its lowest trade is 103.51. Normally read as a four-point repricing between bars, which is what it is. The part to read carefully is the space it left behind: at the default stop and target the target level, 103.09, never traded on that bar, so the exit is booked at the first price that did, the open at 103.80 — 2.36R instead of the 2.00R the level promised. A gap through a target is a gift; the same gap through a stop, one bar later at 100.41, is the −1.72R the stop-market order shows.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range across that stretch from 1.81 points to 4.61 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. Be precise about what expanded: anything computed from closes sees an identical market, and only the touches change — the same target is reached a bar earlier here purely because a high was extended to it.

From bar 21 price first works against the short, reaching 103.65 at bar 26, before declining to 94.37 at bar 49 and closing the sample at 96.09. Normally read as an advance that fails and gives way to lower prices being accepted. The order of events is the reading: about three points of adverse movement arrive before any of the eight the decline eventually offers, so a stop placed inside that first stretch settles the trade before the market does anything the label describes.

Bar 22 opens at 95.73 after bar 21 closed at 99.73, and its lowest trade is 95.43. Normally read as a four-point repricing in the short's favour. It is also where a gap stops being a gift: at the default target of 94.80 the move is not enough to close the trade, bar 23 trades back up to 101.77, and the same gap that would have been read as confirmation is followed by the stop.

Bars 20 to 31 have their highs and lows widened, taking the average bar range there from 1.68 points to 4.48 while every close stays exactly where it was. Normally read as volatility expanding into the entry. What expanded is the recorded extreme and not the path: a stop above the entry is touched by a high that was stretched to it, and a test reading closes alone would report the same market with a different outcome.

The benchmark ends 6.7% above where it started, having reached 113.7 and traded as low as 96.3, with a deepest setback of 11.0%. Normally read as a market that ended higher; the word the line does not support is continued, since the index spent part of the window below its own opening level. That is what the comparison beside it runs against: a strategy is being scored on a path, not on the 6.7%.

The benchmark ends 10.6% lower, reaching 106.9 early and 87.6 late, with a deepest setback of 18.1%. Normally read as lower prices being accepted across the whole market. Worth being exact about what carries that: 137 of the 252 steps close up, so the direction comes from the size of the down steps rather than their count, and a majority of up days under a falling index is not a contradiction.

The benchmark rotates between 93.1 and 107.5 and finishes 3.1% below where it began. Normally read as a market with no sustained direction to lend a strategy or to take away from it. Note also that a 13.4% setback still occurs here with no trend to attribute it to, which is what makes this the sample where an independent return is easiest to see as independent.

The benchmark covers 85.6 to 114.5 and ends 8.2% lower, with annualised volatility of 26.8% against 14.2% in the other samples and a largest single step of 3.89%. Normally read as both sides moving price in size without either holding it. The drift underneath is identical to the balanced sample and only the step size differs, which is precisely why return alone cannot separate the two and a risk-adjusted comparison exists at all.

Create an auditable trade log, reconstruct portfolio equity through time, and measure peak-to-trough loss and recovery duration.
The equity curve is the ordered result of every signal, fill, cost, position, and market movement.
The same average trade can produce very different account stress when losses cluster together.
What to understand
Keep each definition operational so it can be implemented and tested.
Trade log
Store signal, order, fill, quantity, cost, exit, P/L, and reason codes.
Equity curve
Mark open positions and cash consistently through chronological time.
Drawdown
Measure the decline from the previous equity peak and the time required to recover.

The average win is a per-trade statistic; drawdown is a property of the path the account took.

A reason code is a label on a trade; it moves no price.
