clauses.expected: Algorithmic and Automated Trading
Specify automated trading workflows, data and order handling, deployment controls, monitoring, and operational risk procedures.
Subject
Trading
Lessons
Format
Interactive
Overview
What it teaches

How a trading system is split into parts that can be reasoned about separately — strategy rules, signal generation, risk checks, order submission and execution — and how much authority to hand each level of automation. The inputs: historical and streaming data validated, deduplicated and normalized into one model, with late events handled rather than assumed away; and the clock — exchange calendars, time zones, session boundaries, event windows and schedulers that behave the same way twice. The decision itself: a signal engine with explicit state, which is what stops a system repeating, contradicting or acting on a stale signal; and a risk engine that holds cash, positions, exposure, open orders and limits, and is consulted before an order exists. The outside world: a broker adapter that submits, queries, cancels and reconciles while treating every status as asynchronous; order type selection, open-order management and fill quality measured against the decision price; and the whole system run on current data with no capital at risk. The controls: scanning and ranking with deduplicated alerts and decisions that expire; duplicate-safe commands, bounded retries, durable state and reconciliation after a timeout; metrics and traces and an immutable audit trail; scoped credentials, separated environments, rotation and a kill switch; reproducible artifacts, gradual rollout and rollback. AI-Assisted and Agentic Trading Workflows covers AI-assisted and agentic workflows, and Automated Trading System Specification and Production Readiness turns all of it into one versioned specification.
Who it is for

Anyone who has a rule set they trust and no idea what it takes to let it run unattended. It assumes you can read a chart, and that risk per trade, position sizing, expectancy and out-of-sample validation already mean something to you — Trading Risk Management and Backtesting and Trading Systems define them. It assumes nothing about distributed systems: idempotency, reconciliation, traces, secret rotation and rollback are introduced here, from the trading problem they solve rather than from the general engineering literature. It also suits the reader who has decided NOT to automate, and wants to know what they would be signing up for: most of this course is about failure — a timeout with unknown state, a duplicate order, a stale price, a credential with more permission than it needs — and none of that goes away because the strategy is good.
Concept dependencies

Architecture defines the boundaries across which market data and clock events travel. Strategy state and risk limits constrain what broker calls and order management may do. Reliability, observability and security work must account for order status arriving out of order. A missing response creates an uncertain state that the system must reconcile; a good strategy alone does not resolve it.
Where the definitions come from

The labs are simplified on purpose, so lessons close with an official reading link to a primary source rather than to a vendor selling an execution platform: FINRA's Regulatory Notice 15-09 on supervision, testing, controls and documentation for algorithmic trading strategies, and the SEC's own summary of Rule 15c3-5, the market-access rule that requires pre-trade financial and regulatory risk controls. Where the subject is engineering rather than regulation, the source is the project that defines the thing: OpenTelemetry on traces, metrics and logs; Kubernetes on liveness and readiness probes; Docker on build practice; the OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet on storing and rotating credentials; and a broker's own published API documentation for paper trading, streaming market data and working with orders — cited as an example of what such an API looks like, not as a recommendation of that broker.
Every lesson still works with no network at all. Each page is entirely self-contained, and the reference links are the only things on it that point off the site.
Lessons
Explanations, examples, interactive tools, and practice questions.
16 lessons

Educational use only — nothing here is trading advice. This course does not connect to a broker, ingest live market data, place orders, provide trading signals, or claim that any automated strategy will be profitable. It teaches how such a system is structured and controlled; it is not one, and no page here can submit an order.

Data and results scope. All market paths, events, orders, failures, and portfolio states in these lessons are deterministic synthetic examples. The course uses stated conventions — market data, strategy, risk, order and broker responsibilities stay separate; a network timeout represents unknown state until reconciliation; automatic execution is treated as the final level of automation rather than the starting point; AI components produce advisory proposals while deterministic services retain risk and execution authority; and deployment begins with paper, shadow and limited-scope rollout. Every lesson also separates what the market is doing — buyers accepting higher prices, sellers accepting lower ones, price balanced, volatility expanding — from what the system is doing, because latency, a data gap, a risk rejection or an unknown order state is a fact about your software and not about the market.

Encoding the strategy

Before anything runs: what the parts of a trading system are, and how much authority each level of automation actually takes. A strategy that lives in your head produces a different trade every time; a strategy encoded as separate rules, signals, risk checks and orders produces the same decision from the same events — which is the minimum condition for everything that follows. These lessons draw the boundaries, then fill them in: the data model events arrive as, the calendar and scheduler that say when a decision is even allowed, and the signal engine whose state is explicit enough that a repeat or a stale value cannot slip through as a new trade.

The part that touches money. A risk engine that owns cash, positions, exposure, open orders and limits comes first, because it has to be consulted before an order exists rather than after one is rejected. Testing and risk controls

Whether the system may be trusted to run, and what happens when it is wrong. Paper trading runs the whole thing on current data with no capital at risk, which is the first place backtest assumptions meet real signal timing, real latency and real fills. Scanners, alerts and an explicit human approval step are the automation level below automatic, and they have failure modes of their own: duplicated alerts, a thesis the reader cannot reconstruct, a decision acted on an hour after it stopped being true. Then the uncomfortable one — a network that times out leaves you not knowing whether an order exists, and only duplicate-safe commands, durable state and reconciliation get you back to certainty.

Running it accountably. Observability first, because a system you cannot measure is a system you are guessing about: data freshness, decision latency, broker latency, error rate, positions and risk, end-to-end traces, and an immutable record of why each decision was made. AI workflows and system specifications. AI-Assisted and Agentic Trading Workflows explains where AI belongs in this system: research, extraction, classification and trade proposals — with market data, rules, risk, permissions and execution controls kept deterministic and auditable, so a proposal is an input to the risk engine and never a substitute for it. The specification lesson documents an automated trading system. It turns the whole course into one document — what the system trades, where its data comes from, what risk it may take, which broker it speaks to, how it was validated, how it is operated, and what AI is permitted to do — and hands that document back to you as a file, so it can outlive the browser tab it was written in.
Format: automated-trading-system-v1
What comes out of it

Automated Trading System Specification and Production Readiness takes the identity and version you gave the system, the strategy section — type, timeframe, direction, and the automation level, which is one of alert , approval or automatic — the market-data section with its mode, its maximum acceptable age in seconds and whether it is normalized, the risk section with its per-trade and gross-exposure percentages, whether risk is evaluated independently and whether a kill switch exists, the order section covering idempotency, reconciliation and the broker adapter, the validation section with its paper-trading days and shadow-mode flag, the operations section with observability, security scope, rollout percentage and rollback, and the AI section, and exports the whole thing as a JSON document stamped automated-trading-system-v1 .

The schema linked beside this is the contract for that shape. It is worth reading if you would rather keep your systems in your own notebook or repository: match the shape and the same fields carry over. All nine top-level members are required, so a specification that omits its risk section or its validation plan does not validate — those are the two a hurried system leaves out first. Note what the shape deliberately does contain: ai.mode and ai.directExecution are separate fields, because "an AI is involved" and "an AI can place an order" are different claims and the specification is not allowed to blur them. Note also what it does NOT contain: any realized or expected return. A specification records what a system is permitted to do and what had to be true before it was allowed to run — never what it earned. Everything runs in your browser: nothing is uploaded, no broker is contacted, and there is no account anywhere in this course.

Educational course. This course is educational. It does not connect to a broker, ingest live market data, place orders, provide trading signals, or claim that any automated strategy will be profitable, and no page in it can submit an order. All market paths, events, orders, failures and portfolio states in these lessons are deterministic synthetic examples. Automating a strategy does not reduce its risk: it removes the pause in which a person would have noticed a stale price, a duplicated order, a wrong size or a broken assumption, so an automated system can lose money faster and more consistently than a manual one. Real outcomes vary by data source, vendor, venue, asset class, session, liquidity, latency, broker behaviour and the execution you actually get. Confirm the data, the risk limits, the broker's rules and your own obligations before running anything against a live account.

Receive historical and streaming data, validate timestamps and symbols, remove duplicates, handle late events, and expose one normalized market-data model.
A trading decision is only as current and consistent as the data used to produce it.
Buyers can be moving price higher while duplicated, stale, or out-of-order records make the strategy see a false reversal or repeated breakout.
What to understand
Keep the boundaries, state, and authority explicit.
Event time
The time the market event occurred, distinct from the time the system received it.
Normalization
Convert provider-specific messages into one internal schema with consistent units and identifiers.
Data health
Measure gaps, duplicates, lateness, sequence errors, and feed freshness continuously.

Validate before publishing
Downstream strategies should not reimplement provider-specific cleanup.
Receive
Authenticate and capture the original provider message.
Validate
Check schema, sequence, timestamp, price, volume, and freshness.
Publish
Emit a normalized event with provenance and quality status.

Deduplicate with stable event identifiers or sequence rules.

Two timestamps describe one event; they do not create a second one.
Timestamps say when; symbol mapping says what. Keeping both times does not remove the need to identify the instrument.
A second copy of a message costs bandwidth; it never makes the first arrive sooner.
The broker never sees the duplicate event; it sees whatever the strategy did with it, which may be a second order that is accepted.
By then every decision has already been made on un-normalized data; the point is to fix the input before anything consumes it.
Each consumer would then fix the feed its own way and disagree with the others; one model, applied once, is what keeps them consistent.
Arrival order is transport order. The provider's timestamp says the event happened 7.5 s before it arrived.
The event is a real trade and belongs in the record at its event time; what it cannot do is be treated as current, so the feed is flagged stale.

Market Data Ingestion and Normalization

The normalized view draws the reference series whichever defect is selected: the first thirty-five bars hold between 95.13 and 100.81, the last close below that area is bar 46, and from bar 60 onward every print sits between 104.66 and 110.74, ending at 110.39. Normally read as acceptance above the area price had been rotating in, since the level that used to cap it became the floor of everything after it; a close back inside that early band would end the reading. Be precise about what normalization has established, though — the published stream now matches the reference, which is a statement about the data and not evidence about the market.

Nothing on the line changes in this state. A late event carries a receive time and its prices are untouched, so the raw series drawn here is identical to the normalized one: the same rotation to bar 46 and the same acceptance above it. That is the reading worth taking away — a defect a reader cannot see on a chart is still a defect to anything that acts on arrival order or on feed age.

Bar 24 has its close removed, so it is dropped before drawing and the line runs straight from 97.54 to 96.83. There is nothing to read as market behaviour at the gap, which makes this the least misleading defect to look at and one of the more misleading to compute on: the shape around it still reads as the same rotation while anything counting bars or measuring an interval is short a period it does not know is missing.

Bar 24 is published twice, so the line carries a flat step at 97.51 where one bar of the reference sits. Two identical bars are normally read as a pause, an area where price stopped making progress, and here they are one bar recorded twice. The level is untouched and the time axis is not, which is why this one survives review: the damage is to anything that counts bars rather than to the price.

Bars 24 and 25 change places, so the closes run 97.54, 96.83, 97.51 instead of 97.54, 97.51, 96.83. Read literally that is a one-bar bounce inside a decline, and it is an artefact of delivery order rather than anything that traded. Every price in it is a real price from the reference and only the sequence is wrong, which is what makes it hard to see and easy for a state machine to act on.

Bar 24 takes the previous close as its open, high, low and close, so it prints flat at 97.54 with no range at all. A zero-range bar is normally read as a period nobody contested; here it is a feed that stopped updating. The distinction is the whole of the lesson: the level moves by three cents while the bar's range is understated from 0.92 to zero, so anything measuring range or volatility is reading a number the market did not produce.

The defects arrive in a fixed order as the count rises — a duplicated bar first at 24, then a late event, then a missing close, then a swapped pair, then a stale print. Only the duplicate and the swap leave a shape a reader would interpret at all, and both would be read as ordinary pauses or bounces rather than as defects. The rest change the record without changing anything that looks like market behaviour, which is where the quieter damage sits.

clauses.expected: Observability, Logging, and Auditability
Measure data freshness, decision latency, broker latency, error rate, positions, risk, and end-to-end traces while preserving an immutable decision audit trail.
A price loss and a system failure are different events and require different evidence.
Sellers may continue accepting lower prices exactly as the strategy expected, while delayed data or a missing risk response creates an operational loss.
What to understand
Keep the boundaries, state, and authority explicit.
Metrics
Numeric measurements such as feed age, signal count, order latency, rejection rate, and exposure.
Logs and audit
Structured event records containing identities, versions, reasons, and before/after state.
Trace
The causal path from market event through strategy, risk, order, and broker response.
Trading System Observability Lab
Inject a latency or data incident and toggle metrics, logs, traces, and correlation IDs. Measure detection and diagnosis quality.
Trading System Observability Lab
Deterministic synthetic educational data · no broker or live-market connection
Instrument the complete decision path
Telemetry should explain both system health and trading behavior.
Measure
Emit service and domain metrics with clear units and thresholds.
Correlate
Carry event, signal, order, and trace identifiers across components.
Alert
Notify on actionable symptoms and link directly to supporting evidence.
Check your understanding

2. A trace is useful because it:
3. An audit event should include:
4. A trace reads 20, 17, 240, 18 and 24 ms across feed, normalize, strategy, risk and broker. What is the end-to-end time, and which span do you open?
Practical rules
Measure both technical and trading-domain health.
Use correlation IDs across the entire order path.
Alert on stale data, unknown orders, risk breaches, and state divergence.
Common mistakes
Logging only exceptions.
Using unstructured text without stable IDs.
Monitoring process uptime while ignoring feed freshness and broker state.

clauses.expected: Order Management and Execution
Select order types, manage open orders, control participation, and measure fill quality against the decision price and available liquidity.
A correct direction can still produce a poor result when execution consumes the edge.
When buyers are already lifting offers, another large buy order competes for limited liquidity and can push the average fill higher.
What to understand
Keep the boundaries, state, and authority explicit.
Decision price
The market price when the strategy and risk engine approved the trade.
Execution policy
Market, limit, time-sliced, or participation-based instructions with deadlines.

Between the DECISION marker at bar 45 (110.23) and bar 85 (114.74) price works about 409 bps higher, with a highest close of 116.66 inside that window and a deepest close-to-close setback of about 2.1% across the sample; each third holds a higher low than the last — 96.83, 105.48, 113.90 — and the sample ends at 116.98. Normally read as higher prices being accepted across the whole execution window; a close back below 113.90 would end that reading. Which policies read it: the market order fills on the decision bar and never sees the path; the resting limit is left behind by it (the next close is 111.10); the participation order pays for three bars of it (111.10, 111.83, 111.81); the time-sliced order pays for thirty-six — its eight child closes average 113.35, and that is where its slippage comes from.

Across all 100 bars price rotates between 96.92 and 103.89 and ends at 100.56, about 2% above where it opened; between the DECISION marker at bar 45 (102.69) and bar 85 (99.20) it falls roughly 340 bps, a leg inside that rotation rather than a departure from it. The usual interpretation is two-way trade with neither side holding the other's ground, and it stops reading that way when a close holds outside the band instead of turning back into it. The policies read it differently: the three bars after the decision close higher (103.25, 103.63, 103.25), so the participation order pays for the top of the rotation, while the time-sliced order's eight children average 101.67 and it is the only policy whose fill beats the decision price by a wide margin — not because it was cleverer, but because the leg it worked through was falling.

Price holds between 95.39 and 101.46 for the first eighty-five bars and falls from 100.09 at the DECISION marker to 96.80 at bar 85, about 329 bps, with the sample's lowest close, 94.06, arriving at bar 94, after the window. Normally read as lower prices being accepted through the marked window, with the stretch before it showing no such thing; a close back above 101.46 would break that reading. Note where the three bars after the decision went: up, to 100.72, 101.21 and 101.02, so a participation order that finished in three bars paid more than the market order did, and only the time-sliced order that stayed in for thirty-six bars (children averaging 99.61) was rewarded for the decline. A resting limit here fills — the market comes back to it — and is then carried lower, which is the adverse selection this path does not charge for.

Propositional and predicate logic from truth values to written proofs: connectives, truth tables, equivalence, normal forms, quantifiers and their negations, inference rules, and direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and case proofs.
Sets, Relations, and Functions
Sets and their algebra, power sets and Cartesian products, relations and the structures they define, functions and their mapping properties, cardinality, and the pigeonhole principle.

The technique that proves a statement for every natural number by proving one implication: well-ordering, ordinary and strong induction, structural induction, recursive definitions and algorithms, linear and divide-and-conquer recurrences, and loop invariants.

Counting without enumerating: the sum and product rules, permutations and combinations, the binomial theorem, repetition, inclusion and exclusion, derangements, the generalised pigeonhole principle, generating functions and combinatorial proof.

Probability over finite sample spaces: events, the axioms, conditional probability and independence, Bayes' theorem, random variables, expectation and its linearity, variance, and the binomial and geometric distributions.
Number Theory and Cryptography

The arithmetic of remainders, from the division algorithm to RSA: primes and unique factorisation, gcd and the Euclidean algorithm, Bézout's identity, modular arithmetic and exponentiation, linear congruences, the Chinese remainder theorem, Fermat and Euler, and public-key encryption.

Vertices and edges: degree and the handshake theorem, representations, connectivity, isomorphism, bipartite graphs, Euler and Hamilton, search, shortest paths, trees, spanning trees, colouring and planarity.

How to say how long an algorithm takes and why it matters: correctness and termination, growth of functions, big-O with explicit witnesses, analysis of iterative and recursive algorithms, greedy and dynamic programming, complexity classes, and the limits of computation.

The real numbers and the rules for operating on them: order of operations, what a letter and a term mean, the properties that license a rearrangement, integer and rational exponents, radicals, absolute value, and the translation from a stated quantity to an expression.
Linear Equations and Inequalities

Solving for an unknown: what a solution is, the operations that preserve one, one-variable linear equations with fractions and variables on both sides, formulas linear in a named letter, inequalities and their one surprising rule, and absolute value.
Lines, Functions and Graphs

The plane, the line, and the idea of a function: slope and the forms of a linear equation, parallel and perpendicular, what makes a rule a function, domain and range, piecewise definitions, transformations, composition and inverses.

Polynomial arithmetic and the reverse of it: degree and standard form, the four operations, special products, the standard integer-coefficient factoring techniques, long and synthetic division, the remainder and factor theorems, rational roots and polynomial graphs.
Rational and Radical Expressions

Algebraic fractions and roots: domains and the values that break them, simplifying and operating on rational expressions, complex fractions, rational equations and the extraneous solutions they produce, asymptotes, radical arithmetic and radical equations.
Quadratics and Complex Numbers

The quadratic, four ways: factoring, the square root property, completing the square and the formula that completing the square proves. Then the discriminant, the complex numbers that appear when it is negative, parabolas, optimisation and quadratic inequalities.
Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

Growth that compounds, and the function that undoes it: exponential functions and their graphs, decay, the number e, the logarithm as an inverse, the three laws, change of base, solving equations of both kinds, and the scales built on logarithms.

Several equations at once, and the array that makes solving them mechanical: substitution, elimination, three-variable systems, row operations, Gaussian elimination, matrix arithmetic, determinants, inverses, and linear programming.

Ordered lists and the sums of their terms: recursive and closed forms, sigma notation, arithmetic and geometric families, partial sums, infinite geometric series and when they converge, repeating decimals, annuities, Pascal's triangle and the binomial theorem.

clauses.expected: Discrete Mathematics

The mathematics of things you can count, list and check: statements that are true or false, sets and the relations between them, proof by induction, counting without enumerating, probability over finite outcomes, the arithmetic of remainders, graphs, and the analysis of the algorithms that run on all of it. Eight courses and 106 lessons are available.
Courses
Lessons
Level
Beginner → Advanced
Overview

Logic comes first because everything after it is a claim that has to be stated precisely enough to be true or false. A reader who has not settled what ∀x ∃y P(x, y) means cannot read a single theorem in the later courses, and will silently misread several.

Sets, relations and functions come second because they are the vocabulary. An equivalence relation, a bijection and a partial order each appear in four of the six courses that follow; they are introduced once.

Induction is third rather than last because it is the proof technique the rest of the path depends on. Counting arguments, recurrence solutions, graph theorems and algorithm correctness are all induction wearing different clothes.

Counting, probability and number theory then apply that machinery to three specific worlds, and graphs give it an object to act on. Algorithms and complexity comes last because it needs all of them: recurrences from Induction and Recursion, counting from Combinatorics and Counting, and graphs from Graphs and Trees.
Courses

Each course assumes the ones before it and nothing else. Induction and Recursion proves things about the sets built in Sets, Relations, and Functions; Discrete Probability counts the outcomes Combinatorics and Counting taught you to count; Algorithms and Complexity analyses the structures Graphs and Trees built.

Make a statement precise enough to be true or false, then establish it. Connectives and truth tables, logical equivalence, quantifiers and the order they come in, valid inference, and direct, contrapositive, contradiction and case proofs written out in full.

Sets, the operations on them and the identities those obey; relations and the two structures they produce — partitions and orderings; functions, injections, surjections and bijections; countable and uncountable; and the counting principle that follows from all of it.

Logic and Proof ended by showing that checking cases is not proving. This is the answer: prove P(k) → P(k+1) once and the claim holds for every n you could ever check and every one you could not. Then the same idea applied to definitions, to data, to algorithms and to recurrences.

How many? The two basic rules, the four ways to choose r from n , what changes when repetition is allowed, how to correct an over-count, and the double-counting arguments that prove identities without algebra.

Counting with a denominator. Every probability here is a ratio of counts, so Combinatorics and Counting does most of the work — and the parts that go wrong, conditioning and independence, go wrong for reasons that have nothing to do with arithmetic.

Everything follows from one theorem about division with remainder. Primes, gcds, congruences and modular inverses build up to RSA — which is generated, used and then broken here on primes small enough to check by hand.

The discrete structure that models everything with a relation on it: networks, dependencies, maps, molecules, schedules. Every theorem in this course is a claim about all graphs, and the lab lets you try to break each one.

The course the rest of the path was building toward. Recurrences from Induction and Recursion, counting from Combinatorics and Counting and graphs from Graphs and Trees all reappear as the running time of something — and the last two lessons say what no algorithm can do.
Recommended background

School algebra, and nothing beyond it. You need to be comfortable rearranging an equation, working with exponents, and reading summation notation — the first course that uses Σ explains it where it first appears.
No calculus. Nothing on this path takes a limit, a derivative or an integral. Where a growth rate is compared to another, it is compared by an explicit constant and threshold rather than by a limit.

No programming. Algorithms and Complexity reads pseudocode and Number Theory and Cryptography walks through algorithms step by step, but nothing asks you to write or run code. The labs execute in your browser so that you can watch an algorithm rather than implement it.

Patience with definitions. The single largest difficulty in this subject is that its words are used precisely: or is inclusive, some means at least one, and a graph is not a plot. Every one of those is stated where it first matters.

Educational course material. Every figure on this path is computed in your browser from the definition the lesson states — the counting is done in exact integer arithmetic and the probabilities as exact fractions, so the numbers are not approximations. What the labs cannot do is prove anything: checking a statement for the cases on screen is evidence about those cases and nothing more, which is the subject of Induction and Recursion.

clauses.expected: Algebra

The language the rest of mathematics is written in: expressions and the rules for rearranging them, equations and what it means to solve one, functions and their graphs, polynomials and factoring, quadratics and the complex numbers they force into existence, exponentials and logarithms, and systems solved several unknowns at a time, and the sums of ordered lists. Nine courses and 112 lessons are available.
Courses
Lessons
Level
Beginner → Advanced
Overview

Foundations comes first because algebra is arithmetic with the numbers withheld, and every later move is one of a small set of properties applied to an expression. A reader who cannot say why -(x - 3) is -x + 3 will make that error in every course that follows, and will not know they made it.

Equations come second, and functions third, in that order rather than the reverse. Solving is a mechanical skill built on the properties; a function is an idea, and it is far easier to meet once you can already manipulate the formula that defines one.

Factoring sits in the middle of the path because it is the bottleneck. Rational expressions, quadratics, and every polynomial graph after Polynomials and Factoring are stated in terms of factors, and none of those techniques applies to a sum. It is placed where there is still time to practise it.

Exponentials and logarithms come seventh because a logarithm is an inverse function, and inverse functions are Lines, Functions and Graphs. Systems and matrices come last because row reduction is elimination performed on exact fractions, and it is unreadable to anyone not already fluent in both.
Courses

Each course assumes the ones before it and nothing else. Polynomials and Factoring factors the expressions Foundations of Algebra taught you to build; Rational and Radical Expressions cannot start until you can factor; Quadratics and Complex Numbers needs both, and Systems and Matrices needs all of them.

Arithmetic, made general. Why a letter can stand for a number, which rearrangements are always allowed and which only look allowed, and the exponent and radical rules that everything after this course leans on.

Find the value that makes a statement true — and know why each move you made kept it true. Linear equations, literal formulas, inequalities, compound and absolute value statements, and the notation for writing a solution set down.

Put algebra on a picture. Slope and every form of a line, then the definition that organises the rest of the path — a function — with its notation, its domain, the transformations that move its graph, and its inverse.

Multiply out, then learn to go back. The factored form is the one that answers questions — where a graph crosses, when a product is zero — and this course is about producing it reliably rather than by inspection.

What happens when a variable lands in a denominator or under a root. Both put values out of bounds, both create solutions that are not solutions, and both need the domain written down before the algebra starts.

One equation shape, four solution methods, and a number system that has to be extended so that every one of them always finishes. Completing the square is the centre of the course: it derives the formula and it puts a parabola in vertex form.

The variable moves into the exponent, and ordinary algebra stops working. A logarithm is the tool that brings it back down — defined as an inverse, with three laws that are the exponent laws read backwards.

Solve for several unknowns together, then find the notation that removes the bookkeeping. A matrix is elimination with the letters deleted, which is why this course does elimination by hand first and only then writes it down as rows.

A sequence is a function whose input is a position. Arithmetic and geometric families make that idea calculable: both have closed forms for a term and a finite sum, some geometric sums have a limit, and the same indexed notation leads to Pascal's triangle and binomial expansion.
Recommended background

Arithmetic, and specifically arithmetic with fractions and negative numbers. If -3 - (-5) and 2/3 ÷ 4/9 are not automatic, do those first — every course here runs on them, and Systems and Matrices runs on them for pages at a time.

No prior algebra. Foundations of Algebra starts from what a variable is. If you have met some of this before, the labs are still worth opening: they show the step list, and a wrong step list survives a lot of correct answers.
No calculus, and none is used. Quadratics and Complex Numbers finds a maximum with the vertex of a parabola rather than a derivative, which is the honest algebraic method and not a workaround.
No programming. Nothing here asks you to write code. The labs run so that you can change a coefficient and watch what moves, which is the one thing a printed page cannot do.

Educational course material. Every figure on this path is computed in your browser from the definition the lesson states, and the arithmetic is exact — coefficients, solutions and steps are carried as fractions, so 1/3 is 1/3 after twenty operations rather than 0.333 . Curves are drawn by evaluating the function, never from a stored shape. Where a quantity is genuinely irrational the lab says where it rounded.

clauses.expected: Sets, Relations, and Functions

Sets, the operations on them and the identities those obey; relations and the two structures they produce — partitions and orderings; functions, injections, surjections and bijections; countable and uncountable; and the counting principle that follows from all of it.
Subject
Discrete Mathematics
Lessons
Format
Interactive
Overview
What you will be able to do
By the end you have the objects every later course manipulates, and the proof habits from Logic and Proof applied to them.
Prove a set identity
By double inclusion or by a chain of laws — and know exactly when a Venn diagram is a case check (three circles, all eight regions) and when it is only a picture.
Classify a relation
Decide reflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry and transitivity by checking the definition, and recognise the equivalence relations and partial orders.
Work with functions precisely
Distinguish injective from surjective, compose functions in the right order, and say exactly when an inverse exists.
Compare sets by pairing

Show ℤ and ℚ are countable and ℝ is not, using the two arguments that settle both — explicit listing and diagonalisation — and turn the finite half of the same idea, no injection from a larger set into a smaller, into a pigeonhole proof by inventing the boxes yourself.
Lessons
14 lessons
First sets, then relations, then functions, and last the counting consequences that Combinatorics and Counting builds on.
Recommended background
Quantifiers and proof technique.
Practice suggestions
Do the set proofs by double inclusion at least once each, even when a chain of laws is shorter. The habit of proving A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A separately is what makes the later structural proofs writable.

Use the relation lab as a counterexample machine. Almost every claim about relations is refuted by a three-element example, and building one yourself is faster than recalling which property implies which. Start from the empty preset and use as few elements as the claim needs — but the elements you leave untouched still count, so reflexivity fails until every one of them has its loop.
Pay attention to “Cardinality and Countability”. Countability is where intuition about size stops working, and every argument after it depends on accepting bijection as the definition of "same size".
What it does not cover

Axiomatic set theory. Sets here are naive: collections of objects. The Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms, the axiom of choice and the cardinal arithmetic beyond countable versus uncountable are a separate subject.
Russell's paradox is mentioned where it explains a restriction, but the resolution — separating sets from classes — is not developed.
Ordinals, transfinite induction, and the continuum hypothesis. “Cardinality and Countability” stops at the two cardinalities the rest of the path uses.

Sets, Relations, and Functions. The set, relation and function labs on this course decide every property by evaluating its definition over the finite object you built, and name the element or pair that decides it. A property that holds on the handful of elements you can see is a property of those elements; the proofs are what extend it.

baseline_audience.scope: The 'Who it is for' paragraphs of the eight authored Trading Course homes, read once from the baseline commit and carried here. The test that uses them runs under a shallow checkout, where the baseline Git object does not exist; it re-derives from Git and compares only when the object happens to be present.

Market Structure Lab starts from a bare candlestick chart

courses.market-structure: Anyone who can open a chart and wants a vocabulary for what is on it. No prior technical analysis is assumed — Market Structure Lab starts from a bare candlestick chart — and no platform, account, or subscription is needed. The lessons stay useful if you already trade and want a stricter definition of invalidation.
courses.trade-setup-execution: Anyone who can already read a chart and now wants a repeatable procedure for acting on one. Market Structure is the assumed background: this course places stops at structural levels and enters on pullbacks without stopping to define either. It also suits someone who trades already and cannot say, from records rather than memory, which of their setups actually pays.
courses.options-trading: Anyone who can read a chart and now wants to understand the instrument that trades on top of it — including the reader who has bought a call, watched the stock go the right way, and still lost money. It starts from contract terms, so no prior options knowledge is assumed. It also suits someone who already trades options and cannot say, without guessing, which part of a premium is intrinsic and which part is the clock.
courses.technical-indicators: Anyone who has an indicator on their chart and could not, right now, write down its formula or say what makes it lag. It assumes you can read a chart and starts from the calculation, so no prior indicator knowledge is needed. It also suits the reader who has six indicators open and suspects — correctly — that four of them are showing the same thing twice.
courses.volume-and-order-flow: Anyone who has said "that breakout had volume" without being able to say volume relative to what. It assumes you can read a chart and know what a moving average does; it assumes nothing about order books, tape reading or delta. It also suits the reader who has a footprint chart open and is quietly unsure whether the green number means buyers were stronger — the course is explicit that every trade has both a buyer and a seller, and that aggressor classification describes which side crossed the spread, not an unequal number of participants.
courses.trading-risk-management: Anyone who can find a setup and cannot say what it is allowed to cost. It assumes you can read a chart, place a stop and tell a call from a put; it assumes nothing about expectancy, drawdown mathematics, margin mechanics or correlation. It also suits the reader who has been sizing positions by round numbers of shares and has quietly noticed that a wide stop and a narrow stop then risk wildly different amounts — the course is explicit that size is an output, computed from the risk you allowed and the distance to invalidation, and never an input you pick first.
courses.backtesting-and-trading-systems: Anyone who has produced a beautiful equity curve and cannot say why it should be believed. It assumes you can read a chart, and that risk per trade, R-multiples, expectancy and drawdown already mean something to you — Trading Risk Management defines them. It assumes nothing about walk-forward analysis, Monte Carlo resampling or point-in-time data. It also suits the reader who has never written a backtest and wants to know what the result of one is worth: the honest answer is that a simulation is evidence about a past sequence, that costs and timing decide most of it, and that a curve fitted to the data it was chosen on is not evidence at all.
courses.algorithmic-and-automated-trading: Anyone who has a rule set they trust and no idea what it takes to let it run unattended. It assumes you can read a chart, and that risk per trade, position sizing, expectancy and out-of-sample validation already mean something to you — Trading Risk Management and Backtesting and Trading Systems define them. It assumes nothing about distributed systems: idempotency, reconciliation, traces, secret rotation and rollback are introduced here, from the trading problem they solve rather than from the general engineering literature. It also suits the reader who has decided NOT to automate, and wants to know what they would be signing up for: most of this course is about failure — a timeout with unknown state, a duplicate order, a stale price, a credential with more permission than it needs — and none of that goes away because the strategy is good.
